", "end_line": 29, "heading_path": ["Blog hero images", "Size and crop"], "ref": "source_239", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/blog-hero.md", "start_line": 24}, {"content": "### Lab figures

Two product figures come from Wickhold's own lab. Both must carry the phrase "in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026", in the same sentence as the figure.

| Figure | Required form |
|---|---|
| CPU overhead | "under 2% CPU overhead on a typical node in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026" |
| Containment speed | "contains a known-bad process in a median of 38 seconds in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026" |

A footnote does not meet this requirement. An asterisk does not meet it. A qualifier on the slide before does not meet it. In a chart, the phrase goes in the chart title or directly under it. In a talk, the speaker says it aloud.

The figures describe a lab, so they may not be presented as field results or customer averages. "Known-bad process" is part of the claim: it does not extend to unknown processes, novel techniques, or "threats" in general. Reports may repeat the figures only if the benchmark year stays attached. When the 2027 benchmarks run, the year changes and this table is reissued. Nobody edits the year by hand.

Approved:

> Wickhold Quenchline adds under 2% CPU overhead on a typical node in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026.

Not approved:

> Quenchline contains attacks in 38 seconds.

> Under 2% overhead. Guaranteed.

Vaskell Health connected Evenburn to its clusters and began by agreeing on a baseline for workloads in audit scope. That meant writing down what the team expected to be true, so that a difference from it would show up as drift and not as a surprise in an audit meeting.

Three things changed.

**Drift replaced the point-in-time snapshot.** Instead of checking settings once a year, the team could see when a workload stopped matching its baseline, along with when it changed and, where the audit log could show it, who changed it.

**Exceptions gained owners and end dates.** Exceptions had been recorded in tickets and in people's memories. Each one now carries a named owner and a date, so the team can show an auditor what was approved and when it ends.

**Fix order set the pre-audit work.** Before the audit window, the team used exposure paths to find which open issues touched in-scope workloads, and it worked those first.

This is where the two audiences differ most. For engineers, show the thing itself. A short command block costs few words and earns more trust than a paragraph:

> **Install in observe mode**

> The agent attaches to each node. Nothing is contained until you change the mode.

For security leaders, give steps in terms of time and ownership:

> **Week one:** Quenchline runs in observe mode on one cluster.
> **Weeks two to four:** Your team reviews what it would have done.
> **After week four:** You decide which namespaces move to contain mode.

No image contains text produced by an image model or baked into artwork by a tool that does not treat it as live type. Three things do not count as generated text:

- Words that are really in the scene: a printed rack label, a whiteboard someone wrote on, a door sign. Check that they say nothing embarrassing and name nobody outside the company.
- Real interface text in a true product screenshot.
- The wordmark, which is a vector file, placed by a person.

The values are also used by the people team, so marketing should not rephrase them. Quote them exactly as they appear here, in this order, with the full stop after each one. They are short sentences, so treat them as sentences.

", "end_line": 121, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "3. Values", "How the values show up in hiring and reviews"], "ref": "source_265", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 118}, {"content": "### `restrictions`: check it before every use

Read `restrictions` before you use an image, every time, including images you have used before. Restrictions are added after an image enters the library, so last quarter's check does not count.

The field is free text, written by whoever had the reason. There is no fixed vocabulary, so read the sentence instead of searching for a keyword. Three kinds of note turn up in practice:

- **Retirement.** The image is deprecated and must not be used. Some retired files look entirely normal in the grid and carry no other sign. Their tags and titles may even look current.
- **A limited context.** The image may be used in the named context and nowhere else. A note limiting an image to internal use keeps it out of anything a customer, a prospect or the press will see, and that includes sales decks.
- **A person or place.** Something about who or what is shown has changed.

A restriction binds even when the image would be perfect, when a senior person asks for it, and when you found it already published somewhere. If you think one is out of date, ask Brand to change the record. Do not use the image and sort it out later.

An empty `restrictions` field means nobody has recorded a limit. It does not mean the image is on brand. The field is one check among several, and the current-identity rule above still has to pass on your own judgment.

If `restrictions` and `tags` seem to disagree, `restrictions` wins. If `restrictions` and `description` disagree, stop and ask.

", "end_line": 97, "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "The image library and its metadata", "restrictions: check it before every use"], "ref": "source_266", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "start_line": 82}, {"content": "## Customer proof

Lowmoor Credit Union runs Quenchline on 220 nodes. Their time to contain fell from 4 hours to 11 minutes. That is the reference story for mid-sized regulated teams. Use the figures together, with the node count.

", "end_line": 168, "heading_path": ["Wickhold Quenchline: product overview", "Customer proof"], "ref": "source_267", "relative_path": "brand/products/quenchline-overview.md", "start_line": 165}, {"content": "### Worked examples

**Two limits for the same channel.** A general voice document gives one length for a channel and that channel's playbook gives another. The playbook wins, because it sits higher in the list. Use its number, and tell Noor so the other one gets fixed.

**A claim in a deck.** A slide says something about the company that the approved claims do not support. The approved claims win, however recent or confident the slide looks, and however often the line has been used in the field. Sales material is not a source for a claim.

**Copy in this document versus Legal.** If a sentence in these guidelines turns out to conflict with the approved claims, Legal wins, and the guidelines get corrected.

**An old-looking rule with no rival.** A meeting note from the Q2 brand review covers something that the relevant playbook doesn't mention. Nothing conflicts, so the note stands.

**A file that says it's the latest.** File names, version numbers and words like FINAL or CURRENT decide nothing. Neither does the date on a file, on its own. Use this list.

**No source answers the question.** Ask the owner listed below. Do not fill the gap from the 2024 material or from what a competitor does. If the question is likely to come up again, the answer gets written down in the right document.

**Sources at the same level disagree.** Two channel playbooks can conflict on a shared element, such as a campaign running on both email and a landing page. Each playbook governs its own channel. If that doesn't settle it, Noor decides and the decision gets recorded.

", "end_line": 483, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "11. Governance", "Worked examples"], "ref": "source_268", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 468}, {"content": "## 11. Tables, charts and captions

- A table needs a header row and at least two rows of content. One row is a sentence.
- Right-align numbers in tables. Keep units in the header, not in each cell.
- A chart title states the finding in sentence case: "41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident". The axis says what was measured.
- Every chart carries its citation in the same bracket form, set small under the chart, so it survives being cropped into a slide.
- Captions are sentences. They end with a full stop and they don't begin "Figure 1 shows".
- No 3D, no donuts, and no chart for a single number. Write the number.

", "end_line": 201, "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "11. Tables, charts and captions"], "ref": "source_269", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "start_line": 193}, {"content": "### The default containment policy

A new install includes the default containment policy, in observe mode. It covers a short list of high-confidence detections: known cryptominer behavior, a shell spawned from a web-serving process, writes to host paths from an unprivileged container, and attempts to reach the cloud metadata endpoint from a pod that has never done so.

In contain mode, the default containment policy isolates or freezes. It never drains a node. It skips the `kube-system` and `wickhold-system` namespaces. We keep it deliberately short, and product treats a false containment in the default policy as a bug with a release note attached.

", "end_line": 84, "heading_path": ["Wickhold Quenchline: product overview", "How it works", "The default containment policy"], "ref": "source_270", "relative_path": "brand/products/quenchline-overview.md", "start_line": 79}, {"content": "### The market problem

The strongest evidence for this position comes from Wickhold's own research. The Wickhold Containment Report 2026, published April 14, 2026, surveyed 412 platform and security leaders. It found that "41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident" and that "the median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours" [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].

The gap those numbers describe is between finding something and doing something about it. Detection has become cheap and common. Containment still depends on a person with enough access waking up, reading the alert, deciding, and acting. Wickhold's position lives in those hours.

", "end_line": 160, "heading_path": ["Email templates", "T6. Nurture, platform track, first email"], "ref": "source_272", "relative_path": "brand/templates/email-templates.md", "start_line": 142}, {"content": "## Not banned, but expect a comment

Reviewers will ask about these. Sometimes the word survives.

- **solution.** Name the product, or say what it does. The word exists to avoid doing either.
- **visibility.** Seeing isn't the job. If the sentence ends at seeing, ask what happens next.
- **real-time.** Fine with a number next to it. Without one it means nothing.
- **AI-powered.** Tells the reader how something was built and nothing about what it does.
- **comprehensive.** Usually untrue, and a reader will go looking for the gap.
- **threat landscape.** A landscape has no one in it. Say which failure you mean.
- **peace of mind.** Nobody on a rota has ever had this.
- **modern.** Compared with what? Say which setup you mean.
- **mission-critical.** To the person on call, everything is.

", "end_line": 84, "heading_path": ["Landing page imagery", "Review"], "ref": "source_274", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/landing-page-imagery.md", "start_line": 80}, {"content": "## 5. Dates and times

- **Dates:** month, day, year, spelled out: April 14, 2026. No ordinals, no "14th of April".
- **Month and year:** March 2022, no comma. **Year only:** 2026.
- **Ranges:** an en dash with no spaces within a month: September 15–16. Use "to" across months: "March 30 to April 2".
- **Tables, logs, front matter:** ISO, 2026-04-14. Never slashes. 04/10 has already caused one wrong webinar invite, and that's enough.
- **Quarters:** fine internally. In public copy, name the month.
- **Avoid relative dates** in anything that stays online. "Recently", "last year", "this spring" and "soon" all rot. Write the date. Press releases and dated posts can say "today".
- **Roadmap language:** no dates, no "coming soon". Product marketing has a separate process for that.

**Times.** Incident timelines use 24-hour UTC with the zone on every line or at the top of the block: 03:14 UTC. It's how our readers' tools show it. Event and webinar times use 12-hour with the zone: 2:00 p.m. MT. In prose, "3am" with no space is fine as a phrase, and the voice document uses it constantly. It's a figure of speech and shouldn't be used for an actual appointment.

Requests I have already answered. They are listed so that I do not answer them again.

| Request | Ruling |
|---|---|

Wickhold Quenchline is runtime detection and containment for Kubernetes. An eBPF agent runs on every node, watches what workloads do at the kernel level, and takes a containment action when a policy says to. It has been in general availability since September 2020 and is the product most of our customers start with.

This overview is written for marketers, solutions engineers and anyone drafting a page, talk or reply about the product. It runs longer than a datasheet on purpose. Platform engineers will test what we say against a real cluster, so the detail below is what the product does today, including the parts that are awkward.

The isometric style and the line graphic from the 2024 identity have been retired, along with the Cobalt gradient behind them.

", "end_line": 29, "heading_path": ["Email playbook", "What we send"], "ref": "source_284", "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md", "start_line": 16}, {"content": "### The promise at each level

|---|---|
| Company | Small fires stay small. |

", "end_line": 218, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "4. Positioning", "The promise at each level"], "ref": "source_285", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 210}, {"content": "## 3. Banned claims

| Do not say | Say instead, or do this | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| "prevents prompt injection" | "limits what a compromised agent can do" | Leashgate acts on tool calls. It does not read intent and it cannot promise that an agent will not be manipulated. The claim is false as a matter of product design |
| "FedRAMP Authorized", "FedRAMP certified" | See section 4 | Neither is true |
| "GDPR compliant" | Use the regional rules | Regional wording sits there, and the ban is not limited to that region |
| "breach-proof", "unhackable", "impossible to escape" | Describe the containment action | No security product can support an absolute |
| "zero false positives", "100% detection", "catches everything" | Give a sourced figure or say nothing | We hold no such evidence |
| "guarantee", "guaranteed", "warranty" outside a contract | Remove | These words have legal effect. Service credits live in the order form |
| "the leading", "the fastest", "No. 1", "the only" | Remove, or bring me the comparison data | Superlatives need current comparative substantiation, and we do not hold any |
| "certified by", "endorsed by", "partner of" for any standards body or open-source project | Remove | Using eBPF or Helm is not an endorsement from anyone |
| "saves $X", any return-on-investment figure | Remove | We have no approved financial outcome for any customer |

Two refinements, because they keep coming back:

"Helps prevent" is a banned claim dressed up. A qualifier in front of a promise does not make it a limited promise.

"Compliance-ready" and "audit-ready" were requested in June for a trust page and refused. Wickhold can describe what the product records. Whether a customer passes an audit depends on the customer and the auditor.

", "end_line": 98, "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "3. Banned claims"], "ref": "source_286", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md", "start_line": 79}, {"content": "## 8. Technical writing in marketing copy

Kofi Anselm's team reviews anything containing code, and their rules are short.

- **Code formatting** for commands, flags, file names, field names, namespaces, node names and anything a person might type: `kubectl get pods`, `--namespace`, `values.yaml`.
- **Every snippet is run before it's published.** Say which version it was run against. A snippet nobody ran does not go out, even in a slide.
- **Placeholder values** look like placeholders or like real workloads: `payments`, `checkout`, `worker-7`. Don't use `foo`, and don't use the name of a real company, a real customer or a celebrity.
- **Domains and email addresses in examples** use `wickhold.example`.
- **Long output** gets trimmed, with a line saying so. Don't silently edit output.
- **Failure modes** are part of the example. If a command fails in a common way, say how it looks.

Wickhold is a single brand. Products, reports and events all sit under it, and none of them has a logo of its own.

", "end_line": 222, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "5. Brand architecture"], "ref": "source_290", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 219}, {"content": "### Fear is not a sales tool

No threat-actor drama. No ticking clocks.

The rule is simple to state and gets broken constantly, because fear copy is the easiest copy in security to write. It covers attackers portrayed as characters with motives and nicknames, anything of the "while you read this" kind, countdowns, "it's only a matter of time", "every second counts", and any sentence that asks the reader to imagine the phone call to the board. Our readers carry a pager. They do not need help imagining it.

Give the same fact without the dread.

Bad: "Attackers are already inside your cluster, and the clock is ticking."

Good: "41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]."

The second sentence is more uncomfortable than the first, and it did not raise its voice. Trust the number to do that work.

Breach references have their own rules in the claims document. Read them before you mention one.

", "end_line": 56, "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "What Wickhold believes", "Fear is not a sales tool"], "ref": "source_291", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "start_line": 41}, {"content": "# Landing pages

**Noor Eskelund and the web team, April 2026.** Written the week the Containment Report page went live, while the mistakes were fresh. Revised May 2026.

This covers campaign pages, product pages, persona pages and report pages on wickhold.example. The docs site and the blog have their own conventions.

", "end_line": 6, "heading_path": ["Landing pages"], "ref": "source_292", "relative_path": "brand/channels/landing-page-playbook.md", "start_line": 1}, {"content": "## The problem it works on

A runtime incident usually starts small: one pod running a shell it has never run, one process opening a connection nothing else in the namespace opens. The damage comes from the hours between the first signal and someone doing something about it. The 2026 survey gives us the size of that gap:

- 41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]
- the median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]

The survey covered 412 platform and security leaders and was published on April 14, 2026.

Quenchline shortens that gap by moving the first response onto the node. The agent does not wait for a person to read an alert. If the policy allows it, the agent acts on the node and the on-call engineer wakes up to a contained pod and a timeline.

", "end_line": 17, "heading_path": ["Wickhold Quenchline: product overview", "The problem it works on"], "ref": "source_293", "relative_path": "brand/products/quenchline-overview.md", "start_line": 7}, {"content": "## What goes in the frame

**Observe first.** The eBPF agent starts in observe mode and logs what it would have done. Most teams spend two to four weeks here, reading decision records.

**Write the policy.** Start from the default containment policy and decide which detection leads to which containment action. Policies go through your repo like any other change. Every exemption has an expiry date.

**Turn on contain mode where you are ready.** Mode is set per policy. Going back is one line.

A typical landing section might read:

- Page headline, Bricolage Grotesque Bold: "Small fires stay small."
- Subhead, Plex Sans SemiBold: "Wickhold Quenchline contains runtime failures on your Kubernetes nodes, within limits your team sets."
- Body, Plex Sans Regular: one short paragraph.
- Inline literal, Plex Mono: `kubectl get containmentpolicy`.

Four levels is plenty. If a layout seems to need a fifth, the content usually needs editing.

", "end_line": 380, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "8. Typography", "A worked hierarchy"], "ref": "source_1", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 370}, {"content": "# LinkedIn images

Social lead's notes, updated August 2026.

", "end_line": 4, "heading_path": ["LinkedIn images"], "ref": "source_2", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/linkedin-image.md", "start_line": 1}, {"content": "### Claims made in a hurry

Launches and field events are when unapproved language tends to appear, usually from someone trying to help. If you see a claim in circulation that isn't on the approved list, tell Priit the same day, including where you saw it. There is no blame in reporting one. The aim is to get it corrected before it's copied into something else.

", "end_line": 532, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "11. Governance", "Claims made in a hurry"], "ref": "source_3", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 529}, {"content": "## 9. People and companies

- Full name and title on first mention, in this order: Hana Brandvold, CISO, Lowmoor Credit Union.
- After that, surname for external people, in the press-release style: Brandvold said. First name for our founders only where they signed the piece.
- Job titles are capitalized in a byline or attribution line and lowercase in a sentence: "the company's head of developer relations".
- Companies are singular. "Wickhold is", "Ostler Grocers has".
- Use "they" for an unnamed person. "On-call lead", not "on-call guy". "Staffed", not "manned".
- Teams are lowercase: the platform team, the brand team.

", "end_line": 186, "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "9. People and companies"], "ref": "source_4", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "start_line": 178}, {"content": "### Product behavior

Wickhold Quenchline takes a containment action only in contain mode. In observe mode it records what it would have done. Copy describing automatic containment must therefore be true of contain mode and should say so where a reader could assume otherwise. Containment actions are isolating a pod's network, freezing a process and draining a node. Do not add to the list without product confirmation.

Wickhold Evenburn reports drift, exposure paths and a fix order. It does not change a customer's environment by itself, and copy should not imply that it does.

Some topics drag writers back toward the register the rebrand left behind. These are the ones reviewers see most.

**AI agents.** Wickhold Leashgate, in early access, attracts the worst habits in the building, because the whole market is shouting about agents. Treat an agent as a workload with credentials and questionable judgment. Talk about tool calls, agent identity and the blast radius of an agent. Leave the future of work to other people. **Compliance.** Dull on purpose. Certification status is a fact with one correct wording, and legal owns that wording. Copy the approved sentence and do not improve it. A nicer phrasing here is how a company ends up saying something untrue.

**Money.** Prices are stated flatly, with no "just", "only" or "starting from". Core is $18 per node per month. The reader can decide how they feel about that.

**Company news.** Funding, awards, headcount. Nobody is thrilled, excited or proud. The Series B was $46M in June 2024; that is a date and a number, and the sentence after it should say what changed for customers. If nothing changed for customers, ask whether the post needs to exist.

The work took place in four steps, with one security engineer leading and a platform engineer part-time.

First, the team installed the cluster collector and granted read-only roles in its cloud accounts. Nothing on the nodes changed, which made it an easy request for the platform team.

Second, it connected Git and Helm history so that drift had a declared source. As expected, a burst of drift appeared at first, because every undocumented hotfix since the clusters were built showed up at once. Third, it tagged the systems in audit scope and agreed on the baseline with the compliance team. This step took the longest.

Fourth, the team generated evidence reports mapped to HIPAA and SOC 2 controls and reviewed them against the previous year's spreadsheets. Three values.

- `transparent`: no ground at all. The image takes on whatever is behind it, which is why `safe_on` matters so much for these files.
- `solid`: a flat ground is part of the file, such as a logo on its panel or a hero illustration on Tallow.

The voice stays the same. How much of it you get changes with the room.

**Landing pages.** The flattest we get. Mechanical, confident, short. The reader is deciding whether to spend ten more minutes, so tell them what the thing does on a cluster and let them go. "Wickhold Quenchline isolates the pod, freezes the process or drains the node, then writes down what it did."

**Blog.** The most room to think. Brand-voice posts walk through how something fails. Dov's posts can argue, and they should. A good post leaves the reader able to do one thing they could not do before, even if they never buy. Avoid the summary paragraph at the end. If the post worked, the reader was there.

**LinkedIn.** The company page is brand voice. Founder posts are where the personality lives. A post runs about 200 words, which suits one story and one point. Write as a person with a job, not a thought leader: no line breaks after every sentence, no "here's what I learned", no lists of lessons from an outage.

**X.** One fact, or one observation, in a dry tone. The account does not chase the news and does not reply to arguments about vendors. It's fine for a post to be plain. "The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. That is most of a night shift."

**Email.** One person writing to one person who is busy. Say why you are writing in the first sentence. Assume it is being read on a phone in a hallway. No "I hope this finds you well", and since these are brand emails, no "I" at all unless Maren signed it. Customer notices are the exception to everything else in this list and sound like the incident channel at the top of this document.

**Product UI and error text.** The closest thing we have to pure voice. What happened, what state things are in, what to do. "Containment action failed on node `ip-10-2-14-7`: agent unreachable. The pod is still running. Retry or drain the node." Chirpy empty states were tried in 2025 and came out after a customer saw one during a real incident.

**Case studies.** Third person, numbers up front, the customer's team as the subject of most sentences. Enough detail about their environment that a peer recognizes it. A case study that could describe any customer describes none of them.

", "end_line": 122, "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "Tone by channel"], "ref": "source_29", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "start_line": 105}, {"content": "## Start at 3am

Anyone who writes for Wickhold should read an incident channel before writing a line of copy. Kofi Anselm's team keeps a few scrubbed transcripts for new hires. Skip the panic at the top of the thread and find the messages from whoever is running the incident. They tend to look like this:

> 03:14 UTC. A pod in `checkout` started a shell it has no reason to start.
> 03:14 UTC. Wickhold Quenchline froze the process and isolated the pod's network.
> 03:22 UTC. Rest of the namespace is quiet. Still unknown how the shell got there.
> Reading the image history now. Next update 03:45.

That is the voice. It says what happened, what is contained and what is next, in that order, and it stops. It has timestamps where other writers have adjectives. It admits the thing it does not know in the same flat tone as the thing it does. The person writing it is tired and is not going to make their tiredness your problem. Forty people are reading, half of them frightened, and the frightened ones calm down because of how the message is written.

Maren Tolliver and Dov Achterberg were on-call infrastructure leads before they founded this company in Denver in 2019. The voice is theirs by inheritance. The 2026 brand made it official: a wick is the one place a fire is allowed to exist. Production will catch fire in small ways, on ordinary nights, for dull reasons. The mission is to keep small failures from becoming big ones, and the copy should sound like it was written by people who consider that a normal day's work.

Bricolage Grotesque is a display face. Below about 20 px its quirks turn into noise, so it should not be used for body text, buttons or table cells. Limit a page to the two headline weights in the table.

Plex Sans carries nearly everything else. Keep line lengths between 60 and 80 characters. On long pages a wider column is the first thing to go wrong.

Plex Mono has a job beyond code. Commands, flags, file names, YAML keys and other literal strings are set in mono inside body text, so a reader can see what to type. Node counts and timings in a table can also use it, because the digits line up. Do not use it for decoration or to make something feel technical. Engineers notice.

Email is the known exception. Mail clients ignore most web fonts, so the email stack falls back to a system sans-serif, and headlines in an email rely on weight and spacing to do the work.

Italic is for titles of reports and for the occasional stress. All caps are limited to small labels in a layout, and never to whole sentences.

", "end_line": 363, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "8. Typography", "Using them well"], "ref": "source_57", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 352}, {"content": "## 3. Post types

**How-to posts.** A task, steps, and what it looks like when it goes wrong: rolling out contain mode, reading an exposure path, writing a first tool-call policy for Leashgate in early access.

**Founder posts.** Maren, on company decisions and what she learned from them. They're rare and marketing does not ghostwrite them. An editor can tidy.

", "end_line": 48, "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "3. Post types"], "ref": "source_58", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md", "start_line": 37}, {"content": "### Observe mode and contain mode

Every Quenchline policy runs in one of two modes.

**Observe mode** detects and records. For each detection, it writes what it would have done as a decision record, and nothing on the node changes. **Contain mode** carries out the action.

Teams usually spend two to four weeks in observe mode, reading decision records and adding exemptions for the strange things their own tooling does. Backup agents and debug sidecars are the usual suspects. Mode is set per policy, so a team can run contain mode on an internet-facing namespace while the database namespace stays in observe mode.

```bash
kubectl get containmentdecisions -n payments \
  --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp
```

", "end_line": 66, "heading_path": ["Wickhold Quenchline: product overview", "How it works", "Observe mode and contain mode"], "ref": "source_59", "relative_path": "brand/products/quenchline-overview.md", "start_line": 54}, {"content": "## How the sentences go

**Short first.** Most sentences run under twenty words. The long ones earn it by carrying a real sequence of events.

**Verbs do the work.** Name who did what. "Quenchline froze the process" over "the process was frozen". Past tense for incidents, present tense for what the product does.

**End early.** Our most common edit is deleting the last line of a paragraph. Writers tend to add one that restates the point in a nicer rhythm. Readers don't need it. This goes double for the final line of a piece.

**Ration the fire.** The tagline is "Small fires stay small." It carries the metaphor so the copy doesn't have to. A piece gets at most one fire image, and many pieces should have none. Nothing ignites, sparks, blazes or fans the flames. Slow Burn Summit gets to keep its name.

**Plain words for plain things.** "Use", "start", "stop", "run". Reach for the fancier word and the reader assumes something is being hidden.

**Don't argue with the reader's experience.** Telling a platform engineer that alerts are overwhelming is telling them what they had for breakfast. Start from what they know and add something.

Humor depends on the audience, see each persona.

The personas hold the working rules for each reader, including what goes first. What follows is only the register, meaning how the voice sounds once you have chosen your content.

**CISOs.** Level and measured. Assume the reader will forward your paragraph to an audit committee without editing it, and write something they can forward. Risk, time and board language are their native terms: exposure, time to contain, residual risk, ownership. Short sentences, complete ones, no shorthand. Every sentence should survive being read aloud in a room that includes a lawyer.

**Platform engineers.** A good pull-request comment from a colleague you respect. Exact, brief, assumes competence, and shows its working. If there is a YAML snippet that makes the point, the prose can get out of its way. Marketing English reads as noise here and the page will be closed.

**DevSecOps.** These readers sit between the review queue and the pipeline, and they spend their days being the person who says no. Write to someone who is outnumbered: practical, on their side, and specific about what lands in their queue and what stays out of it.

**Compliance leads.** Careful nouns. This reader will notice the difference between "supports" and "meets", and will quote you. Their persona is still being written, so if the piece is aimed mainly at them, ask Noor before guessing.

**Customers mid-incident.** Pure 3am voice. Nothing about the product, nothing about the relationship, no reassurance that isn't backed by a fact. What we see, what we've done, when the next update comes.

**Finance and procurement.** They read a small part of what we write and they read it closely. Plain sentences, the price in the standard form, the terms where they expect them. Anything that sounds like enthusiasm reads to them as a negotiating position.

**Journalists.** Assume no interest in the product and real interest in what is happening to teams. Offer the finding, the method and a person to talk to. Don't send them a story with a hook in it; they have their own.

**Candidates and the community.** Warmer, plainer, and allowed to mention that the work is interesting. The same no-drama rules hold. Nobody here is a rockstar.

These are opinions and we expect some readers to disagree with them. Copy that could have come from any vendor in the category has failed, even if it breaks no rule.

", "end_line": 40, "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "What Wickhold believes"], "ref": "source_64", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "start_line": 37}, {"content": "## 6. Breach and incident references

This section sets how Wickhold may talk about breaches and other public incidents, in any channel.

1. Never name a victim. That covers company names, product names, and descriptions that identify one ("a large regional retailer in the week it made the news").
2. No humor. Not in the copy, not in the image, not in a speaker's aside.
3. Nothing within 30 days of a public incident. Count from the first public disclosure. For the 30 days, Wickhold does not publish, post, send or sponsor anything that refers to the incident or that is plainly timed to it. An incident is not a marketing hook.

After 30 days, a breach may be discussed in general terms only, as a pattern and without identifying anyone. A technical analysis of a technique is fine if it does not rely on the incident for attention.

The rules cover paid media, social, email, blog posts, sales sequences, talks and replies to journalists. They apply to personal LinkedIn accounts when the post mentions Wickhold or its products. Press inquiries about a live incident go to Ilse Varga-Holm, and nobody comments before she has spoken to me.

If a campaign in market could be read as a reaction to a new public incident, whoever notices it pauses it and tells Ilse. Nobody will be criticized for pausing. Sales may answer a direct customer question about an incident with facts about the customer's own deployment. It may not use the question as an opening.

Incidents at Wickhold customers are never discussed without the customer's written approval, whatever their age. The approved Lowmoor material is the model. It has a figure and no drama.

Not approved:

> After last week's breach at a regional bank, can your team afford another six hours?

Approved, more than 30 days after any related event:

> When a pod misbehaves, Wickhold Quenchline in contain mode can isolate its network while the on-call engineer works out what happened.

", "end_line": 150, "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "6. Breach and incident references"], "ref": "source_65", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md", "start_line": 127}, {"content": "## 2. Mission

**Keep small failures from becoming big ones.**

The mission is written for the people who run production. A failed deployment, a process that should not be running, a credential in the wrong place: these happen every week in any serious cluster, and they stay dull when somebody contains them early. The company exists to keep them dull.

Three things follow from that wording, and they are the reasons it was chosen.

It accepts that failures happen. A company that claims failures will not happen has stopped talking to engineers. Founders Maren and Dov spent years as on-call infrastructure leads before starting Wickhold in Denver in March 2019, and neither of them has ever met a system that did not fail.

It measures success by size. A contained incident still gets logged, reviewed and fixed. The win is that it stayed at one pod and did not reach the node, or stayed at one node and did not reach the cluster.

It says "keep", which is ongoing work. Containment is something a team does with good tools, every week. The mission gives the product a role in that work and leaves the credit for the outcome with the customer's on-call team.

Use the mission on recruiting pages, in all-hands decks and in the opening of long-form pieces about the company. It is an internal compass first. It should not be pasted on product pages as a slogan, because the tagline already does that job.

A few sentences show the difference between using the mission and hanging it on the wall.

Good, from a recruiting page: "We build software that keeps small failures from becoming big ones. If you have been paged at 3am, you already know why that matters."

Weak: "Our mission is to revolutionize the way the world thinks about failure." It's bigger than the company, and it says nothing an on-call engineer would recognize.

", "end_line": 82, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "2. Mission"], "ref": "source_66", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 61}, {"content": "## Off the list

- **"Platform".** On the first draft in January, then removed. Half our readers are platform engineers.

", "end_line": 139, "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "Three picks, worked through"], "ref": "source_69", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "start_line": 132}, {"content": "## 10. Accessibility summary

Accessible work is part of the brand standard, and it is checked at review alongside everything else. The reasoning is simple enough: engineers read documentation on bad monitors, on phones and at 3am, and some of them have low vision or are color-blind. Work that only functions in perfect conditions fails the people it is meant for.

In summary, four commitments apply across all marketing work:

- Text is readable against its background. The palette has been measured, and not every pairing is suitable for small text. Ember in particular needs care.
- Images carry a text description, so nobody loses the point of a piece because an image did not load or cannot be seen.
- Meaning is never carried by color alone. A chart or status needs a label, a shape or a pattern too.
- Pages work with a keyboard and at high zoom, and video has captions.

The misses that come up most at review are predictable. A chart legend that relies on Ember versus Verdigris alone is hard to read for some color-blind readers, since those two are close in lightness. An Ember link in a paragraph looks fine on a designer's monitor and is hard to read on a laptop in daylight. Text set into an image can't be read by a screen reader and can't be translated. Video exported from a webinar tool often ships with captions switched off.

Accessibility review belongs to whoever does the brand check on a piece, and it isn't a separate stage. If a template fails, Noor's team fixes the template, so the same miss doesn't come back in every piece made from it.

The specific requirements are in the visual accessibility guidance, and the measured color pairs are in the logo and color addendum. Bricolage Grotesque's limit on small sizes, in section 8, is as much an accessibility point as a matter of taste.

Good: "Wickhold Quenchline can isolate a pod's network the moment a known-bad process starts. Your team sets which actions run on their own."

Good: "Small fires stay small."

Bad: "Total protection for everything you run." This promises what no product can deliver, and it could be anyone's line.

We will have our own bad days: a bad agent release, a late fix, a false containment that drained a node it should have left alone. The values cover this before anything else does. Say what happened. Contain first. Admit limits. Leave it better for the next on-call.

In practice:

- Lead with what happened to the customer's systems, in their terms.
- Use "we" and an active verb. "We shipped a policy update that drained nodes it should not have." "An issue occurred" is not a sentence we publish.
- Apologize once, plainly, in one short sentence. Then get on with the facts.
- Say what is still unknown.

", "end_line": 394, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "9. Photography and illustration direction", "Photography"], "ref": "source_104", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 389}, {"content": "## How to describe it

> Wickhold Quenchline contains runtime incidents on Kubernetes from inside the node.

For a platform engineer, go straight to the mechanism:

> One DaemonSet, eBPF, kernel 5.8 with BTF. It starts in observe mode. Nothing on your nodes changes until you switch a policy to contain mode, and that switch goes through your repo like any other change.

For a CISO, lead with the decision:

> Decide whether a containment action can run before a person is awake. Quenchline lets you make that call per namespace, and every action is recorded.

Examples that do not work:

| Bad example | What is wrong with it |
|---|---|
| "Quenchline makes runtime attacks impossible." | It contains. It makes no such promise, and an engineer will stop reading here |
| "Attackers are already inside your cluster. Every second counts." | Fear is the entire pitch, and the figure is missing |
| "A powerful, intelligent, lightweight platform for modern runtime defense." | Adjectives with nothing behind them. Replace them with the overhead figure and its source |

", "end_line": 15, "heading_path": ["Email playbook", "The short version"], "ref": "source_107", "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md", "start_line": 5}, {"content": "## Banned terms

There are thirteen. They stay out of headlines, body copy, decks, alt text and speaker notes that leave the building. When one shows up in a draft it usually marks the spot where the writer ran out of facts, so deleting it rarely fixes the sentence. Find the fact.

| Term | Why it is out | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| seamless | Putting an eBPF agent on every node has seams: a kernel check, a Helm upgrade, a stretch in observe mode. Platform engineers know this and stop reading when told otherwise. | Say what the rollout takes. |
| robust | Strong against what? The word claims a result and skips the test. | Name the failure the thing survived. |
| leverage | A finance word doing a job that "use" does for free. | Use "use". |
| best-in-class | No class, no judge, no source. It cannot pass "say the number, then stop". | Give the figure and where it came from. |
| next-gen | Every product in this market has been next-gen at some point. The word ages the day it ships. | Say what it does on a node today. |
| single pane of glass | Our readers have been sold this pane many times and own several. It also describes watching, and the job here is containing. | Name the screen and what it shows. |
| holistic | Usually covering for a gap. If something spans cloud and cluster, those two words are shorter and checkable. | List what is covered. |
| unlock | Implies the customer's own work was locked up and we hold the key. Drags padlocks into the room as well. | Say what the reader can now do. |
| empower | The readers already have root. Nobody here hands out power. | Say what changed for them, in a verb they would use. |
| cutting-edge | A claim about us, and an undated one. eBPF is well past being new, and that is one reason it is safe to run in production. | Name the technique. |
| game-changing | An incident is nobody's game, and the claim has no number attached. | Give the before and after. |
| prevent all | A promise no security product can keep. Includes "prevents all", which is the same promise with better grammar. | See the verbs below. |
| stop all | Same promise, same problem. A CISO who reads this line once will discount the rest of the page. | See the verbs below. |

The prose test: if a sentence still reads as true after you swap the product for a toaster, it needed a fact and got an adjective.

", "end_line": 26, "heading_path": ["Word list", "Banned terms"], "ref": "source_108", "relative_path": "brand/voice/word-list.md", "start_line": 5}, {"content": "## 3. Values

There are four, and they are written the way an on-call lead would say them.

**Say what happened.**
Report the event in plain order: what occurred, what was affected, what was done, what is next. This applies to incident reports, release notes, customer emails and the company's own mistakes. When a release goes badly, the customer note says so in the first sentence.

Good: "The last Wickhold Quenchline release raised CPU use on nodes running older kernels. A fix shipped on Tuesday. Here is how to check whether you were affected."

Bad: "We're always working to improve performance, and our latest update includes important enhancements."

**Contain first.**
In an incident, limit the damage before explaining it. In marketing, the same ordering applies: the first thing a reader gets is the thing that helps them, and the story of how it came about can wait. The value also sets the company's posture. Wickhold talks about containing, limiting and slowing. A promise of a world with no incidents is a promise no honest vendor can keep.

Good: "At Lowmoor Credit Union, time to contain fell from 4 hours to 11 minutes across 220 nodes."

That example gives the result with no adjectives around it and leaves the reader to decide what it means.

**Admit limits.**
Every product has edges, and engineers find them within a week. Naming a limit in advance costs less than having a customer discover it during a bad night, and it makes everything else the company says easier to believe.

Good: "Wickhold Quenchline works at runtime. It does not review code before it ships."

**Leave it better for the next on-call.**
This one comes straight from the founders. When an on-call shift ends, the next person should find the runbook updated, the noisy alert tuned and the handoff note written. Inside marketing it means naming source files sensibly, recording why a decision was made, and putting a correction in the document that was wrong and not only in a thread. It is why the "tried and dropped" list in section 1 exists.

", "end_line": 108, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "3. Values"], "ref": "source_109", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 83}, {"content": "## Preferred terms

**Workload, not asset.** Customers run workloads, and that is the word they use in their own runbooks. "Asset" comes from inventory spreadsheets and suggests a thing that sits still. A workload moves, restarts and misbehaves, which is why it needs a runtime product. Inside the marketing team "asset" still means a blog post or an image file; that use never reaches a customer.

**Contain, limit and slow, rather than prevent.** This is the company's argument in three verbs. Something will go wrong on a Tuesday night regardless of what anyone buys. Wickhold Quenchline contains what is already running. Wickhold Evenburn limits exposure. Wickhold Leashgate limits what an agent can reach. "Slow" is the honest verb when the action buys time and does not end the problem. Also keep "eliminate" and "eradicate" out of it; they are "prevent" in a bigger coat.

Use "contain" only when a containment action actually happens. Detection on its own is detection.

One exception came out of a release-notes review. A line saying a patch prevents a crash in the agent is describing our own bug, so it can stay. The rule covers promises about what happens to customers, and a changelog entry makes none.

**Customers, not clients.** Clients have an account manager and a lunch. Customers run our agent in production and page us. A "client" in the software sense stays: `kubectl` is a client, an email client is a client. "Users" is fine when you mean the people logged in to the console, because a customer is the whole company.

", "end_line": 38, "heading_path": ["Word list", "Preferred terms"], "ref": "source_110", "relative_path": "brand/voice/word-list.md", "start_line": 27}, {"content": "### Order of authority

When two sources conflict, the higher one on this list wins:

1. **Legal-approved claims.** The approved claims, certification status, regional rules and customer quote policy owned by Priit Salonen, General Counsel.
2. **These 2026 guidelines**, together with the logo and color addendum, which has the same standing.
3. **Channel playbooks.** The working guides for each channel.
4. **Everything else.** This includes the voice and style documents, messaging, personas, product overviews, templates, sales material, meeting notes and Slack.

So the order is: legal-approved claims, then the 2026 guidelines, then channel playbooks, then everything else.

A lower source is not void. It applies wherever nothing above it speaks to the question. A template's rule, or a decision recorded in meeting notes or Slack by the person who owns the topic, is followed like any other rule until a higher source contradicts it. The order settles conflicts and does not rank importance. If a document at the bottom of the list has the only rule on a subject, that is the rule.

", "end_line": 467, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "11. Governance", "Order of authority"], "ref": "source_111", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 455}, {"content": "## Founder voice and brand voice

There are two voices at Wickhold, and they have one hard line between them.

**Founder voice is first person singular, and it is signed.** Maren writes as "I". Her posts carry her name. She gets to have feelings and doubts, tell a story from a bad night in 2017, and be wrong in public. Dov's technical posts work the same way and are signed "Dov".

**Brand voice never says "I" or "we think".** Website, product pages, company LinkedIn, the company X account, email, decks, reports: no first person singular, ever. "We believe", "we feel" and "in our view" are "we think" in different shoes, and they go too.

**Brand voice uses "Wickhold" or "we" for facts only.** Things that happened, things that are true of the company, things a lawyer could check.

| Fine in brand voice | Not in brand voice |
|---|---|
| We renewed SOC 2 Type II in January 2026. | We think SOC 2 matters. |
| Wickhold serves more than 140 customers. | I've talked to a lot of platform teams. |
| Containment is where incidents are won or lost. | We believe containment is where incidents are won or lost. |

The third row is the useful one. Brand voice still holds opinions. It states them as flat sentences, the way the on-call lead does, and lets the reader disagree. "We think" adds nothing except a hedge.

Practicalities. Nobody else writes as "I" in Wickhold content. Kofi's developer posts and anything from the wider team run in brand voice under a byline, because a byline is credit and a founder post is a person speaking for themselves. Customer quotes are quotes and say whatever was approved. If the content team drafts for Maren, she reads it and changes it before her name goes on, and a post that she has not read does not go out. In the spring a joint Maren-and-Dov byline was tried on one post; "I" became unreadable after two paragraphs, so that was dropped. One author per post.

", "end_line": 104, "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "Founder voice and brand voice"], "ref": "source_112", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "start_line": 85}, {"content": "### Writing your own policy

Policies are a namespaced custom resource, so they go through the same review as everything else in the repo.

```yaml
apiVersion: quenchline.wickhold.example/v1
kind: ContainmentPolicy
metadata:
  name: ledger-api
  namespace: payments
spec:
  mode: contain
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: ledger-api
  rules:
    - detection: shell-in-container
      action: freezeProcess
      holdProbes: true
    - detection: egress-to-new-destination
      action: isolateNetwork
      keepDNS: true
  exemptions:
    - image: registry.wickhold.example/ops/debug-toolbox
      until: "2026-12-01"
```

`until` is required on every exemption. Permanent exemptions were a recurring finding in customer reviews, so the field became mandatory in Quenchline 4.0.

", "end_line": 42, "heading_path": ["Blog hero images", "Choosing by post type"], "ref": "source_115", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/blog-hero.md", "start_line": 30}, {"content": "## Security and compliance of the service

Wickhold holds SOC 2 Type II, renewed in January 2026. Wickhold is pursuing FedRAMP Moderate authorization. Wickhold supports customers' GDPR obligations. ", "end_line": 172, "heading_path": ["Wickhold Quenchline: product overview", "Security and compliance of the service"], "ref": "source_116", "relative_path": "brand/products/quenchline-overview.md", "start_line": 169}, {"content": "## 4. Shape of a post

A title that says what the reader will get. Then the intro. Then three to five sections with descriptive headings. Then an ending that tells the reader what to do on Monday.

Titles we liked:

- Contain mode, one namespace at a time
- What drift looks like after a Helm upgrade
- The six hours after detection
- Writing your first tool-call policy for Wickhold Leashgate, in early access

Titles we rewrote:

- "5 Kubernetes Security Mistakes You're Making Right Now" became "Five findings we see in most new clusters"
- "Everything You Need To Know About eBPF" became "What our eBPF agent can and can't see"

Section headings should still make sense if they're all someone reads. "Background" and "The solution" tell the reader nothing.

End on the practical next step, then one call to action to the most relevant page. Don't summarize what you just said. If the post was good, they remember. Don't add a paragraph about Wickhold at the bottom either, as the footer handles that.

", "end_line": 68, "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "4. Shape of a post"], "ref": "source_117", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md", "start_line": 49}, {"content": "## Changes

", "end_line": 270, "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "Changes"], "ref": "source_118", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "start_line": 263}, {"content": "## 2. First lines

**No rhetorical question as the first line of any asset.** Blog post, landing page hero, email (subject line and first sentence both), LinkedIn post, X post, video script, slide one of a deck.

"Is your cluster ready for the next incident?" tells the reader nothing and asks them to do the writer's work. It's also the most common opening in our category, so it reads as noise. Open on a fact, an event or a claim.

| Don't open with | Open with |
|---|---|
| What would you do if a pod started a shell at 3am? | A pod in `checkout` started a shell at 03:14 UTC. |
| Tired of alert fatigue? | Most alerts at 3am are about something that already stopped mattering. |

Real questions later in a piece are fine. An FAQ section is full of them and that's what it is for, as long as the page opens on a statement.

", "end_line": 48, "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "2. First lines"], "ref": "source_119", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "start_line": 36}, {"content": "### Testing a campaign idea

Before a concept goes to design, Ilse's team asks four questions of it.

1. Could any other security vendor run this with their logo on it? If so, it isn't the position.
2. Does it depend on the reader being scared? If so, drop it.
3. Does it show containment, or only talk about it?
4. Would the customer's on-call lead forward it to a colleague without a sarcastic comment?

The "Quiet night" concept from the 2026 launch passed all four, and it became the opening of the launch film: a dark office, one screen, a log line reading that a pod had been isolated, and an engineer who doesn't appear because she is asleep at home.

", "end_line": 172, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "4. Positioning", "Testing a campaign idea"], "ref": "source_120", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 162}, {"content": "## Advice for other healthcare security teams

Okereke-Voss's team offers three pieces of advice.

Agree on the baseline before you connect anything. The technical setup was the short part of the project, and the conversation about what "correct" meant took longer.

Bring the auditors in early. Show them what the evidence will look like before the audit window opens, so that nobody is surprised by the format.

Keep the exceptions honest. An exception with no end date tends to become permanent. Reviewing them each month took little time and made the audit conversation much shorter.

", "end_line": 70, "heading_path": ["Three weeks back: how Vaskell Health shortened audit preparation", "Advice for other healthcare security teams"], "ref": "source_121", "relative_path": "brand/case-studies/vaskell-health.md", "start_line": 61}, {"content": "## What Evenburn didn't do

Evenburn gives a security team current evidence on configuration and drift. It doesn't replace an auditor, a compliance program or the policies behind it, and it doesn't make any workload compliant by itself. Vaskell Health's team still decides what the baseline should be and still owns every fix. Evidence for controls outside Kubernetes and cloud configuration stays with the tools that already handled it.

", "end_line": 52, "heading_path": ["Three weeks back: how Vaskell Health shortened audit preparation", "What Evenburn didn't do"], "ref": "source_122", "relative_path": "brand/case-studies/vaskell-health.md", "start_line": 49}, {"content": "### Where the category goes wrong

Security marketing has habits that readers have learned to skip. The position is partly defined by not having them.

| Category habit | What Wickhold does |
|---|---|
| Opens with a frightening scenario | Opens with what a team can do about the problem |
| Promises total coverage | Says what is covered and names what is not |
| Sells the dashboard | Shows the containment action and its log entry |
| Treats the on-call engineer as a victim | Treats the on-call engineer as the expert |
| Uses a survey to alarm | Uses a survey to size a problem, then stops |

", "end_line": 161, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "4. Positioning", "Where the category goes wrong"], "ref": "source_123", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 150}, {"content": "### What replaced Cobalt

Cobalt, the primary color from 2024, was retired on February 10, 2026, and **Ember `#C2501F` replaced it as the primary color**. Cobalt should not appear in any new work. Ember is not used the way Cobalt was. Cobalt covered whole slides, hero bands and booth walls. Ember is a small, deliberate point of heat, and a layout built around it should look mostly like Tallow or Soot.

The reasons for the change were practical as well as symbolic. The category is full of blue, and in side-by-side tests of competitor pages Wickhold's old pages were hard to pick out. A warm orange-brown also ties the color to the brand idea, since it is the color of a banked coal. It is deliberately neither a bright hazard orange nor an alarm red, because the brand is not trying to raise a reader's pulse.

", "end_line": 303, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "7. Color", "What replaced Cobalt"], "ref": "source_124", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 298}, {"content": "## T8a. Demo follow-up

", "end_line": 131, "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "Picking an image: the order"], "ref": "source_127", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "start_line": 122}, {"content": "## Before sending

", "end_line": 49, "heading_path": ["Email header images", "Before sending"], "ref": "source_128", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/email-header.md", "start_line": 47}, {"content": "**The Containment Report.** Annual, every April, and the most formal thing we publish. It reads like a clinical note: findings in flat declaratives, method stated early, no pitch in the body. The product can appear at the end, briefly, once the reader has had what they came for.

**Release notes.** Past tense, specific, no selling. A bug we fixed is described as a bug.

**Press.** Third person, plain, one idea per release. The quote from Maren is the only place with any warmth, and she writes it herself.

**Sales decks and talk tracks.** Same facts, same claims, slightly warmer because a person is in the room. If a slide would embarrass the on-call lead, it comes out.

**Webinars and video.** Script it as speech, then cut a third. Two people talking through a real incident timeline beats one person reading slides. No stock intro music with a heartbeat in it, and no voiceover that sounds like a trailer.

**Support replies.** These are written by the support team and we don't police them, but the same habit applies: repeat what you saw, say what you did, say what happens next. A reply that begins by thanking the customer for their patience has already lost them.

**Events.** Slow Burn Summit in Denver is the one place where we are among friends, and it can sound like that. - "GDPR-ready"

- "UK GDPR certified"

Examples:

| Bad | Good |
|---|---|

The agent ships as a DaemonSet from a Helm chart. It loads eBPF programs on each node and attaches to tracepoints, kprobes and LSM hooks covering process execution, file access, network connections and privilege changes. Events move through a BPF ring buffer to a small userspace process that enriches them with pod, namespace, service account and image metadata from containerd and the Kubernetes API.

Requirements:

| Item | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Kernel | Linux 5.8 or later, with BTF enabled |
| Architecture | x86_64 and arm64 |
| cgroups | v2 |
| Container runtime | containerd or CRI-O |
| Kubernetes | The current release and the three before it, self-managed or on a managed Kubernetes service with node access |
| Agent resources | Requests 200m CPU and 256Mi memory, limit 512Mi |

Overhead is under 2% CPU overhead on a typical node in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026. Busy nodes doing a lot of short-lived process execution, such as CI runners, will sit higher than that. Say so if a prospect asks, because they will measure it.

", "end_line": 30, "heading_path": ["Email templates", "Email preheader"], "ref": "source_158", "relative_path": "brand/templates/email-templates.md", "start_line": 23}, {"content": "## Containment actions

| Action | What happens | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| Isolate a pod's network | The pod can no longer reach anything outside it | A workload is talking to something it never has |
| Freeze a process | Execution stops and memory stays intact | You want evidence for a human to read |
| Drain a node | Pods move off the node, within your PodDisruptionBudgets | The node itself is suspect |

", "end_line": 41, "heading_path": ["Runtime containment for Kubernetes, decided before the incident", "Containment actions"], "ref": "source_159", "relative_path": "brand/archive/landing/quenchline-landing-current.md", "start_line": 34}, {"content": "### Containment actions

There are three containment actions.

**Isolate a pod's network.** The agent attaches a cgroup eBPF filter to the pod and drops traffic in both directions, apart from cluster DNS if the policy keeps it. It works regardless of CNI and does not create or edit NetworkPolicy objects, so nothing shows up in a GitOps diff. The pod keeps running, which preserves memory and open files for whoever investigates. Pods with `hostNetwork: true` cannot be isolated this way. The action is refused and the refusal is logged in the decision record, so policies for those pods should use a freeze.

**Freeze a process.** The agent sends SIGSTOP from kernel context to the process and its descendants. With `scope: container`, it writes to `cgroup.freeze` and freezes the whole container. Liveness probes will fail against a frozen container, and the kubelet will eventually restart it, which destroys what you froze. Policies that freeze should set `holdProbes: true` so the agent answers the kubelet's HTTP and gRPC probes itself during an investigation window, 30 minutes by default. Exec probes run inside the container and cannot be held, so a workload that relies on one will restart after the probe's failure threshold. That goes in the policy review, not in a footnote.

**Drain a node.** The agent cordons the node and evicts its pods through the Eviction API, honoring PodDisruptionBudgets up to a configurable timeout. This is the heaviest action and it needs an extra ClusterRole that the chart does not install unless you set `rbac.nodeDrain=true`. Most customers never turn it on.

The agent contains a known-bad process in a median of 38 seconds in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026. That figure is from detection to action on a lab node. It says nothing about how long an entire incident takes, so do not stretch it into a claim about incident response.

", "end_line": 78, "heading_path": ["Wickhold Quenchline: product overview", "How it works", "Containment actions"], "ref": "source_160", "relative_path": "brand/products/quenchline-overview.md", "start_line": 67}, {"content": "### Commissioning imagery

Freelancers and agencies should get the visual guidance before their first sketch. On the launch film, the first round of location photos came back blue and spotless, because the agency had worked from a mood board built on the old identity. Reshooting took a week.

Any generated or composited image gets the same review as a commissioned one. It is held to the same direction, and a person looks at it at full size before it goes anywhere.

", "end_line": 423, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "9. Photography and illustration direction", "Commissioning imagery"], "ref": "source_161", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 416}, {"content": "## How the visual rules are layered

Three layers, read in this order.

1. **This page.** Applies to everything.
2. **The category.** What kind of image is it? Photo, illustration, icon, logo, product screenshot, chart, social graphic, event graphic, legal and trust imagery, anything showing a person.
3. **The content type.** Where is it going? Blog hero, LinkedIn, X, email header, landing page.

Most images touch one rule from each layer, and some touch two categories. A photo of a staff member at a customer site is photography and consent at once, and it has to pass both.

A lower layer can narrow a higher one. The illustration category accepts several formats, for example, and the blog hero page accepts fewer of them. In that case follow the narrower rule for that placement, and the broader rule stays true everywhere else. A lower layer cannot loosen this page. If a content-type page seems to let you do something this page forbids, bring it to Brand, because one of the two pages is wrong and we want to fix it.

Per-campaign exceptions go through Noor's exception log. Without an entry there, if a campaign needs something new, the rule changes for everybody or the campaign changes.

", "end_line": 20, "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "How the visual rules are layered"], "ref": "source_162", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "start_line": 7}, {"content": "## Body

Most of our email has three parts.

1. **What happened or what's new.** One or two sentences.
2. **Why it matters to this reader.** Two to four sentences. Different for a CISO list and a platform list, which is why the tracks are separate.
3. **What to do.** One button or link. Then the sign-off.

The working drafts are in the email templates, and the merge fields there match the sending platform. Start from a template. A blank page tends to produce an email that's 400 words long.

Good body copy, platform track:

> You downloaded the Containment Report, so here's the practical follow-up. Our rollout guide starts with Wickhold Quenchline in observe mode on one namespace, then moves to contain mode once you've read two to four weeks of would-have-acted events.
>
> It takes about an hour, and the failure modes are listed at the end.

Good body copy, CISO track:

> Decide whether your team tracks time to contain today. Your board will ask how long a runtime incident takes to contain. In our survey of 412 platform and security leaders, the median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].
>
> The report sets out how teams measure that number and what they report upward. If your team doesn't track it, section two is a place to start.

Bad body copy:

> Hope you're having a great week! As a valued member of our community, we wanted to reach out and share some exciting content we think you'll love. In today's rapidly evolving threat landscape, security has never been more important.

Four sentences in and the reader has learned nothing. Cut until the first sentence is the news.

Personalization: first name in the greeting when we have it, and role-based copy through segments. Anything else, like company size, industry or recent page views, stays out of the visible copy. Being told what you browsed by a security company is unsettling.

- Every code block must run. An engineer other than the author pastes it into a test cluster before publishing. Kofi keeps a throwaway cluster for this and will give you access.

```bash
# Good: what you ran, and what to look for
kubectl get pods -n payments-api -o wide
# ...
# payments-api-6f9c7d   0/1   Terminating   0   3m   10.2.4.17   node-a

", "end_line": 84, "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "5. Code and commands"], "ref": "source_166", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md", "start_line": 69}, {"content": "## Common questions from the field

**Do we need to change our NetworkPolicies?** No. Isolation sits underneath them.

**Will it conflict with our CNI?** It has been tested with the common eBPF and iptables-based CNIs. The cgroup filter attaches independently of the CNI's own programs. Customers running a heavily customized datapath should test in staging.

**Can it run in a namespace-scoped way, without cluster-wide access?** No. The agent needs privileged access on the node and cluster-wide read on pods. This comes up in almost every security review. The ClusterRole is short and is printed in the chart's `templates/rbac.yaml`, so show it to them.

**What happens during an upgrade?** The DaemonSet rolls one node at a time by default. During the swap a node has a detection gap of a few seconds, and pinned filters remain in place.

**Does it read application payloads?** No. It sees connection metadata and does not decrypt TLS.

Maintained by Product Marketing with the Quenchline engineering team. Last checked against Quenchline 5.3, August 2026.

**Current identity only.** Ember `#C2501F`, Soot `#15181C`, Tallow `#F4EFE6`, with Whetstone `#5E6B73` and Verdigris `#2F8F83` as secondary colors. Bricolage Grotesque, IBM Plex Sans and IBM Plex Mono for any type on an image. Anything leaning on the 2024 blue palette or the 2024 logo is out, however good it looks. Some of those images are still in the library with no flag on them, so your eye is part of this check.

**No third-party marks.** No real product logos on laptop lids, no cloud provider marks on diagrams, no conference logos in a crop unless the agreement with that organizer allows it. Customer marks are a legal matter and go through Legal first.

**No watermarks,** no preview overlays, no leftover crop marks. If an image arrived with a watermark, its rights are not what you think they are.

**Do not stretch, tint or recolor library files.** Crop freely within the category's limits. Stretching breaks the proportions of the art and recoloring breaks the palette. Filters are out too: the warm look comes from the source image, and a filter laid on a cool image only makes it look cool and filtered. If an image needs a color change to fit, it is the wrong image.

**Export for the placement.** WebP or PNG for web, PNG where transparency matters, SVG for logos and icons when the placement accepts it. Keep web images under 400 KB unless the content-type page says otherwise. JPEG artifacts around Ember shapes are very visible, so check flat illustration at full size after compressing.

**Nothing that frightens.** Images follow the same stance as the copy. Show the small fire or the calm room, and skip the alarm. Red alert screens, countdown timers, sirens and skulls have no place here, even as a joke in an engineering post.

", "end_line": 62, "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "Other rules for all images"], "ref": "source_169", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md", "start_line": 49}, {"content": "## 2. The intro

A blog intro must cite a market statistic. Put it in the first two sentences, in the citation format from the style guide, and follow it with one sentence that says why this post exists. The rule is there because engineers are more willing to keep reading once they know the problem is measured and someone has measured it honestly.

Statistics are subject to the age limit in the approved claims, so check the date before you reuse an intro from an older post.

Market statistics are figures about the market or a surveyed population. Our own customer results and benchmark numbers belong further down the post, and they don't satisfy this requirement.

Good:

> The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. Most of the teams we talk to can tell you how long detection took. Far fewer can tell you what happened in the hours after. This post is about those hours.

Good:

> 41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. A lot of that time goes to one question: who is allowed to touch the workload? Here is how to settle that question before the page goes off.

Bad, because it has no statistic and no reason to read on:

> Kubernetes has changed how modern teams ship software, and with that change come new security challenges.

Bad, because a customer result is doing the job of a market statistic:

> Lowmoor Credit Union cut time to contain from 4 hours to 11 minutes. Here's how your team can get the same results.

- **back end** (noun), **back-end** (adjective).
- **cyber:** avoid as a prefix. Say what kind of security you mean.
- **data** is singular in our copy: "the data is".

- **real time** (noun), **real-time** (adjective).

- **third party** (noun), **third-party** (adjective).
- **trade-off:** hyphenated.

The hero says what the product does and who it's for, in that order. Lead with what happens to the reader's workload. Our tagline can sit in the hero of the brand page, but it doesn't describe a product, so product pages shouldn't rely on it.

Good, product page:
