", "heading_path": ["Email templates", "T8c. Renewal notice"], "ref": "s241", "relative_path": "brand/templates/email-templates.md"}, {"chunk_id": "f83751e4-c684-4b91-ae78-8575ba2d6497", "content": "## What we send

**Monthly newsletter.** Goes to everyone opted in, second Tuesday of the month. One lead item, three short items, nothing about us that we wouldn't want to read ourselves. Engineers are the bulk of this list, so it can carry a command or a config snippet.

**Nurture tracks.** Separate tracks for CISOs and platform leads, triggered by report downloads and demo requests. Four to six emails over about six weeks. Sales gets an alert on replies. If a contact opens a sales conversation, the track stops.

**Product announcements.** Goes to customers first, prospects a day later. New capabilities, deprecations, and anything that changes how a customer's agents behave. Deprecations go out at least 60 days ahead.

**Customer notices.** Security advisories, CVE guidance, scheduled maintenance. These bypass frequency caps and unsubscribe groups. Dov or a named engineer signs. Marketing can edit for clarity but never holds one back for scheduling reasons.

**Event email.** Slow Burn Summit and Field Day invites and reminders. The events team writes, lifecycle sends.

**Founder notes.** Maren writes to customers about twice a year, usually around pricing or product direction. It comes from her address. A reply goes to her, and she reads them.

", "heading_path": ["Email playbook", "What we send"], "ref": "s242", "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "ff72767b-3940-4591-a5a3-16502d7c5c5d", "content": "## Retired

The "abandoned demo form" reminder went away in January 2026 because it felt like surveillance. The "We miss you" re-engagement email is also gone, and the replacement is one plain note asking whether to keep sending, with a single "Stay subscribed" button.
", "heading_path": ["Email templates", "Retired"], "ref": "s243", "relative_path": "brand/templates/email-templates.md"}, {"chunk_id": "26f9f996-cd6d-4ef6-b3b8-972d1bd0c6c0", "content": "## 6. Review

| Step | Who | When |
|---|---|---|
| Outline | Editor (Kofi for engineering posts, Noor for the rest) | Before anyone writes 1,000 words |
| Technical read | An engineer who did not write it | Draft complete |
| Copy edit | Brand team | After the technical read |
| Claims check | Priit, for any customer, certification or number, except third-party statistics under section 5 of the approved claims | As the approved claims set out |
| Paste test | Second engineer, code posts only | Day before publish |

Allow two weeks from outline to publish. Report posts in April move faster because Legal has already checked the numbers.

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "6. Review"], "ref": "s244", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "2dfe4ee1-b5b7-475f-aa8a-47e4ee921cb3", "content": "## 1. Length

Blog posts run 900 to 1,400 words. That range counts the body, including captions and code comments you wrote yourself, but not the code output you pasted.

Under 900 words, it's probably a release note or a LinkedIn post. Over 1,400 words, split it in two or cut the history section. We all write the history section first because it's easy, and nobody needs it. The report, the docs and the rollout guide are the place for anything longer.

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "1. Length"], "ref": "s245", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "376c8b2d-e153-46d4-9868-97f9e1c51b3a", "content": "## 3. Post types

**Engineering posts.** Written by Dov, Kofi or an engineer with an editor attached. How the eBPF agent attaches, what we learned from a kernel upgrade, why a containment action took longer than it should have. These carry the blog.

**How-to posts.** A task, steps, and what it looks like when it goes wrong: rolling out contain mode, reading an exposure path, writing a first tool-call policy for Leashgate in early access.

**Report posts.** One finding from the Containment Report, argued properly. We get four or five out of each report. Do not summarize the whole report in one post. That's what the report page does.

**Customer posts.** Built from a published case study, with the customer's own words where we have approval. These need Priit's sign-off every time, even when the numbers are already public.

**Founder posts.** Maren, on company decisions and what she learned from them. They're rare and marketing does not ghostwrite them. An editor can tidy.

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "3. Post types"], "ref": "s246", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "43519095-47d5-42a8-b0b4-9efdf2334158", "content": "# Writing for the Wickhold blog

*Kofi Anselm wrote the first version in May 2026 for the two contractors we brought in after the Containment Report. Noor edited it in July. Send fixes to either of us.*

The blog has one job: get a platform engineer or a security lead to trust that the people here have held the pager. Traffic is a side effect. A post that gets a staff engineer to forward it to their team beats a post that ranks for a keyword and gets skimmed.

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog"], "ref": "s247", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "4a8bc433-313b-48fe-81f1-b9d8798bc8a8", "content": "## 7. Publishing details

- URL slug: lowercase, under 60 characters, no dates.
- Meta description: one plain sentence, under 155 characters.
- Author byline is always a real person. We retired "The Wickhold Team" as a byline in 2025 when we noticed those posts got half the reads.
- Hero images come from the design team. Send the request with your outline, not the day before.
- Tuesdays and Wednesdays. Never the same day as a release note, since they compete in the newsletter.

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "7. Publishing details"], "ref": "s248", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "4cb61d28-8600-42a9-b770-bac22ceba88f", "content": "## 8. Working with engineers who don't want to write

Most of our best material is in the heads of people who would rather fix a kernel bug. Don't send them a blank doc. Book 30 minutes, ask them to walk you through the last hard thing they fixed, and record it with their permission. Write the draft from the recording and send it back for correction. An engineer who won't write 1,000 words will happily rewrite the 200 you got wrong.

Keep their phrasing where you can. If someone says the agent "falls over politely" on a read-only kernel, that goes in. Their name goes on the post, and they read the final version before it goes live. If they ask to take something out, take it out, and don't argue about it in the review thread.

Questions that tend to produce a post:

- What did you assume about this before you got paged?
- What's the command you wish you had run first?
- What does the failure look like from the outside?
- What did you change afterward, and did it hold?

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "8. Working with engineers who don't want to write"], "ref": "s249", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "6fabfd1d-c817-4def-a0d5-bc9821112094", "content": "## 4. Shape of a post

A title that says what the reader will get. Then the intro. Then three to five sections with descriptive headings. Then an ending that tells the reader what to do on Monday.

Titles we liked:

- Contain mode, one namespace at a time
- What drift looks like after a Helm upgrade
- The six hours after detection
- Writing your first tool-call policy for Wickhold Leashgate, in early access

Titles we rewrote:

- "5 Kubernetes Security Mistakes You're Making Right Now" became "Five findings we see in most new clusters"
- "Everything You Need To Know About eBPF" became "What our eBPF agent can and can't see"

Section headings should still make sense if they're all someone reads. "Background" and "The solution" tell the reader nothing.

End on the practical next step, then one call to action to the most relevant page. Don't summarize what you just said. If the post was good, they remember. Don't add a paragraph about Wickhold at the bottom either, as the footer handles that.

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "4. Shape of a post"], "ref": "s250", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "95a3bc17-3a62-42aa-bb1c-70545612062c", "content": "## 5. Code and commands

- Every code block must run. An engineer other than the author pastes it into a test cluster before publishing. Kofi keeps a throwaway cluster for this and will give you access.
- State versions at the top of the block or in the sentence before it: Kubernetes, Helm chart, kernel where it matters.
- Show the output when the output is the point, and trim it with a visible `...`.
- Use real-looking names like `payments-api` and `checkout`. Avoid `foo` and `my-app`, and don't use a customer's actual namespace names, even with permission.
- Say what fails. If `helm upgrade` can leave the agent in `CrashLoopBackOff` on an old kernel, put that in the post.

```bash
# Good: what you ran, and what to look for
kubectl get pods -n payments-api -o wide
# ...
# payments-api-6f9c7d   0/1   Terminating   0   3m   10.2.4.17   node-a
# A pod stuck here after a drain usually has a finalizer. Check that first.
```

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "5. Code and commands"], "ref": "s251", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "9792dec6-922e-42ef-aded-9a7b0bc70f03", "content": "## 2. The intro

A blog intro must cite a market statistic. Put it in the first two sentences, in the citation format from the style guide, and follow it with one sentence that says why this post exists. The rule is there because engineers are more willing to keep reading once they know the problem is measured and someone has measured it honestly.

Statistics are subject to the age limit in the approved claims, so check the date before you reuse an intro from an older post.

Market statistics are figures about the market or a surveyed population. Our own customer results and benchmark numbers belong further down the post, and they don't satisfy this requirement.

Good:

> The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. Most of the teams we talk to can tell you how long detection took. Far fewer can tell you what happened in the hours after. This post is about those hours.

Good:

> 41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. A lot of that time goes to one question: who is allowed to touch the workload? Here is how to settle that question before the page goes off.

Bad, because it has no statistic and no reason to read on:

> Kubernetes has changed how modern teams ship software, and with that change come new security challenges.

Bad, because a customer result is doing the job of a market statistic:

> Lowmoor Credit Union cut time to contain from 4 hours to 11 minutes. Here's how your team can get the same results.

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "2. The intro"], "ref": "s252", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "b0b53749-5be6-4308-8b5a-8b34e65f5020", "content": "## 10. Tried and dropped

Guest posts from partners took more editing than writing one ourselves, and the partners wanted a link in every paragraph. Weekly "news roundups" lasted nine weeks in 2025 and nobody missed them. Keyword-led briefs from an agency produced the "Everything You Need To Know" titles above, and we stopped that contract in the spring.
", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "10. Tried and dropped"], "ref": "s253", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "cde0d081-7f1e-4ee9-a5cb-3a4e3d01ea38", "content": "## 9. Updating old posts

Older posts stay up, but they can mislead. The brand team runs through the top 30 posts by traffic every quarter. Each gets one of three outcomes: leave it, edit it in place with an "Updated" date at the top, or redirect it to a newer post.

Edit in place when a product name, a command or a figure has gone out of date. Redirect when the advice has changed. Never quietly change a claim. If a post said something that turned out to be wrong, add a line saying what changed and when. Engineers notice, and they remember how you handled it.

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "9. Updating old posts"], "ref": "s254", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "06f039a8-673e-4726-a5b1-6b8cbb81dae0", "content": "## Things we tried

Polls brought a lot of votes from people outside our audience and no replies worth reading. Dropped in late 2025.

Document posts and carousels are off the plan. Swipes fell away after the third page.

Paid boosting is decided per post by demand gen. A boosted post goes through the same review as paid copy, even when it started life as an organic one.
", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Things we tried"], "ref": "s255", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "08ed6196-965b-4faa-9751-01ebf0e4f4a2", "content": "# LinkedIn playbook

Noor Eskelund. Last edit 12 August 2026, after the Leashgate early access posts. Ask in the brand channel before you ask me by email.

LinkedIn is the one channel where CISOs, platform leads and our own hiring pipeline all look at the same feed. Most of what we post there is read on a phone, between meetings, by someone who has never heard of us. Write for that person.

", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook"], "ref": "s256", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "1539b083-de00-4738-8643-5b57c2f52acf", "content": "## Examples

Good, report post:

> 41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].
>
> That figure comes from the Wickhold Containment Report 2026, our survey of 412 platform and security leaders. The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].
>
> 7.4 hours is most of an on-call shift, spent on one problem while everything else waits.
>
> Read the report: https://wickhold.example/containment-report

Good, customer post. The numbers are approved and the post leaves them alone:

> Lowmoor Credit Union runs Wickhold Quenchline across 220 nodes. Time to contain fell from 4 hours to 11 minutes.
>
> Quenchline is our runtime detection and containment product for Kubernetes. It uses an eBPF agent to isolate a pod's network, freeze a process or drain a node.
>
> Read the Lowmoor story: https://wickhold.example/customers/lowmoor

Good, product post:

> Wickhold Quenchline contains a known-bad process in a median of 38 seconds in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026.
>
> Lab conditions are kinder than your cluster on a bad night, so start in observe mode and read what it would have done. Then pick the namespaces where contain mode earns its place.
>
> See the rollout guide: https://wickhold.example/docs/rollout

Good, posture post:

> Ostler Grocers cut open critical misconfigurations by 63% in 90 days, across 1,900 nodes.
>
> Wickhold Evenburn tracks drift across cloud and cluster, maps each exposure path, and gives the team a fix order for Monday morning.
>
> Read the Ostler story: https://wickhold.example/customers/ostler

Good openers for founder posts. Only the first lines are shown here because Maren and Dov write the rest themselves:

> The worst page I ever took was for a disk that had filled up with logs about a disk filling up.

> I spent four years on call before we started this company, and I still check my phone at 3:10am.

Bad, from a 2024 draft that came back to the queue last spring:

> We're thrilled to announce an exciting new chapter in our journey! Our amazing team has been working around the clock to bring you the future of cloud security. Stay tuned, big things are coming!

", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Examples"], "ref": "s257", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "3475d85a-d4cb-4436-8cb3-16b2589f01ae", "content": "## Comments and DMs

Reply to real questions within one business day, from the company page, in the same plain voice. Sales inquiries go to the sales queue by DM link. Leave vendor pitches alone. If someone corrects a fact and they're right, say so and fix the post.

", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Comments and DMs"], "ref": "s258", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "3ad8462a-c1af-4958-9ab6-5ba77d64a220", "content": "Nothing happened in that post. No product, no date, no number, and a reader who stops at the cut has learned only that we are thrilled.

Bad, the post with too many jobs:

> Our report is out, we're hiring in Denver, Slow Burn Summit registration is open, and Wickhold Evenburn has a new fix order view. Links in the comments.

That is four posts. Pick the one with a deadline.

", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Examples"], "ref": "s259", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "41f8d6b1-1744-475c-b7dd-9cafc7d5a3e6", "content": "## Structure

Most company posts follow the same order.

1. **The fact.** What shipped, what was measured, what happened. Put the number here if there is one.
2. **The context.** Two or three sentences on why it matters to someone running clusters or answering for them.
3. **The way out.** One link, with a short instruction in front of it.

Then stop. If you have a second point, it is a second post next week.

", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Structure"], "ref": "s260", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "bd7ba1fe-13b7-4692-afd2-ef01d0dc122b", "content": "## Review

| Post contains | Who approves | Turnaround |
|---|---|---|
| No claims, no customers (hiring, event logistics) | Anyone on the brand team | Two business days |
| Product claim from the approved list | Noor | Two business days |
| Customer name or result | Noor and Priit Salonen, plus the customer's contact if we tag them | Five business days |
| Any number we haven't published before, except third-party statistics under section 5 of the approved claims | Priit Salonen | Two business days |

", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Review"], "ref": "s261", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "e4d55076-3313-4cf2-a4af-45a0ab945f2f", "content": "## Format

- A LinkedIn post is 180 words at most. Count everything, including the link line.
- About the first 200 characters show before the "see more" cut on most phones. The news has to fit in that space.
- Short paragraphs, one to three lines each, with a blank line between them.
- One link per post, at the end, on its own line. We tested putting links in the first comment for six weeks in 2025 and could not see a difference, and it annoyed people, so links stay in the post.
- Tag a customer only after their marketing contact has seen the post. Tag people, not company pages, when a named person spoke or wrote the thing.
- Use bullets only for real lists: three containment actions, the tiers, the steps of a rollout. A post that is all bullets reads as a slide.
- Image guidance sits with the visual rules. Every company page post gets one image, except short hiring notes.

", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Format"], "ref": "s262", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "f1e93386-bd9e-4240-9294-b61ce8701dec", "content": "## Who posts

**Company page.** Marketing runs it. Two or three posts a week, Tuesday to Thursday, usually mid-morning Mountain time. Fridays stayed on the calendar through most of 2025 and did nothing, so they came off.

**Maren and Dov.** They post from their own profiles when they have something to say. Marketing can draft, but they rewrite. Do not schedule on their behalf without a yes in writing, and do not reply to comments as them. If a draft of Maren's has been sitting for two weeks, drop it. She has decided.

**Kofi and the DevRel team.** Kofi posts from his own profile about conference talks, open-source eBPF work and whatever broke in the demo cluster. He does not need brand review for those unless a post carries a customer name, a product claim or a number.

**Everyone else.** People can share company posts however they like. We ran an employee amplification program in 2025 with a shared doc of suggested captions. Forty people posted the same sentence on the same morning and it looked exactly like that. We stopped.

Never report a conflict solely because the original brief differs from an accepted answer. Do not require the campaign goal to narrate the correction or its legal justification. An answer is campaign intent, not proof of a factual claim. If a new evidence conflict still needs a decision, ask it explicitly rather than silently overriding the answer. Do not reopen the same question unless relevant evidence or user intent changed, or the answer was ambiguous. Explain the specific change when reopening. Return one field patch per distinct (asset_id, field) in defects. Never return a whole plan. Preserve IDs and all unrelated fields. Do not introduce optional statistics, claims, URLs or examples to repair a hook. Prefer a simple non-factual opening using existing intent. If retaining a statistic, preserve its approved wording, bracket citation and required survey base together. Repair only the concrete defects; use existing candidate facts for incomplete_text, without introducing new claims. For content defects apply original governing rules including exceptions. Return an outline, never full drafts. Do not resolve new conflicts or invent exceptions. Shared evidence is referenced by governing_rules.channels.*.evidence_group references source_groups, whose entries identify evidence.ref. Campaign list fields require list replacements; all other editable fields require strings. Respect the replacement schema character limits. Rewrite concisely as complete sentences; never truncate words or sentences.

", "heading_path": [], "ref": "s0", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "06b9541d-5f83-4479-a802-93cca36f7f44", "content": "## 9. People and companies

- Full name and title on first mention, in this order: Hana Brandvold, CISO, Lowmoor Credit Union.
- After that, surname for external people, in the press-release style: Brandvold said. First name for our founders only where they signed the piece.
- Job titles are capitalized in a byline or attribution line and lowercase in a sentence: "the company's head of developer relations".
- Companies are singular. "Wickhold is", "Ostler Grocers has".
- Use "they" for an unnamed person. "On-call lead", not "on-call guy". "Staffed", not "manned".
- Teams are lowercase: the platform team, the brand team.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "9. People and companies"], "ref": "s1", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "06ede73b-42e2-4a1d-8774-10eb6d36ca3a", "content": "### Product behavior

Wickhold Quenchline takes a containment action only in contain mode. In observe mode it records what it would have done. Copy describing automatic containment must therefore be true of contain mode and should say so where a reader could assume otherwise. Containment actions are isolating a pod's network, freezing a process and draining a node. Do not add to the list without product confirmation.

Wickhold Evenburn reports drift, exposure paths and a fix order. It does not change a customer's environment by itself, and copy should not imply that it does.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "2. Claims that need a qualifier", "Product behavior"], "ref": "s2", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "1642c23e-25ab-42ea-bc7d-815ffe334028", "content": "## 13. Updating published pieces

Blog posts and pages get corrected in place. Add a line at the top: "Updated June 2, 2026: corrected the node count in the second section." Don't change the original publish date, and don't quietly fix a factual error. A typo can be fixed without a note. If the correction changes what the piece argues, Noor decides whether it stays up.

Old posts that use a previous product or company name stay as published until someone updates them for another reason. Don't run find-and-replace across the blog. It was done once in March, and it rewrote a quote.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "13. Updating published pieces"], "ref": "s3", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "1c8464bd-edcd-4e17-81cd-317c32433282", "content": "### Customer results

Keep the node count with the result. The Lowmoor outcome belongs to a 220-node estate and the Ostler outcome to a 1,900-node estate, and neither may be stated as what a new customer should expect. Do not convert the Lowmoor result into a percentage or a multiple. Nobody approved that arithmetic. Do not combine the two results in one sentence, because that reads as a single program with both outcomes. Which customers may be cited, and how, is covered by the logo and quote policy.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "2. Claims that need a qualifier", "Customer results"], "ref": "s4", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "20935a37-7df2-480f-a9e7-2b77fe6fd1fe", "content": "## 14. Bylines and bios

- Blog bylines: full name and title. "By Kofi Anselm, Head of Developer Relations".
- A byline doesn't change the voice. Posts by staff are written like every other piece of company copy. Founder posts have their own treatment, covered in the voice document.
- Bios run one sentence and state a job. Not "passionate about", not "self-described", no hobbies unless the hobby is funny enough for Noor to let it through.
- Don't feature former staff in new pieces. If someone has left, their old byline stays on their old posts.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "14. Bylines and bios"], "ref": "s5", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "20f42450-b663-4c3d-ab3d-76a1f92c69f7", "content": "### Terms we set one way

| Write | Not |
|---|---|
| Kubernetes | K8s, kube (fine in Slack, not in copy) |
| eBPF | EBPF, ebpf, e-BPF |
| containerd | Containerd, ContainerD |
| Helm, Helm chart | helm chart |
| pod, node, cluster, namespace | Pod, Node, Cluster, Namespace (unless it's the literal field or kind in code) |
| runtime (one word, all uses) | run-time, run time |
| on-call (adjective, plus the noun in our value "the next on-call"), on call (otherwise) | oncall |
| open source (noun), open-source (adjective) | opensource |
| cloud-native (adjective) | cloud native |
| tool call (noun), tool-call policy (adjective) | toolcall |
| AI agent | agentic AI, "AI worker", "digital employee" |
| CVE (uppercase, spell the ID in full: CVE-YYYY-NNNNN) | Cve, "a CVE" as a synonym for "an exploit" |
| CIS Benchmarks | CIS benchmarks |
| SOC 2 Type II (space, Roman numerals) | SOC2, SOC 2 Type 2 |
| PCI DSS | PCI-DSS |

Spell out an abbreviation on first use only if the reader might not know it. Platform engineers know what a CVE is. Board-level readers may need "time to contain" rather than an acronym we made up, and we don't use MTTC anywhere, because we'd then have to explain it.

**Security language.** Allowlist and denylist, not whitelist and blacklist. Primary and replica, not master and slave. If Kubernetes itself retains an old term in a literal field name, leave the field as it is.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "8. Technical writing in marketing copy", "Terms we set one way"], "ref": "s6", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "259a4c89-2f19-42d5-8a46-410969bc3808", "content": "## 7. Lists

Bullets are for parallel things. If a list reads like an argument, it's a paragraph.

- Sentences in a list get full stops. Fragments don't. Don't mix them in one list.
- Keep the first word of every item in the same form: all verbs or all nouns.
- Numbered lists are for a real sequence: steps in a runbook, order of operations.
- Five items is usually the end of what a reader holds. A longer list wants grouping.
- Never write a list whose only job is to look thorough. Reviewers will count it.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "7. Lists"], "ref": "s7", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "29f5111a-13f4-4875-bc64-ad77b271291b", "content": "# Approved claims, 2026

Owner: Priit Salonen, General Counsel
Revision 7, 28 September 2026. Replaces revision 6.

This document lists what Wickhold may say about itself, what it may say only with a qualifier, and what it may not say. It governs marketing, sales, developer relations, press and customer success. Founder posts are included. A signature does not change the facts.

If a claim is not listed, it is not approved. That does not mean it is refused. It means nobody has checked it. Send the sentence, the proposed channel and the evidence to priit@wickhold.example. Copy under 500 words comes back within two working days. Reports, press releases and anything with a customer name take five. "Legal said it was fine on a call" is not a record, and I will not recognize it later.

Wording in quotation marks is exact. Do not improve it.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026"], "ref": "s8", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "2c9fa907-d71a-493e-970c-0af9cbc9374b", "content": "## 9. Review, exceptions, and how this document changes

Every piece of external copy containing a claim from section 1 or 2 is reviewed against this document by its author. Copy containing a new claim, a customer name, or a reference to a security incident also comes to me. Press releases and the annual report come to me regardless.

Exceptions are given in writing, for one asset, and expire with that asset. I have given two this year. Neither should be taken as a precedent.

If this document disagrees with a guideline, a playbook, a deck or a comment from a senior colleague, this document wins. If it disagrees with reality, tell me, and I will change it.

Reviewed each quarter with Ilse Varga-Holm and Noor Eskelund.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "9. Review, exceptions, and how this document changes"], "ref": "s9", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "2ed35bac-e511-4a05-b03f-f56a94ab438a", "content": "## 3. Citations

**Citations give the source name, the year and the link, in brackets, right after the claim.**

The shape, exactly:

```text
41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].
```

- Source name in full, as the source spells it.
- Comma, year. Comma, link. The full stop for the sentence goes outside the bracket.
- Link goes to the report or page itself, not a press release about it and not a search result. In a PDF or on a slide print the link out, because hyperlinks do not survive a screenshot.
- Use the same form everywhere, including LinkedIn and X. Yes, it's long on X. Plan the post around it.
- Two sources for one claim: two brackets. Do not merge them.
- A source we did not produce gets its own name in the bracket, even when a Wickhold page quotes it. Cite the original.
- In long pieces (report summaries, the blog), mention the survey base once near the first figure: "a survey of 412 platform and security leaders".

We tried numbered footnotes on the blog through most of 2025 and dropped them. The claim got quoted on LinkedIn, the footnote stayed behind, and the number went around with no source. A bracket travels with the sentence.

Customer results don't take a bracket when the customer is named in the sentence and the case study is linked from the page. Naming them is the source.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "3. Citations"], "ref": "s10", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "33d10c5d-c881-4d79-95fa-1edc60d3c984", "content": "## 1. Claims approved as written

| Topic | Approved wording | Evidence held by |
|---|---|---|
| Customer count | "more than 140 customers" | Finance, reconciled quarterly |
| Market, time to contain | "41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident" | Wickhold Containment Report 2026 |
| Market, median | "the median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours" | Wickhold Containment Report 2026 |
| Lowmoor Credit Union | Time to contain fell from 4 hours to 11 minutes, 220 nodes | Signed customer approval |
| Ostler Grocers | 63% fewer open critical misconfigurations in 90 days, 1,900 nodes | Signed customer approval |
| SOC 2 | Wickhold holds SOC 2 Type II, renewed January 2026 | Legal |
| Agent policy | "limits what a compromised agent can do" | Legal and product |
| Company | Founded in March 2019 in Denver, Colorado | Legal |
| Funding | Series B of $46M in June 2024, led by Marlbank Partners | Legal |

The Containment Report was published on April 14, 2026, and surveyed 412 platform and security leaders. Give the survey size when the copy has room for it. The legal entity is Wickhold, Inc. Contracts, order forms, privacy notices and page footers use that form. Marketing copy uses Wickhold.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "1. Claims approved as written"], "ref": "s11", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "3f1ab036-5423-418c-82f3-db208d02cb8a", "content": "## 6. Breach and incident references

This section sets how Wickhold may talk about breaches and other public incidents, in any channel.

1. Never name a victim. That covers company names, product names, and descriptions that identify one ("a large regional retailer in the week it made the news").
2. No humor. Not in the copy, not in the image, not in a speaker's aside.
3. Nothing within 30 days of a public incident. Count from the first public disclosure. For the 30 days, Wickhold does not publish, post, send or sponsor anything that refers to the incident or that is plainly timed to it. An incident is not a marketing hook.

After 30 days, a breach may be discussed in general terms only, as a pattern and without identifying anyone. A technical analysis of a technique is fine if it does not rely on the incident for attention.

The rules cover paid media, social, email, blog posts, sales sequences, talks and replies to journalists. They apply to personal LinkedIn accounts when the post mentions Wickhold or its products. Press inquiries about a live incident go to Ilse Varga-Holm, and nobody comments before she has spoken to me.

If a campaign in market could be read as a reaction to a new public incident, whoever notices it pauses it and tells Ilse. Nobody will be criticized for pausing. Sales may answer a direct customer question about an incident with facts about the customer's own deployment. It may not use the question as an opening.

Incidents at Wickhold customers are never discussed without the customer's written approval, whatever their age. The approved Lowmoor material is the model. It has a figure and no drama.

Not approved:

> After last week's breach at a regional bank, can your team afford another six hours?

Approved, more than 30 days after any related event:

> When a pod misbehaves, Wickhold Quenchline in contain mode can isolate its network while the on-call engineer works out what happened.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "6. Breach and incident references"], "ref": "s12", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "71d0758e-d528-4a2e-b905-47a466c01082", "content": "## Changes

- **v4, July 2026.** Citation form restated after a run of pieces shipped with no year. Time formats added after the draft summit schedule mixed three of them.
- **v3.2, March 2026.** Product name sheet split out for the web team.
- **v3, February 2026.** Rewritten for the rebrand. Title Case removed. Oxford comma confirmed, again.
- **v2, 2024.** Footnotes adopted for the blog. They didn't last.

Questions: #brand-review. For anything about what a claim may say, ask legal, not this page.
", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "Changes"], "ref": "s13", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "71def5fd-8e65-4813-946c-8576df1c15d3", "content": "## 2. First lines

**No rhetorical question as the first line of any asset.** Blog post, landing page hero, email (subject line and first sentence both), LinkedIn post, X post, video script, slide one of a deck.

"Is your cluster ready for the next incident?" tells the reader nothing and asks them to do the writer's work. It's also the most common opening in our category, so it reads as noise. Open on a fact, an event or a claim.

| Don't open with | Open with |
|---|---|
| What would you do if a pod started a shell at 3am? | A pod in `checkout` started a shell at 03:14 UTC. |
| Tired of alert fatigue? | Most alerts at 3am are about something that already stopped mattering. |

Real questions later in a piece are fine. An FAQ section is full of them and that's what it is for, as long as the page opens on a statement.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "2. First lines"], "ref": "s14", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "76bbbcb1-53e8-43a0-a87a-749d22eecce8", "content": "## 16. Headlines that get sent back

A short list from the last year of review comments, so you can save yourself the round trip.

- "The ultimate guide to" anything. It won't be.
- "X things every platform engineer should know". They know.
- "Why containment matters". Say what it changes.
- "Introducing". The reader can see that it's new. Say what it does.
- Any headline that would also fit a competitor's blog. Swap their name into your mental picture and check.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "16. Headlines that get sent back"], "ref": "s15", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "7ce46d76-f11e-471f-970d-76095f72b3d6", "content": "# Content style guide

The house rules for how Wickhold copy is set on the page. Voice lives elsewhere. This is commas, numbers and headlines. Where a rule here seems fussy, it is usually because somebody spent an afternoon arguing about it and the team would rather not repeat that.

The first three sections are the ones reviewers send back most often.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide"], "ref": "s16", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "819d53ad-e32a-41b3-94ae-7ccd3f1cc7d5", "content": "### Everything else

- **Measurements take digits, always.** Anything with a unit: 220 nodes, 11 minutes, 7.4 hours, 90 days, 38 seconds, 1,900 nodes.
- **Counts of ordinary things** spell out one to nine and use digits from 10: "three clusters", "12 namespaces". Mixed in one sentence, go with digits.
- **Commas from 1,000 up.** No "1.9k nodes", not even on social.
- **Keep the decimal the source gave you.** 7.4 hours stays 7.4 hours. Don't round to "about seven hours", and don't add precision the source lacks.
- **Approved sentences stay as approved.** The report line says "more than six hours", spelled out, and that's how it runs in every piece. The same goes for "more than 140 customers", which never becomes "140+". Legal approved the sentence, and this guide doesn't get to tidy it.
- **Don't do arithmetic on claims.** Lowmoor went from 4 hours to 11 minutes. Do not convert that into a percentage or an "x times faster". The figures we can stand behind are the two figures we were given. Same for adding results from different customers together.
- **No "up to".** "Up to" numbers are a best case wearing a fact's clothes. Give the median, or say which run you mean.
- **No tildes or "approx."** in published copy. If a figure is an estimate, say "about".

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "4. Numbers", "Everything else"], "ref": "s17", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "8873c663-3967-4a15-92f2-c5e65fde3b3c", "content": "### Comparisons

"Faster than" needs a "than what". If the sentence compares to a named thing, that thing must be in the sentence. If it compares to a previous version of our own product, say which version.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "4. Numbers", "Comparisons"], "ref": "s18", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "98588c52-bb4f-4b97-8b2e-da0afede6983", "content": "## 15. Usage notes

- **a/an:** go by sound. An eBPF agent, a SOC 2 report, an SRE.
- **back end** (noun), **back-end** (adjective).
- **cyber:** avoid as a prefix. Say what kind of security you mean.
- **data** is singular in our copy: "the data is".
- **drain:** a verb in Kubernetes and in our copy. "Drained the node."
- **e.g., i.e., etc.:** write "for example", "that is", or finish the list.
- **email:** no hyphen.
- **failover** (noun), **fail over** (verb).
- **in order to:** "to".
- **log in** (verb), **login** (noun). Same pattern for **set up / setup**, **roll out / rollout**, **shut down / shutdown**.
- **real time** (noun), **real-time** (adjective).
- **sidecar, service mesh:** lowercase, one and two words.
- **startup:** one word.
- **third party** (noun), **third-party** (adjective).
- **trade-off:** hyphenated.
- **utilize:** "use".
- **very, really, extremely:** delete and reread.
- **via:** "through", unless it's a technical path.
- **zero-day:** hyphenated, and only for an actual zero-day.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "15. Usage notes"], "ref": "s19", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "a5eca255-6e97-40a8-be37-f50288aba296", "content": "### Money

- Dollars with the symbol: $18, $29. No ".00".
- Node pricing is written in full: "$18 per node per month". Not "/node/mo", not "per-node", not "$18 pnpm", which someone did actually write in a deck.
- Funding and other large sums use a capital M and no space: $46M. Don't write "$46 million" in one place and "$46M" in another; pick the M.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "4. Numbers", "Money"], "ref": "s20", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "b39ffdf9-91aa-4c47-a19d-da6e58b90e6e", "content": "## 12. Social and email formatting

- No emoji in brand posts or email. Founders can do as they like on their own accounts within reason.
- One link per post. Put it where it reads naturally; shortened links are for tracking and shouldn't appear as bare text where the full domain would fit.
- Line breaks on LinkedIn mark real paragraph breaks. No one-sentence-per-line posts.
- Greeting in email: "Hi Sam," with the first name and a comma, or no greeting for a broadcast. No "Dear". No "Hey there".
- Plain sign-off: name, job, company, or the team name on a broadcast. Nobody signs "Cheers" on a customer notice.
- In email, check that the piece reads correctly with images off.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "12. Social and email formatting"], "ref": "s21", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "b7b87728-b779-4387-aded-a12e59f856d7", "content": "## 1. Headlines

**Headlines are in sentence case.** Capitalize the first word and any proper noun. Everything else is lowercase.

This covers page titles, blog titles, section headings, email subject lines, slide titles, buttons, nav labels, form labels, table headers and any text set over an image. If it looks like a heading, it is one.

| Right | Wrong |
|---|---|
| What contain mode does to a running pod | What Contain Mode Does To A Running Pod |
| Wickhold Containment Report 2026 | WICKHOLD CONTAINMENT REPORT 2026 |
| How Ostler Grocers cut its open critical misconfigurations | How Ostler Grocers Cut Its Open Critical Misconfigurations |

Details:

- Product names, event names and the report title keep their capitals, as do Kubernetes, Helm, CVE and the rest of the proper vocabulary. `containerd` and `eBPF` keep their lowercase starts even as the first word, though it's nicer to rewrite so that neither opens a headline.
- The word after a colon is lowercase: "Drift: what it is and how to read it".
- No full stop on headlines. The tagline is the one exception, and it keeps its full stop everywhere.
- No code formatting in headlines. They break in email clients and in link previews.
- Keep a headline to one idea. If it needs a colon and a dash, it's two headlines.

The old sheet used Title Case for everything over 24px. That went in the rebrand, and pages still carrying it get fixed when someone next touches them.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "1. Headlines"], "ref": "s22", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "c1483026-3308-4a52-8cf9-e6314d11b35f", "content": "## 6. Grammar and punctuation

- **American spelling** in all copy, including copy going to UK and EU readers. Containerize, not containerise.
- **Oxford comma**, always. It has settled more than one argument in Kubernetes prose, where lists of nouns can double as lists of objects.
- **Active voice** with a named actor, wherever the actor is known. "Wickhold Quenchline drained the node." If the passive is hiding who did it and that person is us, it goes.
- **Tense.** Past for what happened, present for what the product does, and nothing in the future except where a date is public.
- **Contractions** are fine in the blog, on social and in email. Skip them on legal pages and in anything aimed at a board.
- **Colons** are our favorite punctuation mark and they're doing fine. Use them to introduce the fact.
- **Semicolons** at most once a page. If there are two, one wants to be a full stop.
- **Em dashes** rarely in body copy. Most are a full stop that lost its nerve. Spaced en dashes are not a substitute.
- **Parentheses** for the short aside only. If the aside matters, promote it to a sentence.
- **Quotation marks:** double, with commas and full stops inside, American style, except for literal strings in technical writing where the punctuation would change the meaning. Single quotes only inside double.
- **Italics:** titles of reports and the occasional stress only. They disappear on Soot grounds and in email.
- **Bold:** for scanning in long documents, once or twice per section. Bold on a landing page means the design isn't working.
- **Ampersands:** only in proper names. Plain "and" in headlines too.
- **"And/or"** is a legal term. Pick one.
- **Slashes** as a shortcut ("platform/security teams") get rewritten: "platform and security teams".

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "6. Grammar and punctuation"], "ref": "s23", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "c555aa43-f86c-4b00-af8f-ab621338c84f", "content": "## 4. Certification status

SOC 2 Type II: held. Renewed January 2026. The report is shared under NDA through the account team.

FedRAMP Moderate: in process. The approved sentence is "Wickhold is pursuing FedRAMP Moderate authorization." Never state or imply FedRAMP authorization or certification. The status sheet has the detail and is the first thing to check.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "4. Certification status"], "ref": "s24", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "c6a52d68-5c35-45b0-aceb-b1a1e1b7e799", "content": "## 17. Accepted shortcuts and exceptions

- Internal documents (including this one) don't need to meet the citation form. They do need to be right.
- Slide speaker notes follow the same rules once they go into a shared deck, since decks get forwarded.
- Quoted customer language stays as approved, including its capitalization. If a quote has a problem, go back to the customer through the customer marketing owner; don't fix it in place.
- Text inside a screenshot is not edited. If a screenshot shows something out of date, take a new one.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "17. Accepted shortcuts and exceptions"], "ref": "s25", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "ca3468d9-9da9-4734-a3d6-9c0497716473", "content": "## 5. Statistics: 12-month age limit

A market statistic may not be older than 12 months at publication. This is the limit on how old a statistic can be, and it is measured on the day the piece goes out, not the day it was drafted. A post queued in March for release in May is checked against May.

The limit applies to market and survey statistics only. It covers any figure that describes the industry, the market, or a population of teams. It does not apply to customer results such as the Lowmoor and Ostler outcomes, or to product metrics such as the lab figures, which have their own qualifier.

The age of a statistic runs from the publication date of its source. Fieldwork dates do not matter. A report re-quoted in a newer article keeps its original date, so a 2026 article quoting a 2024 survey is a 2024 statistic.

Applied to our own reports:

| Source | Published | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Wickhold Containment Report 2026 | April 14, 2026 | Usable for publication through April 14, 2027 |
| Wickhold Field Report 2024 | 2024 | Past the 12 months limit |
| Wickhold Field Report 2023 | 2023 | Past the 12 months limit |

The two Containment Report statistics in section 1 are the only market statistics of ours inside the limit today. The Field Report figures still appear in old decks and old posts. That is an archive problem and not a permission. Do not reuse them. Do not reword them to make them feel new, and do not refer to them as "historically" true.

Fresh third-party statistics are allowed without coming to me first, with the source link and the date of the source in the copy. The source must be a named publisher and the figure must appear on the page you link to. A figure found in a vendor's blog, quoting another vendor's blog, gets traced to the original or is dropped. The third party's name still has to clear the competitor rules.

When the 2027 Containment Report is published, section 1 will be updated and the 2026 figures remain usable until they reach the limit. Old assets stay in the archive as they are. They are not re-promoted once a market statistic in them has expired. Paid and email reuse counts as publication.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "5. Statistics: 12-month age limit"], "ref": "s26", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "ca8bf1aa-ced7-4c7e-871d-281a24c0f561", "content": "## 10. Links

Link text names the thing the reader will get: "the 2026 Containment Report", "the Helm values reference". The surrounding sentence should still read correctly if the link is dead. Don't link a whole sentence. Internal pages open in the same tab.

UTM parameters come from the campaign tracker, not from memory. Marketing ops reject hand-typed ones.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "10. Links"], "ref": "s27", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "cd981fdd-c863-4776-8686-3ab4cc8e9dc8", "content": "## 8. Spoken claims, demos and records

Spoken claims count. A webinar is a publication, a sales call can end up quoted in a procurement file, and a recorded conference talk stays available for years. Speakers get the same tables as writers. Questions from the floor that go beyond them are answered with "I will get back to you", and then with an email to me.

Demo environments show synthetic data. A demo may show a containment action in contain mode, and the timing shown on screen is not a claim about customer environments. Presenters should say so if anyone asks. Screenshots from a real customer tenant are not used in any circumstance.

The owner of each asset keeps the published version, or a link to it, and the source for each figure in it for three years. When a claim is withdrawn I will send a list of the assets I know about. I do not know about all of them, so owners should search their own material.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "8. Spoken claims, demos and records"], "ref": "s28", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "cefc4366-9544-4ad9-930d-06a08e27c623", "content": "### Percentages

**Percentages use digits and the % symbol.** Always, including at the start of a sentence, in headlines, in legal-reviewed copy and in speech written for a stage.

- Right: 41% of platform teams, 63% fewer open critical misconfigurations.
- Wrong: forty-one percent, 41 percent, 41 per cent, 63pc.

No space before the symbol. "Percentage points" is written out when you mean the difference between two percentages, and it's rare enough in our copy that a reviewer will ask if you're sure.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "4. Numbers", "Percentages"], "ref": "s29", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "cfd8736c-24f6-4637-a4fe-87e329a80ab5", "content": "### Wickhold Leashgate (early access)

Leashgate is in early access. Claims describe what the early access product does today. They do not describe a roadmap, and they do not give a date.

Permitted vocabulary is tool-call policy, agent identity, and the blast radius of an agent. The approved outcome statement is "limits what a compromised agent can do".

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "2. Claims that need a qualifier", "Wickhold Leashgate (early access)"], "ref": "s30", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "cff1ee61-653f-40b6-b141-8a57f205945f", "content": "### Market statistics

Name the source and the year each time. A market statistic in a headline needs its source on the same screen or page section. See section 5 for how long a statistic stays usable.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "2. Claims that need a qualifier", "Market statistics"], "ref": "s31", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "d5917474-5628-4710-bcee-8fc4d508b8f4", "content": "### Lab figures

Two product figures come from Wickhold's own lab. Both must carry the phrase "in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026", in the same sentence as the figure.

| Figure | Required form |
|---|---|
| CPU overhead | "under 2% CPU overhead on a typical node in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026" |
| Containment speed | "contains a known-bad process in a median of 38 seconds in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026" |

A footnote does not meet this requirement. An asterisk does not meet it. A qualifier on the slide before does not meet it. In a chart, the phrase goes in the chart title or directly under it. In a talk, the speaker says it aloud.

The figures describe a lab, so they may not be presented as field results or customer averages. "Known-bad process" is part of the claim: it does not extend to unknown processes, novel techniques, or "threats" in general. Reports may repeat the figures only if the benchmark year stays attached. When the 2027 benchmarks run, the year changes and this table is reissued. Nobody edits the year by hand.

Approved:

> Wickhold Quenchline adds under 2% CPU overhead on a typical node in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026.

Not approved:

> Quenchline contains attacks in 38 seconds.

> Under 2% overhead. Guaranteed.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "2. Claims that need a qualifier", "Lab figures"], "ref": "s32", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "d62a25c1-8dcf-4f5f-9fca-e5ace68eb593", "content": "### Change log

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "9. Review, exceptions, and how this document changes", "Change log"], "ref": "s33", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "dd77c0c2-9cd8-4804-84c6-5405807045df", "content": "### Customer count

The only approved claim is "more than 140 customers". The following are not approved: "140+ customers", "nearly 150 customers", "hundreds of customers", "thousands of engineers", or any count of nodes, clusters or workloads summed across the customer base. Finance reconciles the number each quarter against active contracts. Pilots, lapsed accounts, open-source users, and companies that attended Slow Burn Summit are not customers for this purpose.

When the reconciled number supports a higher claim, this document will change. Until it does, the number in a sales deck, a conference bio or a partner page is the number here. If you have seen a larger figure in circulation, it is wrong, and I would like to know where you saw it.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "1. Claims approved as written", "Customer count"], "ref": "s34", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "dde20031-29bf-4c0b-91c9-c5d802e24e23", "content": "## 2. Claims that need a qualifier

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "2. Claims that need a qualifier"], "ref": "s35", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "ea87fb35-66f8-4d07-ae6d-704ad1b44df1", "content": "## 11. Tables, charts and captions

- A table needs a header row and at least two rows of content. One row is a sentence.
- Right-align numbers in tables. Keep units in the header, not in each cell.
- A chart title states the finding in sentence case: "41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident". The axis says what was measured.
- Every chart carries its citation in the same bracket form, set small under the chart, so it survives being cropped into a slide.
- Captions are sentences. They end with a full stop and they don't begin "Figure 1 shows".
- No 3D, no donuts, and no chart for a single number. Write the number.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "11. Tables, charts and captions"], "ref": "s36", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "eef6d698-d3bd-4e2e-a928-14c6f517a9c1", "content": "## 5. Dates and times

- **Dates:** month, day, year, spelled out: April 14, 2026. No ordinals, no "14th of April".
- **Month and year:** March 2022, no comma. **Year only:** 2026.
- **Ranges:** an en dash with no spaces within a month: September 15–16. Use "to" across months: "March 30 to April 2".
- **Tables, logs, front matter:** ISO, 2026-04-14. Never slashes. 04/10 has already caused one wrong webinar invite, and that's enough.
- **Quarters:** fine internally. In public copy, name the month.
- **Avoid relative dates** in anything that stays online. "Recently", "last year", "this spring" and "soon" all rot. Write the date. Press releases and dated posts can say "today".
- **Roadmap language:** no dates, no "coming soon". Product marketing has a separate process for that.

**Times.** Incident timelines use 24-hour UTC with the zone on every line or at the top of the block: 03:14 UTC. It's how our readers' tools show it. Event and webinar times use 12-hour with the zone: 2:00 p.m. MT. In prose, "3am" with no space is fine as a phrase, and the voice document uses it constantly. It's a figure of speech and shouldn't be used for an actual appointment.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "5. Dates and times"], "ref": "s37", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "f336e33c-84c9-43ae-8e01-ca9e18cefc0a", "content": "## 7. Rulings from this year

Requests I have already answered. They are listed so that I do not answer them again.

| Request | Ruling |
|---|---|
| "Trusted by more than 140 customers" | Allowed. The count stays exact |
| "Trusted by credit unions" | Refused. One customer is not a plural |
| "Agentless" or "agent-free" for Quenchline | Refused. It uses an eBPF agent. Say so |
| "Lightweight" | Allowed only next to the CPU overhead figure and its qualifier |
| "Real-time" for Quenchline | Allowed for detection. For containment, use the lab figure or leave it out |
| "Stops the attack" | Refused. Name the containment action: isolate a pod's network, freeze a process, drain a node |
| "Automatic remediation" for Evenburn | Refused. Evenburn gives a fix order and people do the fixing |
| "AI-powered" for any product | Refused unless product confirms in writing what the model does. Writing about AI agents does not make the product AI-powered |
| "Secures your AI" or "safe AI" for Leashgate | Refused. Describe tool-call policy and agent identity |
| "SOC 2 certified" | Refused. Say "holds SOC 2 Type II" |
| "Used by your peers" in a sector email | Refused unless a named, approved customer in that sector is shown |
| "Battle-tested" | Refused. It implies a history of incidents at customers that we have not disclosed and may not disclose |

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "7. Rulings from this year"], "ref": "s38", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "f85915ac-8ed5-47a1-b0b7-df460f5be9ef", "content": "## 3. Banned claims

| Do not say | Say instead, or do this | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| "prevents prompt injection" | "limits what a compromised agent can do" | Leashgate acts on tool calls. It does not read intent and it cannot promise that an agent will not be manipulated. The claim is false as a matter of product design |
| "FedRAMP Authorized", "FedRAMP certified" | See section 4 | Neither is true |
| "GDPR compliant" | Use the regional rules | Regional wording sits there, and the ban is not limited to that region |
| "breach-proof", "unhackable", "impossible to escape" | Describe the containment action | No security product can support an absolute |
| "zero false positives", "100% detection", "catches everything" | Give a sourced figure or say nothing | We hold no such evidence |
| "guarantee", "guaranteed", "warranty" outside a contract | Remove | These words have legal effect. Service credits live in the order form |
| "the leading", "the fastest", "No. 1", "the only" | Remove, or bring me the comparison data | Superlatives need current comparative substantiation, and we do not hold any |
| "certified by", "endorsed by", "partner of" for any standards body or open-source project | Remove | Using eBPF or Helm is not an endorsement from anyone |
| "saves $X", any return-on-investment figure | Remove | We have no approved financial outcome for any customer |

Two refinements, because they keep coming back:

"Helps prevent" is a banned claim dressed up. A qualifier in front of a promise does not make it a limited promise.

"Compliance-ready" and "audit-ready" were requested in June for a trust page and refused. Wickhold can describe what the product records. Whether a customer passes an audit depends on the customer and the auditor.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "3. Banned claims"], "ref": "s39", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "f9008b51-bf82-4c69-90da-d9e64bb8490d", "content": "## 8. Technical writing in marketing copy

Kofi Anselm's team reviews anything containing code, and their rules are short.

- **Code formatting** for commands, flags, file names, field names, namespaces, node names and anything a person might type: `kubectl get pods`, `--namespace`, `values.yaml`.
- **Every snippet is run before it's published.** Say which version it was run against. A snippet nobody ran does not go out, even in a slide.
- **Placeholder values** look like placeholders or like real workloads: `payments`, `checkout`, `worker-7`. Don't use `foo`, and don't use the name of a real company, a real customer or a celebrity.
- **Domains and email addresses in examples** use `wickhold.example`.
- **Long output** gets trimmed, with a line saying so. Don't silently edit output.
- **Failure modes** are part of the example. If a command fails in a common way, say how it looks.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "8. Technical writing in marketing copy"], "ref": "s40", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "f9297cda-c4e2-4687-81ea-30232d69aa3f", "content": "## 4. Numbers

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "4. Numbers"], "ref": "s41", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "26f9f996-cd6d-4ef6-b3b8-972d1bd0c6c0", "content": "## 6. Review

| Step | Who | When |
|---|---|---|
| Outline | Editor (Kofi for engineering posts, Noor for the rest) | Before anyone writes 1,000 words |
| Technical read | An engineer who did not write it | Draft complete |
| Copy edit | Brand team | After the technical read |
| Claims check | Priit, for any customer, certification or number, except third-party statistics under section 5 of the approved claims | As the approved claims set out |
| Paste test | Second engineer, code posts only | Day before publish |

Allow two weeks from outline to publish. Report posts in April move faster because Legal has already checked the numbers.

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "6. Review"], "ref": "s42", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "2dfe4ee1-b5b7-475f-aa8a-47e4ee921cb3", "content": "## 1. Length

Blog posts run 900 to 1,400 words. That range counts the body, including captions and code comments you wrote yourself, but not the code output you pasted.

Under 900 words, it's probably a release note or a LinkedIn post. Over 1,400 words, split it in two or cut the history section. We all write the history section first because it's easy, and nobody needs it. The report, the docs and the rollout guide are the place for anything longer.

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "1. Length"], "ref": "s43", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "376c8b2d-e153-46d4-9868-97f9e1c51b3a", "content": "## 3. Post types

**Engineering posts.** Written by Dov, Kofi or an engineer with an editor attached. How the eBPF agent attaches, what we learned from a kernel upgrade, why a containment action took longer than it should have. These carry the blog.

**How-to posts.** A task, steps, and what it looks like when it goes wrong: rolling out contain mode, reading an exposure path, writing a first tool-call policy for Leashgate in early access.

**Report posts.** One finding from the Containment Report, argued properly. We get four or five out of each report. Do not summarize the whole report in one post. That's what the report page does.

**Customer posts.** Built from a published case study, with the customer's own words where we have approval. These need Priit's sign-off every time, even when the numbers are already public.

**Founder posts.** Maren, on company decisions and what she learned from them. They're rare and marketing does not ghostwrite them. An editor can tidy.

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "3. Post types"], "ref": "s44", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "43519095-47d5-42a8-b0b4-9efdf2334158", "content": "# Writing for the Wickhold blog

*Kofi Anselm wrote the first version in May 2026 for the two contractors we brought in after the Containment Report. Noor edited it in July. Send fixes to either of us.*

The blog has one job: get a platform engineer or a security lead to trust that the people here have held the pager. Traffic is a side effect. A post that gets a staff engineer to forward it to their team beats a post that ranks for a keyword and gets skimmed.

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog"], "ref": "s45", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "4a8bc433-313b-48fe-81f1-b9d8798bc8a8", "content": "## 7. Publishing details

- URL slug: lowercase, under 60 characters, no dates.
- Meta description: one plain sentence, under 155 characters.
- Author byline is always a real person. We retired "The Wickhold Team" as a byline in 2025 when we noticed those posts got half the reads.
- Hero images come from the design team. Send the request with your outline, not the day before.
- Tuesdays and Wednesdays. Never the same day as a release note, since they compete in the newsletter.

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "7. Publishing details"], "ref": "s46", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "4cb61d28-8600-42a9-b770-bac22ceba88f", "content": "## 8. Working with engineers who don't want to write

Most of our best material is in the heads of people who would rather fix a kernel bug. Don't send them a blank doc. Book 30 minutes, ask them to walk you through the last hard thing they fixed, and record it with their permission. Write the draft from the recording and send it back for correction. An engineer who won't write 1,000 words will happily rewrite the 200 you got wrong.

Keep their phrasing where you can. If someone says the agent "falls over politely" on a read-only kernel, that goes in. Their name goes on the post, and they read the final version before it goes live. If they ask to take something out, take it out, and don't argue about it in the review thread.

Questions that tend to produce a post:

- What did you assume about this before you got paged?
- What's the command you wish you had run first?
- What does the failure look like from the outside?
- What did you change afterward, and did it hold?

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "8. Working with engineers who don't want to write"], "ref": "s47", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "6fabfd1d-c817-4def-a0d5-bc9821112094", "content": "## 4. Shape of a post

A title that says what the reader will get. Then the intro. Then three to five sections with descriptive headings. Then an ending that tells the reader what to do on Monday.

Titles we liked:

- Contain mode, one namespace at a time
- What drift looks like after a Helm upgrade
- The six hours after detection
- Writing your first tool-call policy for Wickhold Leashgate, in early access

Titles we rewrote:

- "5 Kubernetes Security Mistakes You're Making Right Now" became "Five findings we see in most new clusters"
- "Everything You Need To Know About eBPF" became "What our eBPF agent can and can't see"

Section headings should still make sense if they're all someone reads. "Background" and "The solution" tell the reader nothing.

End on the practical next step, then one call to action to the most relevant page. Don't summarize what you just said. If the post was good, they remember. Don't add a paragraph about Wickhold at the bottom either, as the footer handles that.

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "4. Shape of a post"], "ref": "s48", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "95a3bc17-3a62-42aa-bb1c-70545612062c", "content": "## 5. Code and commands

- Every code block must run. An engineer other than the author pastes it into a test cluster before publishing. Kofi keeps a throwaway cluster for this and will give you access.
- State versions at the top of the block or in the sentence before it: Kubernetes, Helm chart, kernel where it matters.
- Show the output when the output is the point, and trim it with a visible `...`.
- Use real-looking names like `payments-api` and `checkout`. Avoid `foo` and `my-app`, and don't use a customer's actual namespace names, even with permission.
- Say what fails. If `helm upgrade` can leave the agent in `CrashLoopBackOff` on an old kernel, put that in the post.

```bash
# Good: what you ran, and what to look for
kubectl get pods -n payments-api -o wide
# ...
# payments-api-6f9c7d   0/1   Terminating   0   3m   10.2.4.17   node-a
# A pod stuck here after a drain usually has a finalizer. Check that first.
```

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "5. Code and commands"], "ref": "s49", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "9792dec6-922e-42ef-aded-9a7b0bc70f03", "content": "## 2. The intro

A blog intro must cite a market statistic. Put it in the first two sentences, in the citation format from the style guide, and follow it with one sentence that says why this post exists. The rule is there because engineers are more willing to keep reading once they know the problem is measured and someone has measured it honestly.

Statistics are subject to the age limit in the approved claims, so check the date before you reuse an intro from an older post.

Market statistics are figures about the market or a surveyed population. Our own customer results and benchmark numbers belong further down the post, and they don't satisfy this requirement.

Good:

> The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. Most of the teams we talk to can tell you how long detection took. Far fewer can tell you what happened in the hours after. This post is about those hours.

Good:

> 41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. A lot of that time goes to one question: who is allowed to touch the workload? Here is how to settle that question before the page goes off.

Bad, because it has no statistic and no reason to read on:

> Kubernetes has changed how modern teams ship software, and with that change come new security challenges.

Bad, because a customer result is doing the job of a market statistic:

> Lowmoor Credit Union cut time to contain from 4 hours to 11 minutes. Here's how your team can get the same results.

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "2. The intro"], "ref": "s50", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "b0b53749-5be6-4308-8b5a-8b34e65f5020", "content": "## 10. Tried and dropped

Guest posts from partners took more editing than writing one ourselves, and the partners wanted a link in every paragraph. Weekly "news roundups" lasted nine weeks in 2025 and nobody missed them. Keyword-led briefs from an agency produced the "Everything You Need To Know" titles above, and we stopped that contract in the spring.
", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "10. Tried and dropped"], "ref": "s51", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "cde0d081-7f1e-4ee9-a5cb-3a4e3d01ea38", "content": "## 9. Updating old posts

Older posts stay up, but they can mislead. The brand team runs through the top 30 posts by traffic every quarter. Each gets one of three outcomes: leave it, edit it in place with an "Updated" date at the top, or redirect it to a newer post.
