", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "Reading old copy"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s189", "content": "## 5. Statistics: 12-month age limit

A market statistic may not be older than 12 months at publication. This is the limit on how old a statistic can be, and it is measured on the day the piece goes out, not the day it was drafted. A post queued in March for release in May is checked against May.

The limit applies to market and survey statistics only. It covers any figure that describes the industry, the market, or a population of teams. It does not apply to customer results such as the Lowmoor and Ostler outcomes, or to product metrics such as the lab figures, which have their own qualifier.

The age of a statistic runs from the publication date of its source. Fieldwork dates do not matter. A report re-quoted in a newer article keeps its original date, so a 2026 article quoting a 2024 survey is a 2024 statistic.

Applied to our own reports:

| Source | Published | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Wickhold Containment Report 2026 | April 14, 2026 | Usable for publication through April 14, 2027 |
| Wickhold Field Report 2024 | 2024 | Past the 12 months limit |
| Wickhold Field Report 2023 | 2023 | Past the 12 months limit |

The two Containment Report statistics in section 1 are the only market statistics of ours inside the limit today. The Field Report figures still appear in old decks and old posts. That is an archive problem and not a permission. Do not reuse them. Do not reword them to make them feel new, and do not refer to them as "historically" true.

Fresh third-party statistics are allowed without coming to me first, with the source link and the date of the source in the copy. The source must be a named publisher and the figure must appear on the page you link to. A figure found in a vendor's blog, quoting another vendor's blog, gets traced to the original or is dropped. The third party's name still has to clear the competitor rules.

When the 2027 Containment Report is published, section 1 will be updated and the 2026 figures remain usable until they reach the limit. Old assets stay in the archive as they are. They are not re-promoted once a market statistic in them has expired. Paid and email reuse counts as publication.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "5. Statistics: 12-month age limit"], "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s190", "content": "## Regional rules: EU and UK copy

Priit Salonen, with notes from the field marketing review, August 2026

Applies to anything aimed at readers in the EU or the UK: campaigns, event pages, email sends, localized landing pages, press outreach, partner co-marketing. If a global asset will run in those regions, it is regional copy too.

", "heading_path": ["Regional rules: EU and UK copy"], "relative_path": "brand/legal/regional-rules-eu-uk.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s191", "content": "## CTA format for all channels

This lives here because the email team wrote it down first, and it now applies to every channel: email, landing pages, paid, social, the blog, event pages.

A CTA, the call to action on a button or a link, is at most four words, and it starts with a verb. The same CTA wording rules apply wherever the button sits. "Learn more" and "Click here" are banned everywhere, including as link text inside a sentence.

| Fine | Not fine |
|---|---|
| Read the report | Learn more |
| Book a demo | Click here |
| See the rollout guide | Click here to see the rollout guide |
| Request early access | Early access request |
| Save your seat | Your seat is waiting for you |

Say what happens on the other side of the click. "Get started" is allowed but weak, so use something more specific if you can.

", "heading_path": ["Email templates", "CTA format for all channels"], "relative_path": "brand/templates/email-templates.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s192", "content": "## 10. Links

Link text names the thing the reader will get: "the 2026 Containment Report", "the Helm values reference". The surrounding sentence should still read correctly if the link is dead. Don't link a whole sentence. Internal pages open in the same tab.

UTM parameters come from the campaign tracker, not from memory. Marketing ops reject hand-typed ones.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "10. Links"], "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s193", "content": "## Not cleared

**Vaskell Health is not cleared.** Do not use the name, logo, people, quotes or results in anything external, and do not use them in a customer-facing deck. "A large health system" does not help, because the draft material is specific enough to identify them. The draft case study in the folder stays a draft. No approval was given, and a finished-looking layout does not change that.

Everyone else is not cleared by default. Companies seen in a contract, in a support ticket, or in a Slow Burn Summit attendee list are not references.

", "heading_path": ["Customer logo and quote policy", "Not cleared"], "relative_path": "brand/legal/customer-logo-and-quote-policy.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s194", "content": "## The character

Wickhold is someone who has been paged more often than you have and is not going to bring it up.

**Unhurried.** Nothing in our copy is urgent. A page that hurries the reader is using the same trick as the alert fatigue they came to us to get away from.

**Exact.** "Isolated the pod's network" beats "took action". "220 nodes" beats "at scale". If two engineers would argue over what a sentence means, it isn't finished.

**Unimpressed by itself.** The product is useful. Copy that gasps at it reads as though the writer has not seen it fail. We have seen it fail, and the release notes say so.

**On your side of the pager.** The reader is a peer on the same rota, and we write to them as someone who could take the next shift. No lecturing, no "did you know", no explaining Kubernetes to people who run it.

When the character slips, it usually slips into one of four people:

- **The hero.** Rushes in, saves the day, gets the credit. Early rebrand drafts leaned on firefighters and helmets until Maren pointed out that a firefighter arriving means it already went badly. The customer's on-call team is the competent party in every story we tell.
- **The prophet.** Sees doom everywhere and sells shelter from it. The whole security industry's default register, which makes it invisible to the people we want to reach.
- **The buddy.** "Hey there, Kubernetes friends." Nobody paged at 3am wants a pal.
- **The analyst.** "In today's rapidly evolving threat landscape." Sentences with no one in them. If nothing would change when the paragraph is deleted, delete it.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "The character"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s195", "content": "### Raising a conflict

If two documents disagree, don't quietly pick one and move on, because the next person will hit the same thing. Follow the order of authority for the piece in hand, ship it, and then send a short note to the owner of the lower document.

A useful note says three things and takes a minute to write:

> "These two documents give different answers on the same point. I used the higher one. Can the other be updated?"

The owner corrects the lower document or explains why it stands. If the higher document is the one that's out of date, the owner of that document changes it. Nobody overrides it locally.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "11. Governance", "Raising a conflict"], "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s196", "content": "## 8. Spoken claims, demos and records

Spoken claims count. A webinar is a publication, a sales call can end up quoted in a procurement file, and a recorded conference talk stays available for years. Speakers get the same tables as writers. Questions from the floor that go beyond them are answered with "I will get back to you", and then with an email to me.

Demo environments show synthetic data. A demo may show a containment action in contain mode, and the timing shown on screen is not a claim about customer environments. Presenters should say so if anyone asks. Screenshots from a real customer tenant are not used in any circumstance.

The owner of each asset keeps the published version, or a link to it, and the source for each figure in it for three years. When a claim is withdrawn I will send a list of the assets I know about. I do not know about all of them, so owners should search their own material.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "8. Spoken claims, demos and records"], "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s197", "content": "## 9. Updating old posts

Older posts stay up, but they can mislead. The brand team runs through the top 30 posts by traffic every quarter. Each gets one of three outcomes: leave it, edit it in place with an "Updated" date at the top, or redirect it to a newer post.

Edit in place when a product name, a command or a figure has gone out of date. Redirect when the advice has changed. Never quietly change a claim. If a post said something that turned out to be wrong, add a line saying what changed and when. Engineers notice, and they remember how you handled it.

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "9. Updating old posts"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s198", "content": "### Product imagery

Screenshots and diagrams show the real product and real terms. When a choice exists between a clever visual metaphor and a clear view of what the product did, show the product.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "9. Photography and illustration direction", "Product imagery"], "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s199", "content": "### Percentages

**Percentages use digits and the % symbol.** Always, including at the start of a sentence, in headlines, in legal-reviewed copy and in speech written for a stage.

- Right: 41% of platform teams, 63% fewer open critical misconfigurations.
- Wrong: forty-one percent, 41 percent, 41 per cent, 63pc.

No space before the symbol. "Percentage points" is written out when you mean the difference between two percentages, and it's rare enough in our copy that a reviewer will ask if you're sure.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "4. Numbers", "Percentages"], "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s200", "content": "## Spec

**600px wide. No text in the image.**

The file itself is 600px wide. We tried a 1200px source scaled down in the HTML, and a couple of older desktop mail apps rendered it at full width and broke the layout. So: exactly 600, height between 150 and 240, under 150 KB.

No text means none, and it is stricter than other placements that allow overlay set in design. A large share of readers load email with images off, and headers get blocked first. If the headline is in the picture, those readers get an empty box. Headlines, dates and CTAs go in live HTML. A header image that says "Slow Burn Summit" in type is out, even when a designer set it properly and even if the art is otherwise approved. Put the event name in the first line of the HTML.

That also rules out the social templates, which all carry type, and charts, which need labels.

", "heading_path": ["Email header images", "Spec"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/email-header.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s201", "content": "### Wickhold Leashgate (early access)

Leashgate is in early access. Claims describe what the early access product does today. They do not describe a roadmap, and they do not give a date.

Permitted vocabulary is tool-call policy, agent identity, and the blast radius of an agent. The approved outcome statement is "limits what a compromised agent can do".

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "2. Claims that need a qualifier", "Wickhold Leashgate (early access)"], "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s202", "content": "### Market statistics

Name the source and the year each time. A market statistic in a headline needs its source on the same screen or page section. See section 5 for how long a statistic stays usable.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "2. Claims that need a qualifier", "Market statistics"], "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s203", "content": "## Anonymous examples

An unnamed customer story needs the same evidence as a named one and Legal's review of the wording. Keep the sector broad and leave out numbers that could be traced. Do not invent a composite customer.

", "heading_path": ["Customer logo and quote policy", "Anonymous examples"], "relative_path": "brand/legal/customer-logo-and-quote-policy.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s204", "content": "### Why the company rebranded

The 2024 brand made a promise about watching. It suited a company that sold visibility, and it stopped fitting as the product moved on. By 2025 the feature customers talked about in renewals was the moment Wickhold Quenchline isolated a pod's network at 3am and nobody had to get out of bed. Sales calls kept going the same way: the prospect would say every tool they owned could see a problem, and then ask what happens next.

Ilse Varga-Holm, who owns the rebrand, started the work in spring 2025 with a set of about 30 customer and on-call interviews. Maren Tolliver and Dov Achterberg sat in on most of them. The clearest finding was that nobody wanted another thing watching them. They wanted the blast of an incident to be smaller and the morning after to be shorter. That finding drove every decision below.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "1. What changed in 2026", "Why the company rebranded"], "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s205", "content": "## Transparency and dark mode

Do not use transparent PNGs in email headers. Spot illustrations and other `background: transparent` files are out here, whatever their `safe_on` says. Several mail apps darken the message in dark mode, and they do it unevenly: some swap the ground and leave images alone, and some invert parts of both. A flat ground inside the image keeps the header predictable. Always send a `solid` or `scene` image.

The wordmark sits in its own table cell above the header image, as a panel variant, with alt text. Do not bake the logo into the header picture, since the header is blocked more often than a small logo and you lose the sender's identity with it.

", "heading_path": ["Email header images", "Transparency and dark mode"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/email-header.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s206", "content": "## Lists and segments

| Segment | Who | Tone in one line | Usual sends |
|---|---|---|---|
| Platform | Platform engineers, SREs, DevSecOps | Practical, can carry code | Newsletter, platform nurture, product announcements |
| Security leadership | CISOs, security directors | Short and plain | CISO nurture, report, Summit invite |
| Customers, technical | Named admins and on-call contacts | Facts and steps | Product announcements, customer notices |
| Customers, executive | Sponsors on the account | Short, rarely | Founder notes, Summit invite |
| Event-local | Contacts within driving distance of a Field Day | Friendly, practical | Field Day invite and reminder |

Role tags come from enrichment and are wrong about one time in ten. If a reply says "I'm not a CISO", fix the contact on the day. Never merge the platform and security leadership lists to reach a volume target. We did that for the 2025 report and the CISO list's unsubscribe rate doubled in a single send.

", "heading_path": ["Email playbook", "Lists and segments"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s207", "content": "### Mistakes seen since launch

The single most common mistake since launch is treating Ember as the "main" color because the table calls it primary. Primary means most important, and it does not mean most area.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "7. Color", "Mistakes seen since launch"], "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s208", "content": "## Size and crop

Export at 1600x900. Most library heroes and photos are 3:2, so you will lose some height. Crop from the top and bottom, then check that the focal point has survived. A hero illustration's focal element usually sits off center and the quiet part can go. Some platforms crop preview cards further, so keep the focal point out of the outer tenth of the frame.

Do not upscale. A 1536-wide source enlarged to 1600 is about the limit, and it should look clean at full size.

", "heading_path": ["Blog hero images", "Size and crop"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/blog-hero.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s209", "content": "### Lab figures

Two product figures come from Wickhold's own lab. Both must carry the phrase "in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026", in the same sentence as the figure.

| Figure | Required form |
|---|---|
| CPU overhead | "under 2% CPU overhead on a typical node in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026" |
| Containment speed | "contains a known-bad process in a median of 38 seconds in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026" |

A footnote does not meet this requirement. An asterisk does not meet it. A qualifier on the slide before does not meet it. In a chart, the phrase goes in the chart title or directly under it. In a talk, the speaker says it aloud.

The figures describe a lab, so they may not be presented as field results or customer averages. "Known-bad process" is part of the claim: it does not extend to unknown processes, novel techniques, or "threats" in general. Reports may repeat the figures only if the benchmark year stays attached. When the 2027 benchmarks run, the year changes and this table is reissued. Nobody edits the year by hand.

Approved:

> Wickhold Quenchline adds under 2% CPU overhead on a typical node in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026.

Not approved:

> Quenchline contains attacks in 38 seconds.

> Under 2% overhead. Guaranteed.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "2. Claims that need a qualifier", "Lab figures"], "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s210", "content": "## Legal pages carry no people

Terms, privacy, subprocessors, the DPA page, and the like: no people in any image on these pages. That covers portraits, illustrated silhouettes, hands in a shot and a team in the footer strip. The same applies to the legal section of any combined page.

This is where the two audiences differ most. For engineers, show the thing itself. A short command block costs few words and earns more trust than a paragraph:

> **Install in observe mode**
> `helm install quenchline wickhold/quenchline --set agent.mode=observe`
> The agent attaches to each node. Nothing is contained until you change the mode.

For security leaders, give steps in terms of time and ownership:

> **Week one:** Quenchline runs in observe mode on one cluster.
> **Weeks two to four:** Your team reviews what it would have done.
> **After week four:** You decide which namespaces move to contain mode.

Both describe the same rollout. Neither should use a diagram that needs a paragraph to explain it.

", "heading_path": ["Landing pages", "How-it-works blocks"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/landing-page-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s214", "content": "## Further down the page

Sections below the hero have more room. Spot illustrations work in feature rows. Check each section's ground, since landing pages usually alternate Tallow and Soot bands, and a `safe_on: light` file dropped in a Soot band disappears. Nav and footer logos need checking band by band as well.

Screenshots in the body can run larger and carry callouts. Keep one image per section at most.

Customer logo strips: only what Legal has approved, and no more than the approved set, even when a strip looks empty. Keep them in one tone. Do not recolor logos in Ember.

Quote portraits go through the people and consent check first.

", "heading_path": ["Landing page imagery", "Further down the page"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/landing-page-imagery.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s215", "content": "## Build and review

1. Brief, with Noor's OK on audience and goal.
2. Copy in a shared doc with a word count at the top. Over 500 goes back.
3. Claims check by Priit, with sources pasted next to each claim.
4. Design and build. Web team needs five business days for a new layout and two for an existing one.
5. Staging review on a phone first. Most paid traffic arrives there.
6. Launch, then a check at two weeks: is anyone completing the form, and where do they drop off?

Use the existing layouts when you can. We have three (product, campaign and report) and each has been tested for load speed and for the mobile form. A page built from scratch needs a reason, and "it's a special campaign" isn't one.

", "heading_path": ["Landing pages", "Build and review"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/landing-page-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s216", "content": "## Timing against the event calendar

Dated images age badly. A card that names a date comes down from the scheduled queue the moment the date moves. After the event, do not reuse it. Set `restrictions` on the record when you file it, as with any time-limited card.

Hero image under 250 KB on the wire. Serve WebP with sizes set, and do not lazy-load the hero. SVG for logos and icons. Everything below the fold lazy-loads. A slow page is a credibility problem for a company that sells to platform engineers, and they will open dev tools.

", "heading_path": ["Landing page imagery", "Performance"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/landing-page-imagery.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s220", "content": "### Containment is the whole argument

Something will get through. Every serious engineer already knows this, and the companies who claim otherwise are talking to someone else. Wickhold's position is that the useful question is how far a failure gets and how fast it stops spreading. The whole product line follows from that, and so does most of our vocabulary. If a draft reads as though nothing bad will ever happen to the customer, it's arguing for a different company.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "What Wickhold believes", "Containment is the whole argument"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s221", "content": "## T8d. Deprecation notice

**Subject:** {{feature}} ends on {{date}}
**Preheader:** What's changing, who is affected and how to move before then.

Hi {{first_name}},

On {{date}} we're removing {{feature}} from {{product}}.

**Who is affected.** Clusters running {{condition}}.

**What to do.** {{numbered_steps}}

**What happens if you don't.** {{plain_failure_mode}}

Reply to this email if the date doesn't work for your change window, and we'll talk.

**[Read the migration guide]**

The Wickhold team

No image contains text produced by an image model or baked into artwork by a tool that does not treat it as live type. Models misspell product names, invent letterforms and produce near-English that survives one quick look and then gets screenshotted by a customer. We had a test hero in spring where a wall sign read almost like "Quenchline". Nobody caught it until it was in a review deck.

Text in a Wickhold image is set by a person, in the design tool, in the brand typefaces, as a separate layer over finished art. That covers overlays, labels, chart annotations and callouts.

Three things do not count as generated text:

- Words that are really in the scene: a printed rack label, a whiteboard someone wrote on, a door sign. Check that they say nothing embarrassing and name nobody outside the company.
- Real interface text in a true product screenshot.
- The wordmark, which is a vector file, placed by a person.

Some placements allow no overlay at all and others cap it. The content-type page has the number.

", "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "The two rules that come up every week", "No generated text in any image"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s223", "content": "### Tagline

The current tagline is **Small fires stay small.**

It is written with sentence case and a full stop, and the full stop is part of it. Do not vary it, translate it into a campaign pun, or extend it with a second clause. It can stand alone under the logo, close a piece, or sit at the end of a deck. It does not need to appear in every piece, and one use per piece is the limit.

The retired 2024 tagline should not appear in anything new, including "then and now" pieces, without a request to Brand.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "4. Positioning", "Tagline"], "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s224", "content": "## Asking for something new

If the library has nothing suitable, do not borrow from the web, do not pull an image from a past deck, and do not take it from a teammate's desktop. Files outside the library have no record and nobody can check their rights.

Requests go to the brand designers through the design queue with the placement, the deadline and one sentence on what the image should show. Allow five working days for illustration and more for photography that needs a shoot. Anything made for you gets a metadata record before it ships.

", "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "Asking for something new"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s225", "content": "### Customer count

The only approved claim is "more than 140 customers". The following are not approved: "140+ customers", "nearly 150 customers", "hundreds of customers", "thousands of engineers", or any count of nodes, clusters or workloads summed across the customer base. Finance reconciles the number each quarter against active contracts. Pilots, lapsed accounts, open-source users, and companies that attended Slow Burn Summit are not customers for this purpose.

When the reconciled number supports a higher claim, this document will change. Until it does, the number in a sales deck, a conference bio or a partner page is the number here. If you have seen a larger figure in circulation, it is wrong, and I would like to know where you saw it.

Anything superseded is meant to move to the archive, and in practice that lags. Brand reviews every new image and every first use of a library image in paid, press and homepage work. Anything else can ship on the owner's own check against this page, and Brand samples it monthly. Pull anything that fails the sample, even if it has already gone out.

Legal review is separate. It looks at claims, customer marks and consent. A pass from Legal is not a pass from Brand, and the other way around.
", "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "Review"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s230", "content": "## Format

- A LinkedIn post is 180 words at most. Count everything, including the link line.
- About the first 200 characters show before the "see more" cut on most phones. The news has to fit in that space.
- Short paragraphs, one to three lines each, with a blank line between them.
- One link per post, at the end, on its own line. We tested putting links in the first comment for six weeks in 2025 and could not see a difference, and it annoyed people, so links stay in the post.
- Tag a customer only after their marketing contact has seen the post. Tag people, not company pages, when a named person spoke or wrote the thing.
- Use bullets only for real lists: three containment actions, the tiers, the steps of a rollout. A post that is all bullets reads as a slide.
- Image guidance sits with the visual rules. Every company page post gets one image, except short hiring notes.

", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Format"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s231", "content": "## T7. Nurture, CISO track, first email

**Preheader:** The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours.

Hi {{first_name}},

The decision for you is whether your team measures how long it takes to contain a runtime incident, and who owns that number. You will be asked for it. In our survey of 412 platform and security leaders, the median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].

**[Read the report]**

The Wickhold team

Each page needs its own preview image, built from the hero crop. A preview with a product crop needs a larger, simpler view of the same action. Paid campaign pages should reuse the same hero as the ad, so that the click feels continuous.

Region-specific pages use the same imagery unless Legal says otherwise. Do not localize by swapping in a landmark photo.

The values are also used by the people team, so marketing should not rephrase them. Quote them exactly as they appear here, in this order, with the full stop after each one. They are short sentences, so treat them as sentences.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "3. Values", "How the values show up in hiring and reviews"], "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s234", "content": "### `restrictions`: check it before every use

Read `restrictions` before you use an image, every time, including images you have used before. Restrictions are added after an image enters the library, so last quarter's check does not count.

The field is free text, written by whoever had the reason. There is no fixed vocabulary, so read the sentence instead of searching for a keyword. Three kinds of note turn up in practice:

- **Retirement.** The image is deprecated and must not be used. Some retired files look entirely normal in the grid and carry no other sign. Their tags and titles may even look current.
- **A limited context.** The image may be used in the named context and nowhere else. A note limiting an image to internal use keeps it out of anything a customer, a prospect or the press will see, and that includes sales decks.
- **A person or place.** Something about who or what is shown has changed.

A restriction binds even when the image would be perfect, when a senior person asks for it, and when you found it already published somewhere. If you think one is out of date, ask Brand to change the record. Do not use the image and sort it out later.

An empty `restrictions` field means nobody has recorded a limit. It does not mean the image is on brand. The field is one check among several, and the current-identity rule above still has to pass on your own judgment.

If `restrictions` and `tags` seem to disagree, `restrictions` wins. If `restrictions` and `description` disagree, stop and ask.

", "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "The image library and its metadata", "restrictions: check it before every use"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s235", "content": "### Worked examples

**Two limits for the same channel.** A general voice document gives one length for a channel and that channel's playbook gives another. The playbook wins, because it sits higher in the list. Use its number, and tell Noor so the other one gets fixed.

**A claim in a deck.** A slide says something about the company that the approved claims do not support. The approved claims win, however recent or confident the slide looks, and however often the line has been used in the field. Sales material is not a source for a claim.

**Copy in this document versus Legal.** If a sentence in these guidelines turns out to conflict with the approved claims, Legal wins, and the guidelines get corrected.

**An old-looking rule with no rival.** A meeting note from the Q2 brand review covers something that the relevant playbook doesn't mention. Nothing conflicts, so the note stands.

**A file that says it's the latest.** File names, version numbers and words like FINAL or CURRENT decide nothing. Neither does the date on a file, on its own. Use this list.

**No source answers the question.** Ask the owner listed below. Do not fill the gap from the 2024 material or from what a competitor does. If the question is likely to come up again, the answer gets written down in the right document.

**Sources at the same level disagree.** Two channel playbooks can conflict on a shared element, such as a campaign running on both email and a landing page. Each playbook governs its own channel. If that doesn't settle it, Noor decides and the decision gets recorded.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "11. Governance", "Worked examples"], "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s236", "content": "## 11. Tables, charts and captions

- A table needs a header row and at least two rows of content. One row is a sentence.
- Right-align numbers in tables. Keep units in the header, not in each cell.
- A chart title states the finding in sentence case: "41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident". The axis says what was measured.
- Every chart carries its citation in the same bracket form, set small under the chart, so it survives being cropped into a slide.
- Captions are sentences. They end with a full stop and they don't begin "Figure 1 shows".
- No 3D, no donuts, and no chart for a single number. Write the number.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "11. Tables, charts and captions"], "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s237", "content": "### The market problem

The strongest evidence for this position comes from Wickhold's own research. The Wickhold Containment Report 2026, published April 14, 2026, surveyed 412 platform and security leaders. It found that "41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident" and that "the median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours" [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].

The gap those numbers describe is between finding something and doing something about it. Detection has become cheap and common. Containment still depends on a person with enough access waking up, reading the alert, deciding, and acting. Wickhold's position lives in those hours.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "4. Positioning", "The market problem"], "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s238", "content": "## T6. Nurture, platform track, first email

Owner: lifecycle. Trigger: report download by a contact tagged platform.

**Subject:** A first namespace in contain mode
**Preheader:** Start in observe mode on one namespace. The guide takes about an hour.

Hi {{first_name}},

You read the Containment Report, so here's the practical follow-up.

Our rollout guide starts Wickhold Quenchline in observe mode on one namespace. After two to four weeks you'll see what it would have done. Then you move that namespace to contain mode, with one containment action turned on.

Most of the guide is flags and failure modes. It also covers what to do if the agent can't attach on an old kernel.

**[See the rollout guide]**

The Wickhold team

", "heading_path": ["Email templates", "T6. Nurture, platform track, first email"], "relative_path": "brand/templates/email-templates.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s239", "content": "## Not banned, but expect a comment

Reviewers will ask about these. Sometimes the word survives.

- **solution.** Name the product, or say what it does. The word exists to avoid doing either.
- **visibility.** Seeing isn't the job. If the sentence ends at seeing, ask what happens next.
- **real-time.** Fine with a number next to it. Without one it means nothing.
- **AI-powered.** Tells the reader how something was built and nothing about what it does.
- **comprehensive.** Usually untrue, and a reader will go looking for the gap.
- **threat landscape.** A landscape has no one in it. Say which failure you mean.
- **peace of mind.** Nobody on a rota has ever had this.
- **modern.** Compared with what? Say which setup you mean.
- **mission-critical.** To the person on call, everything is.

", "heading_path": ["Word list", "Not banned, but expect a comment"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/word-list.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s240", "content": "## Review

Every landing page hero is a first use for that page and goes through Brand. Paid landing pages also go to Legal for the claims on the page, and the image goes along with them, because a screenshot can make a claim too.

Allow two working days for Brand. Campaign deadlines are not exempt, so book it when the page is scoped.
", "heading_path": ["Landing page imagery", "Review"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/landing-page-imagery.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s241", "content": "## 5. Dates and times

- **Dates:** month, day, year, spelled out: April 14, 2026. No ordinals, no "14th of April".
- **Month and year:** March 2022, no comma. **Year only:** 2026.
- **Ranges:** an en dash with no spaces within a month: September 15–16. Use "to" across months: "March 30 to April 2".
- **Tables, logs, front matter:** ISO, 2026-04-14. Never slashes. 04/10 has already caused one wrong webinar invite, and that's enough.
- **Quarters:** fine internally. In public copy, name the month.
- **Avoid relative dates** in anything that stays online. "Recently", "last year", "this spring" and "soon" all rot. Write the date. Press releases and dated posts can say "today".
- **Roadmap language:** no dates, no "coming soon". Product marketing has a separate process for that.

**Times.** Incident timelines use 24-hour UTC with the zone on every line or at the top of the block: 03:14 UTC. It's how our readers' tools show it. Event and webinar times use 12-hour with the zone: 2:00 p.m. MT. In prose, "3am" with no space is fine as a phrase, and the voice document uses it constantly. It's a figure of speech and shouldn't be used for an actual appointment.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "5. Dates and times"], "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s242", "content": "## Who posts

**Company page.** Marketing runs it. Two or three posts a week, Tuesday to Thursday, usually mid-morning Mountain time. Fridays stayed on the calendar through most of 2025 and did nothing, so they came off.

**Maren and Dov.** They post from their own profiles when they have something to say. Marketing can draft, but they rewrite. Do not schedule on their behalf without a yes in writing, and do not reply to comments as them. If a draft of Maren's has been sitting for two weeks, drop it. She has decided.

**Kofi and the DevRel team.** Kofi posts from his own profile about conference talks, open-source eBPF work and whatever broke in the demo cluster. He does not need brand review for those unless a post carries a customer name, a product claim or a number.

**Everyone else.** People can share company posts however they like. We ran an employee amplification program in 2025 with a shared doc of suggested captions. Forty people posted the same sentence on the same morning and it looked exactly like that. We stopped.

", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Who posts"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s243", "content": "### Partners

Wickhold does not run a sub-brand for partners, resellers or integrations. A partner may say that it works with Wickhold, once the partner agreement is in place and Priit's team has reviewed the wording. There is no "Wickhold certified" badge, and there is no plan for one.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "5. Brand architecture", "Partners"], "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s244", "content": "## 7. Rulings from this year

Requests I have already answered. They are listed so that I do not answer them again.

| Request | Ruling |
|---|---|
| "Trusted by more than 140 customers" | Allowed. The count stays exact |
| "Trusted by credit unions" | Refused. One customer is not a plural |
| "Agentless" or "agent-free" for Quenchline | Refused. It uses an eBPF agent. Say so |
| "Lightweight" | Allowed only next to the CPU overhead figure and its qualifier |
| "Real-time" for Quenchline | Allowed for detection. For containment, use the lab figure or leave it out |
| "Stops the attack" | Refused. Name the containment action: isolate a pod's network, freeze a process, drain a node |
| "Automatic remediation" for Evenburn | Refused. Evenburn gives a fix order and people do the fixing |
| "AI-powered" for any product | Refused unless product confirms in writing what the model does. Writing about AI agents does not make the product AI-powered |
| "Secures your AI" or "safe AI" for Leashgate | Refused. Describe tool-call policy and agent identity |
| "SOC 2 certified" | Refused. Say "holds SOC 2 Type II" |
| "Used by your peers" in a sector email | Refused unless a named, approved customer in that sector is shown |
| "Battle-tested" | Refused. It implies a history of incidents at customers that we have not disclosed and may not disclose |

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "7. Rulings from this year"], "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s245", "content": "### Illustration

Illustration is flat cut-paper shapes with one Ember focal element on Tallow or Soot, and no gradients. The cut-paper style was chosen because it looks made by hand and sits comfortably next to the warm photography. It also holds up small. Shapes should be simple enough to be cut with scissors, which is a good test when a design starts picking up detail.

Illustration tends to work best for ideas that have no honest photograph, such as a policy, a blast radius or an exposure path. Containment is the recurring theme: something small, held inside something that keeps it there.

The isometric style and the line graphic from the 2024 identity have been retired, along with the Cobalt gradient behind them.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "9. Photography and illustration direction", "Illustration"], "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s246", "content": "## T8c. Renewal notice

Localized landing pages use the consent banner supplied by web ops. Don't add a new tag, pixel or form tool to an EU or UK page without asking first. Paid retargeting on EU and UK traffic stays off unless the banner has recorded consent. A partner's tracking link is a new tag.

", "heading_path": ["Regional rules: EU and UK copy", "Analytics, cookies and tracking"], "relative_path": "brand/legal/regional-rules-eu-uk.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s248", "content": "### Agencies and freelancers

Outside partners work to the same order of authority, and the person who hired them is responsible for making sure they have it. At kickoff they receive these guidelines, the addendum, the relevant playbook and the current logo package. They do not receive older guidelines or old campaign files as reference, unless Brand has reviewed what's being sent. ", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "11. Governance", "Agencies and freelancers"], "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s249", "content": "## What we send

**Monthly newsletter.** Goes to everyone opted in, second Tuesday of the month. One lead item, three short items, nothing about us that we wouldn't want to read ourselves. Engineers are the bulk of this list, so it can carry a command or a config snippet.

**Nurture tracks.** Separate tracks for CISOs and platform leads, triggered by report downloads and demo requests. Four to six emails over about six weeks. Sales gets an alert on replies. If a contact opens a sales conversation, the track stops.

**Product announcements.** Goes to customers first, prospects a day later. New capabilities, deprecations, and anything that changes how a customer's agents behave. Deprecations go out at least 60 days ahead.

**Customer notices.** Security advisories, CVE guidance, scheduled maintenance. These bypass frequency caps and unsubscribe groups. Dov or a named engineer signs. Marketing can edit for clarity but never holds one back for scheduling reasons.

**Event email.** Slow Burn Summit and Field Day invites and reminders. The events team writes, lifecycle sends.

**Founder notes.** Maren writes to customers about twice a year, usually around pricing or product direction. It comes from her address. A reply goes to her, and she reads them.

", "heading_path": ["Email playbook", "What we send"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s250", "content": "### The promise at each level

| Level | What is promised |
|---|---|
| Company | Small fires stay small. |
| Quenchline | When something goes wrong at runtime, a defined containment action happens quickly and the team sees exactly what it did |
| Evenburn | The team sees where the drift and exposure paths are, and gets a fix order |
| Leashgate | AI agents work inside a tool-call policy, so the blast radius of an agent is known in advance |

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "4. Positioning", "The promise at each level"], "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s251", "content": "## 3. Banned claims

| Do not say | Say instead, or do this | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| "prevents prompt injection" | "limits what a compromised agent can do" | Leashgate acts on tool calls. It does not read intent and it cannot promise that an agent will not be manipulated. The claim is false as a matter of product design |
| "FedRAMP Authorized", "FedRAMP certified" | See section 4 | Neither is true |
| "GDPR compliant" | Use the regional rules | Regional wording sits there, and the ban is not limited to that region |
| "breach-proof", "unhackable", "impossible to escape" | Describe the containment action | No security product can support an absolute |
| "zero false positives", "100% detection", "catches everything" | Give a sourced figure or say nothing | We hold no such evidence |
| "guarantee", "guaranteed", "warranty" outside a contract | Remove | These words have legal effect. Service credits live in the order form |
| "the leading", "the fastest", "No. 1", "the only" | Remove, or bring me the comparison data | Superlatives need current comparative substantiation, and we do not hold any |
| "certified by", "endorsed by", "partner of" for any standards body or open-source project | Remove | Using eBPF or Helm is not an endorsement from anyone |
| "saves $X", any return-on-investment figure | Remove | We have no approved financial outcome for any customer |

Two refinements, because they keep coming back:

"Helps prevent" is a banned claim dressed up. A qualifier in front of a promise does not make it a limited promise.

"Compliance-ready" and "audit-ready" were requested in June for a trust page and refused. Wickhold can describe what the product records. Whether a customer passes an audit depends on the customer and the auditor.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "3. Banned claims"], "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s252", "content": "## 8. Technical writing in marketing copy

Kofi Anselm's team reviews anything containing code, and their rules are short.

- **Code formatting** for commands, flags, file names, field names, namespaces, node names and anything a person might type: `kubectl get pods`, `--namespace`, `values.yaml`.
- **Every snippet is run before it's published.** Say which version it was run against. A snippet nobody ran does not go out, even in a slide.
- **Placeholder values** look like placeholders or like real workloads: `payments`, `checkout`, `worker-7`. Don't use `foo`, and don't use the name of a real company, a real customer or a celebrity.
- **Domains and email addresses in examples** use `wickhold.example`.
- **Long output** gets trimmed, with a line saying so. Don't silently edit output.
- **Failure modes** are part of the example. If a command fails in a common way, say how it looks.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "8. Technical writing in marketing copy"], "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s253", "content": "## 4. Numbers

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "4. Numbers"], "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s254", "content": "### Color in common pieces

| Piece | Ground | Where Ember goes |
|---|---|---|
| Website page | Tallow, with Soot bands for pacing | The primary button, or one key figure |
| Sales or conference deck | Soot for title and section slides, Tallow for content | One point on a slide, or none |
| Report | Tallow pages, Soot cover | Chart highlights and one rule on the cover |
| Product documentation | Follows the docs theme | Links are not Ember on small text |
| Booth | Soot backwall, Tallow counter | The dot in the logo and one line of type |
| Swag | Soot or undyed fabric | The dot |

Dark layouts should use Soot, and pure black should not stand in for it. Soot has a slight cool cast that keeps Ember from buzzing against it. On Tallow pages, photographs and screenshots sit best with a thin Whetstone rule around them, since a light screenshot can otherwise dissolve into the page.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "7. Color", "Color in common pieces"], "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s255", "content": "## 5. Brand architecture

Wickhold is a single brand. Products, reports and events all sit under it, and none of them has a logo of its own.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "5. Brand architecture"], "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s256", "content": "### Fear is not a sales tool

No threat-actor drama. No ticking clocks.

The rule is simple to state and gets broken constantly, because fear copy is the easiest copy in security to write. It covers attackers portrayed as characters with motives and nicknames, anything of the "while you read this" kind, countdowns, "it's only a matter of time", "every second counts", and any sentence that asks the reader to imagine the phone call to the board. Our readers carry a pager. They do not need help imagining it.

Give the same fact without the dread.

Bad: "Attackers are already inside your cluster, and the clock is ticking."

Good: "41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]."

The second sentence is more uncomfortable than the first, and it did not raise its voice. Trust the number to do that work.

Breach references have their own rules in the claims document. Read them before you mention one.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "What Wickhold believes", "Fear is not a sales tool"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s257", "content": "# Landing pages

**Noor Eskelund and the web team, April 2026.** Written the week the Containment Report page went live, while the mistakes were fresh. Revised May 2026.

This covers campaign pages, product pages, persona pages and report pages on wickhold.example. The docs site and the blog have their own conventions.

", "heading_path": ["Landing pages"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/landing-page-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s258", "content": "## What goes in the frame

Use, in rough order of how well they have done for us:

1. A photo of real work, with no overlay at all
2. A stat card from the social templates. Quote cards rarely fit the cap
3. A short product crop showing one action, large enough to read in the feed
4. A hero illustration, cropped

Library images are 3:2, so a 1200x627 crop loses about a fifth of the height. Keep the focal point near the vertical center. Spot illustrations should sit on a solid Tallow or Soot layout from the template. They are transparent and LinkedIn will show them on its own background if you upload them as they are.

Do not run overlay text across a photo's focal point. Text goes on a solid band or in the quiet side of the frame.

", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn images", "What goes in the frame"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/linkedin-image.md"}, {"chunk_id": "s259", "content": "## Common hero rejections

{"brand_rules": {"evidence": [{"chunk_id": "383000ed-25fc-4fa8-8a32-0a9cb7da5f80", "content": "## How the sentences go

**Short first.** Most sentences run under twenty words. The long ones earn it by carrying a real sequence of events.

**Verbs do the work.** Name who did what. "Quenchline froze the process" over "the process was frozen". Past tense for incidents, present tense for what the product does.

**End early.** Our most common edit is deleting the last line of a paragraph. Writers tend to add one that restates the point in a nicer rhythm. Readers don't need it. This goes double for the final line of a piece.

**Ration the fire.** The tagline is "Small fires stay small." It carries the metaphor so the copy doesn't have to. A piece gets at most one fire image, and many pieces should have none. Nothing ignites, sparks, blazes or fans the flames. Slow Burn Summit gets to keep its name.

**Plain words for plain things.** "Use", "start", "stop", "run". Reach for the fancier word and the reader assumes something is being hidden.

**Don't argue with the reader's experience.** Telling a platform engineer that alerts are overwhelming is telling them what they had for breakfast. Start from what they know and add something.

", "end_line": 222, "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "How the sentences go"], "ref": "383000ed-25fc-4fa8-8a32-0a9cb7da5f80", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "start_line": 209}]}}

{"channel_rules": {"evidence": [{"chunk_id": "2dfe4ee1-b5b7-475f-aa8a-47e4ee921cb3", "content": "## 1. Length

Blog posts run 900 to 1,400 words. That range counts the body, including captions and code comments you wrote yourself, but not the code output you pasted.

Under 900 words, it's probably a release note or a LinkedIn post. Over 1,400 words, split it in two or cut the history section. We all write the history section first because it's easy, and nobody needs it. The report, the docs and the rollout guide are the place for anything longer.

", "end_line": 12, "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "1. Length"], "ref": "2dfe4ee1-b5b7-475f-aa8a-47e4ee921cb3", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md", "start_line": 7}, {"chunk_id": "43519095-47d5-42a8-b0b4-9efdf2334158", "content": "# Writing for the Wickhold blog

*Kofi Anselm wrote the first version in May 2026 for the two contractors we brought in after the Containment Report. Noor edited it in July. Send fixes to either of us.*

The blog has one job: get a platform engineer or a security lead to trust that the people here have held the pager. Traffic is a side effect. A post that gets a staff engineer to forward it to their team beats a post that ranks for a keyword and gets skimmed.

", "end_line": 6, "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog"], "ref": "43519095-47d5-42a8-b0b4-9efdf2334158", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md", "start_line": 1}, {"chunk_id": "6fabfd1d-c817-4def-a0d5-bc9821112094", "content": "## 4. Shape of a post

A title that says what the reader will get. Then the intro. Then three to five sections with descriptive headings. Then an ending that tells the reader what to do on Monday.

Titles we liked:

- Contain mode, one namespace at a time
- What drift looks like after a Helm upgrade
- The six hours after detection
- Writing your first tool-call policy for Wickhold Leashgate, in early access

Titles we rewrote:

- "5 Kubernetes Security Mistakes You're Making Right Now" became "Five findings we see in most new clusters"
- "Everything You Need To Know About eBPF" became "What our eBPF agent can and can't see"

Section headings should still make sense if they're all someone reads. "Background" and "The solution" tell the reader nothing.

End on the practical next step, then one call to action to the most relevant page. Don't summarize what you just said. If the post was good, they remember. Don't add a paragraph about Wickhold at the bottom either, as the footer handles that.

", "end_line": 68, "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "4. Shape of a post"], "ref": "6fabfd1d-c817-4def-a0d5-bc9821112094", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md", "start_line": 49}, {"chunk_id": "9792dec6-922e-42ef-aded-9a7b0bc70f03", "content": "## 2. The intro

A blog intro must cite a market statistic. Put it in the first two sentences, in the citation format from the style guide, and follow it with one sentence that says why this post exists. The rule is there because engineers are more willing to keep reading once they know the problem is measured and someone has measured it honestly.

Statistics are subject to the age limit in the approved claims, so check the date before you reuse an intro from an older post.

Market statistics are figures about the market or a surveyed population. Our own customer results and benchmark numbers belong further down the post, and they don't satisfy this requirement.

Good:

> The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. Most of the teams we talk to can tell you how long detection took. Far fewer can tell you what happened in the hours after. This post is about those hours.

Good:

> 41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. A lot of that time goes to one question: who is allowed to touch the workload? Here is how to settle that question before the page goes off.

Bad, because it has no statistic and no reason to read on:

> Kubernetes has changed how modern teams ship software, and with that change come new security challenges.

Bad, because a customer result is doing the job of a market statistic:

> Lowmoor Credit Union cut time to contain from 4 hours to 11 minutes. Here's how your team can get the same results.

", "end_line": 36, "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "2. The intro"], "ref": "9792dec6-922e-42ef-aded-9a7b0bc70f03", "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md", "start_line": 13}]}}

Wickhold Quenchline takes a containment action only in contain mode. In observe mode it records what it would have done. Copy describing automatic containment must therefore be true of contain mode and should say so where a reader could assume otherwise. Containment actions are isolating a pod's network, freezing a process and draining a node. Do not add to the list without product confirmation.

Wickhold Evenburn reports drift, exposure paths and a fix order. It does not change a customer's environment by itself, and copy should not imply that it does.

", "end_line": 72, "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "2. Claims that need a qualifier", "Product behavior"], "ref": "06ede73b-42e2-4a1d-8774-10eb6d36ca3a", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md", "start_line": 67}, {"chunk_id": "1475f7bc-8d87-4eb3-9fc9-4dece12a6a55", "content": "## Approved

|---|---|---|---|

| Ostler Grocers | Approved | Rafe Mulcahy, VP Infrastructure. Approved | 63% fewer open critical misconfigurations in 90 days, 1,900 nodes |

The written approval sits with Legal. If someone on the list changes jobs, stop using the quote until Legal has confirmed it.

Approvals cover website, email, social, sales decks, reports and event slides. They do not cover paid advertising or press releases. Each of those goes back to the customer through the account owner, one asset at a time.

Logos come from the brand library, in the supplied one-color versions. Don't recolor one, crop it, or take it from the customer's website. On a logo wall, keep the customers in alphabetical order so that nobody reads an endorsement ranking into it. Don't tag either company, or its people, on social unless the account owner has checked first. Sales emails may mention an approved customer by name, and may attach the approved case study, but may not offer a customer's contact details. Reference calls go through the account owner.

Citations

**Citations give the source name, the year and the link, in brackets, right after the claim.**

The shape, exactly:

```text
41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].
```

- Source name in full, as the source spells it.
- Comma, year. Comma, link. The full stop for the sentence goes outside the bracket.
- Link goes to the report or page itself, not a press release about it and not a search result. In a PDF or on a slide print the link out, because hyperlinks do not survive a screenshot.
- Use the same form everywhere, including LinkedIn and X. Yes, it's long on X. Plan the post around it.
- Two sources for one claim: two brackets. Do not merge them.
- A source we did not produce gets its own name in the bracket, even when a Wickhold page quotes it. Cite the original.
- In long pieces (report summaries, the blog), mention the survey base once near the first figure: "a survey of 412 platform and security leaders".

We tried numbered footnotes on the blog through most of 2025 and dropped them. The claim got quoted on LinkedIn, the footnote stayed behind, and the number went around with no source. A bracket travels with the sentence.

Customer results don't take a bracket when the customer is named in the sentence and the case study is linked from the page. Naming them is the source.

", "end_line": 70, "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "3. Citations"], "ref": "2ed35bac-e511-4a05-b03f-f56a94ab438a", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md", "start_line": 49}, {"chunk_id": "33d10c5d-c881-4d79-95fa-1edc60d3c984", "content": "## 1. Claims approved as written

| SOC 2 | Wickhold holds SOC 2 Type II, renewed January 2026 | Legal |
| Agent policy | "limits what a compromised agent can do" | Legal and product |
| Company | Founded in March 2019 in Denver, Colorado | Legal |
| Funding | Series B of $46M in June 2024, led by Marlbank Partners | Legal |

The Containment Report was published on April 14, 2026, and surveyed 412 platform and security leaders. Give the survey size when the copy has room for it. The legal entity is Wickhold, Inc. Contracts, order forms, privacy notices and page footers use that form. Marketing copy uses Wickhold.

Claims approved as written"], "ref": "33d10c5d-c881-4d79-95fa-1edc60d3c984", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md", "start_line": 12}, {"chunk_id": "3b54ef64-c087-4b32-a84a-a649f3d76cd6", "content": "## Tone by audience

Humor depends on the audience, see each persona.

The personas hold the working rules for each reader, including what goes first. What follows is only the register, meaning how the voice sounds once you have chosen your content.

**CISOs.** Level and measured. Assume the reader will forward your paragraph to an audit committee without editing it, and write something they can forward. Risk, time and board language are their native terms: exposure, time to contain, residual risk, ownership. Short sentences, complete ones, no shorthand. Every sentence should survive being read aloud in a room that includes a lawyer.

**Platform engineers.** A good pull-request comment from a colleague you respect. Exact, brief, assumes competence, and shows its working. If there is a YAML snippet that makes the point, the prose can get out of its way. Marketing English reads as noise here and the page will be closed.

**DevSecOps.** These readers sit between the review queue and the pipeline, and they spend their days being the person who says no. Write to someone who is outnumbered: practical, on their side, and specific about what lands in their queue and what stays out of it.

**Compliance leads.** Careful nouns. This reader will notice the difference between "supports" and "meets", and will quote you. Their persona is still being written, so if the piece is aimed mainly at them, ask Noor before guessing.

**Customers mid-incident.** Pure 3am voice. Nothing about the product, nothing about the relationship, no reassurance that isn't backed by a fact. What we see, what we've done, when the next update comes.

**Finance and procurement.** They read a small part of what we write and they read it closely. Plain sentences, the price in the standard form, the terms where they expect them. Anything that sounds like enthusiasm reads to them as a negotiating position.

**Journalists.** Assume no interest in the product and real interest in what is happening to teams. Offer the finding, the method and a person to talk to. Don't send them a story with a hook in it; they have their own.

**Candidates and the community.** Warmer, plainer, and allowed to mention that the work is interesting. The same no-drama rules hold. Nobody here is a rockstar.

Last checked 2 October 2026.

Sales, this is the sheet to use before you answer a security questionnaire. If a deck or an old email says something different, the deck or the email is out of date.

| Program | Status | What you may say |
|---|---|---|
| SOC 2 Type II | Held. Renewed January 2026 | "Wickhold holds SOC 2 Type II." |
| FedRAMP Moderate | In process. Not held | "Wickhold is pursuing FedRAMP Moderate authorization." |

**FedRAMP.** Never claim FedRAMP authorization or certification. The approved wording above is the only wording. It goes in copy exactly as written, including the word "pursuing".

These are banned in every channel, spoken or written: "FedRAMP Authorized", "FedRAMP certified", "FedRAMP Ready", "FedRAMP compliant", "FedRAMP equivalent", "built to FedRAMP standards". Agency buyers read those words literally, and a false statement to a federal buyer is a contract and legal problem, whatever the deal size.

The status changes when authorization is complete and published, and this sheet says so. An assessor's visit, a sponsor conversation, or a positive meeting does not change it. Do not give prospects a target date. We do not publish one. If a federal prospect presses, the answer is the sentence above and an offer to connect them with me.

Good, in an answer to a questionnaire:

> Wickhold holds SOC 2 Type II, renewed January 2026. Wickhold is pursuing FedRAMP Moderate authorization. We can share the SOC 2 report under NDA.

Bad:

> We're basically FedRAMP Authorized, the paperwork is just finishing up.

**SOC 2.** The report goes out under NDA through the account team, never by public link. Say "Type II" every time. Say "held" or "renewed", and do not say "SOC 2 certified", because SOC 2 ends in an attestation report and not a certificate.

**Questionnaires and RFPs.** Security questionnaires go through the account team, and any answer about certifications is copied from this sheet. If a form offers only "Yes" or "No" for FedRAMP, answer "No", and use the comments box for the approved sentence. Do not tick a box in the hope of explaining later.

One of the company values, and the one marketing finds hardest. Every product we sell has an edge. Wickhold Evenburn finds drift and exposure paths; it does not contain anything. Grammar and punctuation

- **American spelling** in all copy, including copy going to UK and EU readers. Containerize, not containerise.
- **Oxford comma**, always. It has settled more than one argument in Kubernetes prose, where lists of nouns can double as lists of objects.
- **Active voice** with a named actor, wherever the actor is known. "Wickhold Quenchline drained the node." If the passive is hiding who did it and that person is us, it goes.
- **Tense.** Past for what happened, present for what the product does, and nothing in the future except where a date is public.
- **Contractions** are fine in the blog, on social and in email. Skip them on legal pages and in anything aimed at a board.
- **Colons** are our favorite punctuation mark and they're doing fine. Use them to introduce the fact.
- **Semicolons** at most once a page. If there are two, one wants to be a full stop.
- **Em dashes** rarely in body copy. Most are a full stop that lost its nerve. Spaced en dashes are not a substitute.
- **Parentheses** for the short aside only. If the aside matters, promote it to a sentence.
- **Quotation marks:** double, with commas and full stops inside, American style, except for literal strings in technical writing where the punctuation would change the meaning. Single quotes only inside double.
- **Italics:** titles of reports and the occasional stress only. They disappear on Soot grounds and in email.
- **Bold:** for scanning in long documents, once or twice per section. Bold on a landing page means the design isn't working.
- **Ampersands:** only in proper names. Plain "and" in headlines too.
- **"And/or"** is a legal term. Pick one.
- **Slashes** as a shortcut ("platform/security teams") get rewritten: "platform and security teams".

Statistics: 12-month age limit

A market statistic may not be older than 12 months at publication. This is the limit on how old a statistic can be, and it is measured on the day the piece goes out, not the day it was drafted. A post queued in March for release in May is checked against May.

The limit applies to market and survey statistics only. It covers any figure that describes the industry, the market, or a population of teams. It does not apply to customer results such as the Lowmoor and Ostler outcomes, or to product metrics such as the lab figures, which have their own qualifier.

The age of a statistic runs from the publication date of its source. Fieldwork dates do not matter. A report re-quoted in a newer article keeps its original date, so a 2026 article quoting a 2024 survey is a 2024 statistic.

| Source | Published | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Wickhold Containment Report 2026 | April 14, 2026 | Usable for publication through April 14, 2027 |
| Wickhold Field Report 2024 | 2024 | Past the 12 months limit |

The two Containment Report statistics in section 1 are the only market statistics of ours inside the limit today. The Field Report figures still appear in old decks and old posts. That is an archive problem and not a permission. Do not reuse them. Do not reword them to make them feel new, and do not refer to them as "historically" true.

Fresh third-party statistics are allowed without coming to me first, with the source link and the date of the source in the copy. The source must be a named publisher and the figure must appear on the page you link to. A figure found in a vendor's blog, quoting another vendor's blog, gets traced to the original or is dropped. The third party's name still has to clear the competitor rules.

When the 2027 Containment Report is published, section 1 will be updated and the 2026 figures remain usable until they reach the limit. Old assets stay in the archive as they are. They are not re-promoted once a market statistic in them has expired. Paid and email reuse counts as publication.

| Do not say | Say instead, or do this | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| "prevents prompt injection" | "limits what a compromised agent can do" | Leashgate acts on tool calls. It does not read intent and it cannot promise that an agent will not be manipulated. The claim is false as a matter of product design |

| "the leading", "the fastest", "No. 1", "the only" | Remove, or bring me the comparison data | Superlatives need current comparative substantiation, and we do not hold any |

| "saves $X", any return-on-investment figure | Remove | We have no approved financial outcome for any customer |

"Helps prevent" is a banned claim dressed up. A qualifier in front of a promise does not make it a limited promise.

"Compliance-ready" and "audit-ready" were requested in June for a trust page and refused. Wickhold can describe what the product records. Whether a customer passes an audit depends on the customer and the auditor.

{"title":"Assess vendor status and organize posture work","subject":null,"preheader":null,"sender_name":null,"byline":null,"body":"Wickhold is pursuing FedRAMP Moderate authorization. The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. This post explains how regulated security teams can assess vendor status and organize posture work. The report surveyed 412 platform and security leaders.

## Separate a vendor’s status from your own readiness

A vendor’s documented status and your organization’s audit preparation answer different questions. Start by asking what the vendor holds or is pursuing, which service or product the statement covers, and what documentation the vendor can provide. Record the answer in the vendor review rather than translating it into a broader conclusion.

Wickhold holds SOC 2 Type II, renewed January 2026. Wickhold is pursuing FedRAMP Moderate authorization. These are two distinct statements. Neither, on its own, establishes that a customer’s environment meets an audit requirement or that a particular deployment fits a customer’s needs.

For a review, keep the wording and evidence together. Note the date you checked the status, who confirmed it, and which service or scope the evidence describes. If a status is still in process, record that accurately. Don’t turn a plan, conversation, or pending step into a completed authorization. If the vendor provides a report under agreed access terms, note where your team stores it and who can review it.

Then make the internal decision explicit: what evidence does your organization need before it approves the vendor, and who owns that decision? Security, procurement, legal, and the service owner may need different details. A short record of the question, evidence, owner, and next step gives the review a clear path without implying that the vendor’s status completes your work.

## Keep audit preparation in your own workflow

Your team controls its own preparation. Begin with the systems, owners, and evidence your review actually covers. A useful working record can include the system or service, the relevant control or requirement, the evidence location, its owner, and the next review date. Keep gaps visible rather than smoothing them into a general status like “ready.”

For each finding, assign a person to assess it and a next action. Some findings need investigation. Others need a change, a documented exception, or a decision from the control owner. Record what the team chose and why. A report can help people see what to examine, but your team still decides how to address a finding and what evidence supports that decision.

This distinction matters when several teams share responsibility. A security leader may own the review process; a platform engineer may understand the affected workload; and an application owner may know the operational impact of a change. Give each person a defined part of the work. Agree on how the team will track decisions and when it will revisit open items.

Treat the record as a working tool, not a promise about an audit outcome. The usefulness of the process depends on your organization’s scope, evidence, and decisions. A clear list of owners and next actions can make posture work easier to coordinate without claiming that a vendor or a product makes the organization audit-ready.

## Use posture reporting to decide what to investigate

Wickhold Evenburn reports drift, exposure paths, and a fix order. That gives a team information to review and prioritize. It does not change a customer’s environment by itself. Engineers and security owners still need to assess the reported issue, decide what action fits their environment, and make or approve that change.

A practical review starts with the report, not an assumption about what the product has done. Confirm what the finding describes and which workload or configuration it concerns. Check the path and the surrounding context. Then decide whether the suggested order fits your team’s risk, ownership, and current work. If it does not, record the reason and the decision-maker rather than treating the order as an automatic instruction.

That process can connect posture work to an existing review queue. Assign an owner, note what evidence the owner needs, and track the decision and follow-up. If the team accepts a fix, it can manage that change through its normal workflow. If it defers the work, record who accepted the risk and when the team will review it again. The report helps inform the decision; it does not make the decision for you.

## Keep containment separate from posture work

Wickhold Quenchline provides supporting context for runtime containment, which is different from Evenburn’s reporting role. Quenchline takes a containment action only in contain mode. In observe mode, it records what it would have done. Its actions are isolating a pod’s network, freezing a process, and draining a node.

That distinction helps teams assess what they are evaluating. Evenburn reports drift and exposure paths; it does not contain anything. Quenchline can take the listed containment actions in contain mode; it does not patch the image an application came from. Keep those functions separate in a review, and ask which workflow, operating mode, and team decision apply to the task in front of you.

## Set the next step before the review ends

On Monday, choose one vendor review or posture queue to examine. Write down the question the team needs to answer, the evidence it will check, and the person responsible for the next action. Keep the vendor’s documented status separate from your organization’s audit preparation, and use posture reports as input to your team’s decisions.
