{"brand_rules": {"evidence": [{"chunk_id": "383000ed-25fc-4fa8-8a32-0a9cb7da5f80", "content": "## How the sentences go

**Short first.** Most sentences run under twenty words. The long ones earn it by carrying a real sequence of events.

**Verbs do the work.** Name who did what. "Quenchline froze the process" over "the process was frozen". Past tense for incidents, present tense for what the product does.

**End early.** Our most common edit is deleting the last line of a paragraph. Writers tend to add one that restates the point in a nicer rhythm. Readers don't need it. This goes double for the final line of a piece.

**Ration the fire.** The tagline is "Small fires stay small." It carries the metaphor so the copy doesn't have to. A piece gets at most one fire image, and many pieces should have none. Nothing ignites, sparks, blazes or fans the flames. Slow Burn Summit gets to keep its name.

**Plain words for plain things.** "Use", "start", "stop", "run". Reach for the fancier word and the reader assumes something is being hidden.

**Don't argue with the reader's experience.** Telling a platform engineer that alerts are overwhelming is telling them what they had for breakfast. Start from what they know and add something.

", "end_line": 222, "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "How the sentences go"], "ref": "383000ed-25fc-4fa8-8a32-0a9cb7da5f80", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "start_line": 209}]}}

{"channel_rules": {"evidence": [{"chunk_id": "459b9ef8-bddf-4cff-908d-53322e51e731", "content": "## Sender and footer

- Default from name: `Wickhold`, from `hello@wickhold.example`. Replies go to a monitored queue.
- Newsletter from name: `Kofi at Wickhold`.
- Founder notes: `Maren Tolliver`, from `maren@wickhold.example`.
- Customer notices: `Wickhold Customer Notices`, from `notices@wickhold.example`.
- Footer carries the legal entity, Wickhold, Inc., a Denver postal address and the unsubscribe link.

", "end_line": 99, "heading_path": ["Email playbook", "Sender and footer"], "ref": "459b9ef8-bddf-4cff-908d-53322e51e731", "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md", "start_line": 92}, {"chunk_id": "5f590c06-fa98-48f5-82ff-5c20b8a3ac8f", "content": "# Email playbook

Owner: Ilse Varga-Holm's team (lifecycle). Rewritten for the March 2026 platform migration, revised September 2026.

", "end_line": 4, "heading_path": ["Email playbook"], "ref": "5f590c06-fa98-48f5-82ff-5c20b8a3ac8f", "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md", "start_line": 1}, {"chunk_id": "60fd8029-020c-42ea-8ffa-c11621d95fe2", "content": "## The short version

| Thing | Limit |
|---|---|
| Email length | 220 words at most, body text, including the sign-off |
| Subject line | 48 characters at most, counted with spaces |
| Links | One main action. More links are fine in a newsletter, and a second link is fine in a customer notice |
| Sends per contact | Two marketing sends a week at most, customer notices excluded |

The 48-character limit comes from the phone inbox preview, where the back half of a longer subject gets cut. We pulled a sample of opens in early 2026 and most were on phones, so the preview is the version people actually read.

", "end_line": 15, "heading_path": ["Email playbook", "The short version"], "ref": "60fd8029-020c-42ea-8ffa-c11621d95fe2", "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md", "start_line": 5}, {"chunk_id": "8e229f98-1ea5-4a28-8b10-5f4b455449ff", "content": "## Email preheader

Every email has a preheader of at most 90 characters. It shows beside or under the subject line in most inboxes, so treat it as the second half of the subject. It must add something. Don't repeat the subject, and don't leave the field empty, or the client will fill it with the first text in the email, which for us is often the "view in browser" line.

Good: `Survey of 412 platform and security leaders on what happens after detection.`

Bad: `Containment Report 2026 is out. Read the Containment Report 2026 today.`

", "end_line": 30, "heading_path": ["Email templates", "Email preheader"], "ref": "8e229f98-1ea5-4a28-8b10-5f4b455449ff", "relative_path": "brand/templates/email-templates.md", "start_line": 23}, {"chunk_id": "9444a373-5e1b-44c8-b229-396932ea45d4", "content": "## Body

Most of our email has three parts.

1. **What happened or what's new.** One or two sentences.
2. **Why it matters to this reader.** Two to four sentences. Different for a CISO list and a platform list, which is why the tracks are separate.
3. **What to do.** One button or link. Then the sign-off.

The working drafts are in the email templates, and the merge fields there match the sending platform. Start from a template. A blank page tends to produce an email that's 400 words long.

Good body copy, platform track:

> You downloaded the Containment Report, so here's the practical follow-up. Our rollout guide starts with Wickhold Quenchline in observe mode on one namespace, then moves to contain mode once you've read two to four weeks of would-have-acted events.
>
> It takes about an hour, and the failure modes are listed at the end.

Good body copy, CISO track:

> Decide whether your team tracks time to contain today. Your board will ask how long a runtime incident takes to contain. In our survey of 412 platform and security leaders, the median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].
>
> The report sets out how teams measure that number and what they report upward. If your team doesn't track it, section two is a place to start.

Bad body copy:

> Hope you're having a great week! As a valued member of our community, we wanted to reach out and share some exciting content we think you'll love. In today's rapidly evolving threat landscape, security has never been more important.

Four sentences in and the reader has learned nothing. Cut until the first sentence is the news.

Personalization: first name in the greeting when we have it, and role-based copy through segments. Anything else, like company size, industry or recent page views, stays out of the visible copy. Being told what you browsed by a security company is unsettling.

", "end_line": 85, "heading_path": ["Email playbook", "Body"], "ref": "9444a373-5e1b-44c8-b229-396932ea45d4", "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md", "start_line": 56}, {"chunk_id": "ca65b949-2e3b-43fc-b1a9-0f6770fb82d8", "content": "## CTA format for all channels

This lives here because the email team wrote it down first, and it now applies to every channel: email, landing pages, paid, social, the blog, event pages.

A CTA, the call to action on a button or a link, is at most four words, and it starts with a verb. The same CTA wording rules apply wherever the button sits. "Learn more" and "Click here" are banned everywhere, including as link text inside a sentence.

| Fine | Not fine |
|---|---|
| Read the report | Learn more |
| Book a demo | Click here |
| See the rollout guide | Click here to see the rollout guide |
| Request early access | Early access request |
| Save your seat | Your seat is waiting for you |

Say what happens on the other side of the click. "Get started" is allowed but weak, so use something more specific if you can.

", "end_line": 22, "heading_path": ["Email templates", "CTA format for all channels"], "ref": "ca65b949-2e3b-43fc-b1a9-0f6770fb82d8", "relative_path": "brand/templates/email-templates.md", "start_line": 7}]}}

{"brand_rules": {"evidence": [{"chunk_id": "383000ed-25fc-4fa8-8a32-0a9cb7da5f80", "content": "## How the sentences go

**Short first.** Most sentences run under twenty words. The long ones earn it by carrying a real sequence of events.

**Verbs do the work.** Name who did what. "Quenchline froze the process" over "the process was frozen". Past tense for incidents, present tense for what the product does.

**End early.** Our most common edit is deleting the last line of a paragraph. Writers tend to add one that restates the point in a nicer rhythm. Readers don't need it. This goes double for the final line of a piece.

**Ration the fire.** The tagline is "Small fires stay small." It carries the metaphor so the copy doesn't have to. A piece gets at most one fire image, and many pieces should have none. Nothing ignites, sparks, blazes or fans the flames. Slow Burn Summit gets to keep its name.

**Plain words for plain things.** "Use", "start", "stop", "run". Reach for the fancier word and the reader assumes something is being hidden.

**Don't argue with the reader's experience.** Telling a platform engineer that alerts are overwhelming is telling them what they had for breakfast. Start from what they know and add something.

", "end_line": 222, "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "How the sentences go"], "ref": "383000ed-25fc-4fa8-8a32-0a9cb7da5f80", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "start_line": 209}]}}

{"channel_rules": {"evidence": [{"chunk_id": "333c68ed-7bd9-491d-9020-93f7cb39c911", "content": "## Hard limit

A landing page is 500 words at most. That counts every word a visitor can read on the page: headline, subheads, body, proof, form labels and the FAQ. Navigation and the site footer don't count.

If the page runs over, cut sections. Don't shrink the type or tuck copy into tabs and accordions. It still counts, and the page is still doing too many things. Long-form material belongs in the report, a blog post or the docs, and the page links there.

", "end_line": 12, "heading_path": ["Landing pages", "Hard limit"], "ref": "333c68ed-7bd9-491d-9020-93f7cb39c911", "relative_path": "brand/channels/landing-page-playbook.md", "start_line": 7}, {"chunk_id": "39544f3e-3ce8-49ae-b7bb-0c805ed0fe8c", "content": "## Every page has one job

Before anyone writes copy, the brief answers three things.

- Who lands here, and from where (paid search, a nurture email, a Field Day QR code)
- What they should do next
- What proof they need to do it

A page aimed at both a CISO and a platform engineer ends up serving neither. We build two pages and route by campaign. The rollout guide page for engineers shows commands and flags above the fold. The executive page for the same product leads with what the decision is and what it costs in time.

", "end_line": 22, "heading_path": ["Landing pages", "Every page has one job"], "ref": "39544f3e-3ce8-49ae-b7bb-0c805ed0fe8c", "relative_path": "brand/channels/landing-page-playbook.md", "start_line": 13}, {"chunk_id": "a1cb5f0e-a0a0-4e46-9bcf-3ae99202023b", "content": "## Hero copy

The hero says what the product does and who it's for, in that order. Lead with what happens to the reader's workload. Our tagline can sit in the hero of the brand page, but it doesn't describe a product, so product pages shouldn't rely on it.

Good, product page:

> **Contain runtime failures before they spread**
> Wickhold Quenchline detects bad behavior in Kubernetes and isolates a pod, freezes a process or drains a node, under the policy you set.
> [Book a demo]

Good, posture page:

> **Know which misconfiguration to fix first**
> Wickhold Evenburn tracks drift across cloud and cluster, finds each exposure path and gives your team a fix order.
> [See a sample report]

Good, early access page:

> **Set policy for what AI agents can call**
> Wickhold Leashgate, in early access, applies tool-call policy at runtime and limits what a compromised agent can do.
> [Request early access]

Good, report page:

> **The Wickhold Containment Report 2026**
> A survey of 412 platform and security leaders on how long containment takes, and where the hours go.
> [Read the report]

Good, brand page:

> **Small fires stay small.**
> Wickhold is the runtime security company for teams that run Kubernetes.
> [See how it works]

Bad, from a 2025 agency concept:

> **Next-level cloud security for the modern enterprise**
> One powerful platform. Total confidence. Peace of mind at every layer of your stack.

Nothing in that hero says what the software does. It would fit a mattress company if you swapped "stack" for "bed".

", "end_line": 78, "heading_path": ["Landing pages", "Hero copy"], "ref": "a1cb5f0e-a0a0-4e46-9bcf-3ae99202023b", "relative_path": "brand/channels/landing-page-playbook.md", "start_line": 38}, {"chunk_id": "c1079d42-ff19-496b-9bbf-e72c382dc03d", "content": "## Page skeleton and word budget

| Section | Budget (words) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Hero: headline, one sentence, CTA | 40 | Must make sense with no scrolling |
| Proof strip: customer logos or one number | 25 | One row, no carousel |
| What it does: three blocks at most | 150 | Concrete actions, not themes |
| How it works or how you roll it out | 100 | Steps. Commands if the audience is technical |
| Customer proof: one result, one quote | 70 | A full sentence with the number and the source |
| FAQ: three questions at most | 80 | Real questions from sales calls |
| Closing CTA | 15 | Same action as the hero |
| **Total** | **480** | Leaves 20 words of slack |

CTAs follow the shared CTA format in the email templates. Use one primary CTA per page, repeated at the top and bottom with the same wording. A secondary link is allowed for a technical reader who is not ready for a form, like the docs or the rollout guide.

", "end_line": 37, "heading_path": ["Landing pages", "Page skeleton and word budget"], "ref": "c1079d42-ff19-496b-9bbf-e72c382dc03d", "relative_path": "brand/channels/landing-page-playbook.md", "start_line": 23}, {"chunk_id": "fb4da63f-2def-4f97-a867-73a2a7d2fe81", "content": "# Landing pages

**Noor Eskelund and the web team, April 2026.** Written the week the Containment Report page went live, while the mistakes were fresh. Revised May 2026.

This covers campaign pages, product pages, persona pages and report pages on wickhold.example. The docs site and the blog have their own conventions.

", "end_line": 6, "heading_path": ["Landing pages"], "ref": "fb4da63f-2def-4f97-a867-73a2a7d2fe81", "relative_path": "brand/channels/landing-page-playbook.md", "start_line": 1}]}}

|---|---|---|

**FedRAMP.** Never claim FedRAMP authorization or certification. The approved wording above is the only wording. It goes in copy exactly as written, including the word "pursuing".

These are banned in every channel, spoken or written: "FedRAMP Authorized", "FedRAMP certified", "FedRAMP Ready", "FedRAMP compliant", "FedRAMP equivalent", "built to FedRAMP standards". Good, in an answer to a questionnaire:

> Wickhold holds SOC 2 Type II, renewed January 2026. Wickhold is pursuing FedRAMP Moderate authorization. We can share the SOC 2 report under NDA.

Bad:

> We're basically FedRAMP Authorized, the paperwork is just finishing up.

- **Measurements take digits, always.** Anything with a unit: 220 nodes, 11 minutes, 7.4 hours, 90 days, 38 seconds, 1,900 nodes.
- **Counts of ordinary things** spell out one to nine and use digits from 10: "three clusters", "12 namespaces". Mixed in one sentence, go with digits.
- **Commas from 1,000 up.** No "1.9k nodes", not even on social.

- **Approved sentences stay as approved.** The report line says "more than six hours", spelled out, and that's how it runs in every piece. The same goes for "more than 140 customers", which never becomes "140+". Legal approved the sentence, and this guide doesn't get to tidy it.

Grammar and punctuation

- **American spelling** in all copy, including copy going to UK and EU readers. Containerize, not containerise.
- **Oxford comma**, always. It has settled more than one argument in Kubernetes prose, where lists of nouns can double as lists of objects.

- **Contractions** are fine in the blog, on social and in email. Skip them on legal pages and in anything aimed at a board.
- **Colons** are our favorite punctuation mark and they're doing fine. Use them to introduce the fact.
- **Semicolons** at most once a page. If there are two, one wants to be a full stop.

- **Bold:** for scanning in long documents, once or twice per section. Bold on a landing page means the design isn't working.
- **Ampersands:** only in proper names. Plain "and" in headlines too.
- **"And/or"** is a legal term. Pick one.
- **Slashes** as a shortcut ("platform/security teams") get rewritten: "platform and security teams".

| "GDPR compliant" | Use the regional rules | Regional wording sits there, and the ban is not limited to that region |

| "zero false positives", "100% detection", "catches everything" | Give a sourced figure or say nothing | We hold no such evidence |
| "guarantee", "guaranteed", "warranty" outside a contract | Remove | These words have legal effect. Service credits live in the order form |
| "the leading", "the fastest", "No. 1", "the only" | Remove, or bring me the comparison data | Superlatives need current comparative substantiation, and we do not hold any |
| "certified by", "endorsed by", "partner of" for any standards body or open-source project | Remove | Using eBPF or Helm is not an endorsement from anyone |
| "saves $X", any return-on-investment figure | Remove | We have no approved financial outcome for any customer |

Two refinements, because they keep coming back:

"Helps prevent" is a banned claim dressed up. A qualifier in front of a promise does not make it a limited promise.

"Compliance-ready" and "audit-ready" were requested in June for a trust page and refused. Wickhold can describe what the product records. Whether a customer passes an audit depends on the customer and the auditor.

Wickhold Quenchline takes a containment action only in contain mode. In observe mode it records what it would have done. Copy describing automatic containment must therefore be true of contain mode and should say so where a reader could assume otherwise. Containment actions are isolating a pod's network, freezing a process and draining a node. Do not add to the list without product confirmation.

Wickhold Evenburn reports drift, exposure paths and a fix order. It does not change a customer's environment by itself, and copy should not imply that it does.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "2. Claims that need a qualifier", "Product behavior"], "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "1475f7bc-8d87-4eb3-9fc9-4dece12a6a55", "content": "## Approved

| Customer | Name and logo | Quote | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lowmoor Credit Union | Approved | Hana Brandvold, CISO. Approved | Time to contain fell from 4 hours to 11 minutes, 220 nodes |
| Ostler Grocers | Approved | Rafe Mulcahy, VP Infrastructure. Approved | 63% fewer open critical misconfigurations in 90 days, 1,900 nodes |

Use the quote as it stands in the signed approval, with the person's name, title and company. Do not trim it so that the meaning shifts, stitch two quotes together, or update a title without asking. The written approval sits with Legal. If someone on the list changes jobs, stop using the quote until Legal has confirmed it.

Approvals cover website, email, social, sales decks, reports and event slides. They do not cover paid advertising or press releases. Each of those goes back to the customer through the account owner, one asset at a time.

Logos come from the brand library, in the supplied one-color versions. Don't recolor one, crop it, or take it from the customer's website. On a logo wall, keep the customers in alphabetical order so that nobody reads an endorsement ranking into it. Don't tag either company, or its people, on social unless the account owner has checked first. Sales emails may mention an approved customer by name, and may attach the approved case study, but may not offer a customer's contact details. Reference calls go through the account owner.

Keep the node count with the result. The Lowmoor outcome belongs to a 220-node estate and the Ostler outcome to a 1,900-node estate, and neither may be stated as what a new customer should expect. Do not convert the Lowmoor result into a percentage or a multiple. Nobody approved that arithmetic. Do not combine the two results in one sentence, because that reads as a single program with both outcomes. Which customers may be cited, and how, is covered by the logo and quote policy.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "2. Claims that need a qualifier", "Customer results"], "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "33d10c5d-c881-4d79-95fa-1edc60d3c984", "content": "## 1. Claims approved as written

| Topic | Approved wording | Evidence held by |
|---|---|---|
| Customer count | "more than 140 customers" | Finance, reconciled quarterly |
| Market, time to contain | "41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident" | Wickhold Containment Report 2026 |
| Market, median | "the median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours" | Wickhold Containment Report 2026 |
| Lowmoor Credit Union | Time to contain fell from 4 hours to 11 minutes, 220 nodes | Signed customer approval |
| Ostler Grocers | 63% fewer open critical misconfigurations in 90 days, 1,900 nodes | Signed customer approval |
| SOC 2 | Wickhold holds SOC 2 Type II, renewed January 2026 | Legal |
| Agent policy | "limits what a compromised agent can do" | Legal and product |
| Company | Founded in March 2019 in Denver, Colorado | Legal |
| Funding | Series B of $46M in June 2024, led by Marlbank Partners | Legal |

The Containment Report was published on April 14, 2026, and surveyed 412 platform and security leaders. Give the survey size when the copy has room for it. The legal entity is Wickhold, Inc. Contracts, order forms, privacy notices and page footers use that form. Marketing copy uses Wickhold.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "1. Claims approved as written"], "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "383000ed-25fc-4fa8-8a32-0a9cb7da5f80", "content": "## How the sentences go

**Short first.** Most sentences run under twenty words. The long ones earn it by carrying a real sequence of events.

**Verbs do the work.** Name who did what. "Quenchline froze the process" over "the process was frozen". Past tense for incidents, present tense for what the product does.

**End early.** Our most common edit is deleting the last line of a paragraph. Writers tend to add one that restates the point in a nicer rhythm. Readers don't need it. This goes double for the final line of a piece.

**Ration the fire.** The tagline is "Small fires stay small." It carries the metaphor so the copy doesn't have to. A piece gets at most one fire image, and many pieces should have none. Nothing ignites, sparks, blazes or fans the flames. Slow Burn Summit gets to keep its name.

**Plain words for plain things.** "Use", "start", "stop", "run". Reach for the fancier word and the reader assumes something is being hidden.

**Don't argue with the reader's experience.** Telling a platform engineer that alerts are overwhelming is telling them what they had for breakfast. Start from what they know and add something.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "How the sentences go"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "412b98db-a59b-4fa4-afb4-aada12ba8243", "content": "Certification status: sheet kept by Priit Salonen. Last checked 2 October 2026.

Sales, this is the sheet to use before you answer a security questionnaire. If a deck or an old email says something different, the deck or the email is out of date.

| Program | Status | What you may say |
|---|---|---|
| SOC 2 Type II | Held. Renewed January 2026 | "Wickhold holds SOC 2 Type II." |
| FedRAMP Moderate | In process. Not held | "Wickhold is pursuing FedRAMP Moderate authorization." |

**FedRAMP.** Never claim FedRAMP authorization or certification. The approved wording above is the only wording. It goes in copy exactly as written, including the word "pursuing".

These are banned in every channel, spoken or written: "FedRAMP Authorized", "FedRAMP certified", "FedRAMP Ready", "FedRAMP compliant", "FedRAMP equivalent", "built to FedRAMP standards". Agency buyers read those words literally, and a false statement to a federal buyer is a contract and legal problem, whatever the deal size.

The status changes when authorization is complete and published, and this sheet says so. An assessor's visit, a sponsor conversation, or a positive meeting does not change it. Do not give prospects a target date. We do not publish one. If a federal prospect presses, the answer is the sentence above and an offer to connect them with me.

Good, in an answer to a questionnaire:

> Wickhold holds SOC 2 Type II, renewed January 2026. Wickhold is pursuing FedRAMP Moderate authorization. We can share the SOC 2 report under NDA.

Bad:

> We're basically FedRAMP Authorized, the paperwork is just finishing up.

**SOC 2.** The report goes out under NDA through the account team, never by public link. Say "Type II" every time. Say "held" or "renewed", and do not say "SOC 2 certified", because SOC 2 ends in an attestation report and not a certificate.

**Questionnaires and RFPs.** Security questionnaires go through the account team, and any answer about certifications is copied from this sheet. If a form offers only "Yes" or "No" for FedRAMP, answer "No", and use the comments box for the approved sentence. Do not tick a box in the hope of explaining later.

", "heading_path": [], "relative_path": "brand/legal/certifications-status.md"}, {"chunk_id": "459b9ef8-bddf-4cff-908d-53322e51e731", "content": "## Sender and footer

- Default from name: `Wickhold`, from `hello@wickhold.example`. Replies go to a monitored queue.
- Newsletter from name: `Kofi at Wickhold`.
- Founder notes: `Maren Tolliver`, from `maren@wickhold.example`.
- Customer notices: `Wickhold Customer Notices`, from `notices@wickhold.example`.
- Footer carries the legal entity, Wickhold, Inc., a Denver postal address and the unsubscribe link.

", "heading_path": ["Email playbook", "Sender and footer"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "5145b09f-4795-4c18-8ba2-f71cc42dda0e", "content": "## Testing and approvals

Test one thing per send, on lists over about 5,000 contacts. Subject lines first, send time second. We no longer test emoji, since they lost every round in 2025.

Before anything goes out:

1. Send a proof to the seed list, which covers phone, desktop and text-only clients.
2. Click every link. Check that the UTM tags are in place.
3. Check word count and subject length.
4. Lifecycle reviews. Noor reviews any new template or any new claim.
5. Priit reviews customer names, new numbers, and anything about certifications.

Suppressions: exclude open opportunities from nurture, exclude churned customers from product mail, and always exclude contacts on the do-not-contact list that sales keeps. Lists are pulled the morning of the send, not the night before.

", "heading_path": ["Email playbook", "Testing and approvals"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "52f1185e-856d-4a13-a2e9-79463e3620d2", "content": "# Customer logo and quote policy

Maintained by Legal. Reviewed by Priit Salonen and Noor Eskelund, July 2026.

Cite only customers listed as approved below. That covers names, logos, quotes, results, case studies and any description that would let a reader work out who the customer is. A customer who likes us on a call has not approved anything.

", "heading_path": ["Customer logo and quote policy"], "relative_path": "brand/legal/customer-logo-and-quote-policy.md"}, {"chunk_id": "5f590c06-fa98-48f5-82ff-5c20b8a3ac8f", "content": "# Email playbook

Owner: Ilse Varga-Holm's team (lifecycle). Rewritten for the March 2026 platform migration, revised September 2026.

", "heading_path": ["Email playbook"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "60fd8029-020c-42ea-8ffa-c11621d95fe2", "content": "## The short version

| Thing | Limit |
|---|---|
| Email length | 220 words at most, body text, including the sign-off |
| Subject line | 48 characters at most, counted with spaces |
| Links | One main action. More links are fine in a newsletter, and a second link is fine in a customer notice |
| Sends per contact | Two marketing sends a week at most, customer notices excluded |

The 48-character limit comes from the phone inbox preview, where the back half of a longer subject gets cut. We pulled a sample of opens in early 2026 and most were on phones, so the preview is the version people actually read.

", "heading_path": ["Email playbook", "The short version"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "668f858f-133e-4581-b3b0-c0ca0a2f6f13", "content": "## Founder voice and brand voice

There are two voices at Wickhold, and they have one hard line between them.

**Founder voice is first person singular, and it is signed.** Maren writes as "I". Her posts carry her name. She gets to have feelings and doubts, tell a story from a bad night in 2017, and be wrong in public. Dov's technical posts work the same way and are signed "Dov".

**Brand voice never says "I" or "we think".** Website, product pages, company LinkedIn, the company X account, email, decks, reports: no first person singular, ever. "We believe", "we feel" and "in our view" are "we think" in different shoes, and they go too.

**Brand voice uses "Wickhold" or "we" for facts only.** Things that happened, things that are true of the company, things a lawyer could check.

| Fine in brand voice | Not in brand voice |
|---|---|
| We renewed SOC 2 Type II in January 2026. | We think SOC 2 matters. |
| Wickhold serves more than 140 customers. | I've talked to a lot of platform teams. |
| Containment is where incidents are won or lost. | We believe containment is where incidents are won or lost. |

The third row is the useful one. Brand voice still holds opinions. It states them as flat sentences, the way the on-call lead does, and lets the reader disagree. "We think" adds nothing except a hedge.

Practicalities. Nobody else writes as "I" in Wickhold content. Kofi's developer posts and anything from the wider team run in brand voice under a byline, because a byline is credit and a founder post is a person speaking for themselves. Customer quotes are quotes and say whatever was approved. If the content team drafts for Maren, she reads it and changes it before her name goes on, and a post that she has not read does not go out. In the spring a joint Maren-and-Dov byline was tried on one post; "I" became unreadable after two paragraphs, so that was dropped. One author per post.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "Founder voice and brand voice"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "8e229f98-1ea5-4a28-8b10-5f4b455449ff", "content": "## Email preheader

Every email has a preheader of at most 90 characters. It shows beside or under the subject line in most inboxes, so treat it as the second half of the subject. It must add something. Don't repeat the subject, and don't leave the field empty, or the client will fill it with the first text in the email, which for us is often the "view in browser" line.

Good: `Survey of 412 platform and security leaders on what happens after detection.`

Bad: `Containment Report 2026 is out. Read the Containment Report 2026 today.`

", "heading_path": ["Email templates", "Email preheader"], "relative_path": "brand/templates/email-templates.md"}, {"chunk_id": "9444a373-5e1b-44c8-b229-396932ea45d4", "content": "## Body

Most of our email has three parts.

1. **What happened or what's new.** One or two sentences.
2. **Why it matters to this reader.** Two to four sentences. Different for a CISO list and a platform list, which is why the tracks are separate.
3. **What to do.** One button or link. Then the sign-off.

The working drafts are in the email templates, and the merge fields there match the sending platform. Start from a template. A blank page tends to produce an email that's 400 words long.

Good body copy, platform track:

> You downloaded the Containment Report, so here's the practical follow-up. Our rollout guide starts with Wickhold Quenchline in observe mode on one namespace, then moves to contain mode once you've read two to four weeks of would-have-acted events.
>
> It takes about an hour, and the failure modes are listed at the end.

Good body copy, CISO track:

> Decide whether your team tracks time to contain today. Your board will ask how long a runtime incident takes to contain. In our survey of 412 platform and security leaders, the median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].
>
> The report sets out how teams measure that number and what they report upward. If your team doesn't track it, section two is a place to start.

Bad body copy:

> Hope you're having a great week! As a valued member of our community, we wanted to reach out and share some exciting content we think you'll love. In today's rapidly evolving threat landscape, security has never been more important.

Four sentences in and the reader has learned nothing. Cut until the first sentence is the news.

Personalization: first name in the greeting when we have it, and role-based copy through segments. Anything else, like company size, industry or recent page views, stays out of the visible copy. Being told what you browsed by a security company is unsettling.

", "heading_path": ["Email playbook", "Body"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/email-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "b39ffdf9-91aa-4c47-a19d-da6e58b90e6e", "content": "## 12. Social and email formatting

- No emoji in brand posts or email. Founders can do as they like on their own accounts within reason.
- One link per post. Put it where it reads naturally; shortened links are for tracking and shouldn't appear as bare text where the full domain would fit.
- Line breaks on LinkedIn mark real paragraph breaks. No one-sentence-per-line posts.
- Greeting in email: "Hi Sam," with the first name and a comma, or no greeting for a broadcast. No "Dear". No "Hey there".
- Plain sign-off: name, job, company, or the team name on a broadcast. Nobody signs "Cheers" on a customer notice.
- In email, check that the piece reads correctly with images off.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "12. Social and email formatting"], "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "ca65b949-2e3b-43fc-b1a9-0f6770fb82d8", "content": "## CTA format for all channels

This lives here because the email team wrote it down first, and it now applies to every channel: email, landing pages, paid, social, the blog, event pages.

A CTA, the call to action on a button or a link, is at most four words, and it starts with a verb. The same CTA wording rules apply wherever the button sits. "Learn more" and "Click here" are banned everywhere, including as link text inside a sentence.

| Fine | Not fine |
|---|---|
| Read the report | Learn more |
| Book a demo | Click here |
| See the rollout guide | Click here to see the rollout guide |
| Request early access | Early access request |
| Save your seat | Your seat is waiting for you |

Say what happens on the other side of the click. "Get started" is allowed but weak, so use something more specific if you can.

", "heading_path": ["Email templates", "CTA format for all channels"], "relative_path": "brand/templates/email-templates.md"}, {"chunk_id": "f85915ac-8ed5-47a1-b0b7-df460f5be9ef", "content": "## 3. Banned claims

| Do not say | Say instead, or do this | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| "prevents prompt injection" | "limits what a compromised agent can do" | Leashgate acts on tool calls. It does not read intent and it cannot promise that an agent will not be manipulated. The claim is false as a matter of product design |
| "FedRAMP Authorized", "FedRAMP certified" | See section 4 | Neither is true |
| "GDPR compliant" | Use the regional rules | Regional wording sits there, and the ban is not limited to that region |
| "breach-proof", "unhackable", "impossible to escape" | Describe the containment action | No security product can support an absolute |
| "zero false positives", "100% detection", "catches everything" | Give a sourced figure or say nothing | We hold no such evidence |
| "guarantee", "guaranteed", "warranty" outside a contract | Remove | These words have legal effect. Service credits live in the order form |
| "the leading", "the fastest", "No. 1", "the only" | Remove, or bring me the comparison data | Superlatives need current comparative substantiation, and we do not hold any |
| "certified by", "endorsed by", "partner of" for any standards body or open-source project | Remove | Using eBPF or Helm is not an endorsement from anyone |
| "saves $X", any return-on-investment figure | Remove | We have no approved financial outcome for any customer |

Two refinements, because they keep coming back:

"Helps prevent" is a banned claim dressed up. A qualifier in front of a promise does not make it a limited promise.

"Compliance-ready" and "audit-ready" were requested in June for a trust page and refused. Wickhold can describe what the product records. Whether a customer passes an audit depends on the customer and the auditor.

Wickhold Quenchline takes a containment action only in contain mode. In observe mode it records what it would have done. Copy describing automatic containment must therefore be true of contain mode and should say so where a reader could assume otherwise. Containment actions are isolating a pod's network, freezing a process and draining a node. Do not add to the list without product confirmation.

Wickhold Evenburn reports drift, exposure paths and a fix order. It does not change a customer's environment by itself, and copy should not imply that it does.

|---|---|---|---|

Use the quote as it stands in the signed approval, with the person's name, title and company. Do not trim it so that the meaning shifts, stitch two quotes together, or update a title without asking. The written approval sits with Legal. If someone on the list changes jobs, stop using the quote until Legal has confirmed it.

Approvals cover website, email, social, sales decks, reports and event slides. They do not cover paid advertising or press releases. Each of those goes back to the customer through the account owner, one asset at a time.

Logos come from the brand library, in the supplied one-color versions. Don't recolor one, crop it, or take it from the customer's website. On a logo wall, keep the customers in alphabetical order so that nobody reads an endorsement ranking into it. Don't tag either company, or its people, on social unless the account owner has checked first. Every piece of external copy containing a claim from section 1 or 2 is reviewed against this document by its author. Copy containing a new claim, a customer name, or a reference to a security incident also comes to me. Press releases and the annual report come to me regardless.

Exceptions are given in writing, for one asset, and expire with that asset. I have given two this year. Neither should be taken as a precedent.

If this document disagrees with a guideline, a playbook, a deck or a comment from a senior colleague, this document wins. If it disagrees with reality, tell me, and I will change it.

Reviewed each quarter with Ilse Varga-Holm and Noor Eskelund.

A landing page is 500 words at most. That counts every word a visitor can read on the page: headline, subheads, body, proof, form labels and the FAQ. Navigation and the site footer don't count.

If the page runs over, cut sections. Don't shrink the type or tuck copy into tabs and accordions. It still counts, and the page is still doing too many things. Long-form material belongs in the report, a blog post or the docs, and the page links there.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "1. Claims approved as written"], "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "383000ed-25fc-4fa8-8a32-0a9cb7da5f80", "content": "## How the sentences go

**Short first.** Most sentences run under twenty words. The long ones earn it by carrying a real sequence of events.

**Verbs do the work.** Name who did what. "Quenchline froze the process" over "the process was frozen". Past tense for incidents, present tense for what the product does.

**End early.** Our most common edit is deleting the last line of a paragraph. Writers tend to add one that restates the point in a nicer rhythm. Readers don't need it. This goes double for the final line of a piece.

**Ration the fire.** The tagline is "Small fires stay small." It carries the metaphor so the copy doesn't have to. A piece gets at most one fire image, and many pieces should have none. Nothing ignites, sparks, blazes or fans the flames. Slow Burn Summit gets to keep its name.

**Plain words for plain things.** "Use", "start", "stop", "run". Reach for the fancier word and the reader assumes something is being hidden.

**Don't argue with the reader's experience.** Telling a platform engineer that alerts are overwhelming is telling them what they had for breakfast. Start from what they know and add something.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "How the sentences go"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "39544f3e-3ce8-49ae-b7bb-0c805ed0fe8c", "content": "## Every page has one job

Before anyone writes copy, the brief answers three things.

- Who lands here, and from where (paid search, a nurture email, a Field Day QR code)
- What they should do next
- What proof they need to do it

A page aimed at both a CISO and a platform engineer ends up serving neither. We build two pages and route by campaign. The rollout guide page for engineers shows commands and flags above the fold. The executive page for the same product leads with what the decision is and what it costs in time.

", "heading_path": ["Landing pages", "Every page has one job"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/landing-page-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "412b98db-a59b-4fa4-afb4-aada12ba8243", "content": "Certification status: sheet kept by Priit Salonen. Last checked 2 October 2026.

Sales, this is the sheet to use before you answer a security questionnaire. If a deck or an old email says something different, the deck or the email is out of date.

| Program | Status | What you may say |
|---|---|---|
| SOC 2 Type II | Held. Renewed January 2026 | "Wickhold holds SOC 2 Type II." |
| FedRAMP Moderate | In process. Not held | "Wickhold is pursuing FedRAMP Moderate authorization." |

**FedRAMP.** Never claim FedRAMP authorization or certification. The approved wording above is the only wording. It goes in copy exactly as written, including the word "pursuing".

These are banned in every channel, spoken or written: "FedRAMP Authorized", "FedRAMP certified", "FedRAMP Ready", "FedRAMP compliant", "FedRAMP equivalent", "built to FedRAMP standards". Agency buyers read those words literally, and a false statement to a federal buyer is a contract and legal problem, whatever the deal size.

The status changes when authorization is complete and published, and this sheet says so. An assessor's visit, a sponsor conversation, or a positive meeting does not change it. Do not give prospects a target date. We do not publish one. If a federal prospect presses, the answer is the sentence above and an offer to connect them with me.

Good, in an answer to a questionnaire:

> Wickhold holds SOC 2 Type II, renewed January 2026. Wickhold is pursuing FedRAMP Moderate authorization. We can share the SOC 2 report under NDA.

Bad:

> We're basically FedRAMP Authorized, the paperwork is just finishing up.

**SOC 2.** The report goes out under NDA through the account team, never by public link. Say "Type II" every time. Say "held" or "renewed", and do not say "SOC 2 certified", because SOC 2 ends in an attestation report and not a certificate.

**Questionnaires and RFPs.** Security questionnaires go through the account team, and any answer about certifications is copied from this sheet. If a form offers only "Yes" or "No" for FedRAMP, answer "No", and use the comments box for the approved sentence. Do not tick a box in the hope of explaining later.

", "heading_path": [], "relative_path": "brand/legal/certifications-status.md"}, {"chunk_id": "4efa700b-1645-41eb-89bc-1d8aeb1b7fb2", "content": "### Review before publishing

Most work needs one reviewer. Riskier work needs more.

| Type of work | Review |
|---|---|
| Routine social post or email from an approved template | A peer in marketing |
| New blog post or landing page | Peer, plus Noor's team for brand |
| Any technical how-to or product detail | Developer relations |
| Anything with a new claim, statistic, customer name or certification mention | Legal, before design starts, except third-party statistics under section 5 of the approved claims |
| Anything signed by a founder | The founder personally, with no exceptions |
| Press releases | Ilse and Legal |

Legal's turnaround is set in the approved claims. Brand review takes two working days. If a deadline can't take that, say so at the start of the work and not the night before. Anything already on the approved claims list needs no further sign-off for the claim itself, which is the reason to use it word for word.

Maintained by Legal. Reviewed by Priit Salonen and Noor Eskelund, July 2026.

Cite only customers listed as approved below. That covers names, logos, quotes, results, case studies and any description that would let a reader work out who the customer is. A customer who likes us on a call has not approved anything.

", "heading_path": ["Customer logo and quote policy"], "relative_path": "brand/legal/customer-logo-and-quote-policy.md"}, {"chunk_id": "5b924c2e-d5ac-458e-9271-f95a845d565a", "content": "### Admit limits

One of the company values, and the one marketing finds hardest. Every product we sell has an edge. Wickhold Evenburn finds drift and exposure paths; it does not contain anything. Quenchline contains what is running; it does not patch the image it came from. Saying so costs a little in the moment and buys a lot of belief for the next claim on the page. Engineers look for the catch. When they find we already named it, they keep reading.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "What Wickhold believes", "Admit limits"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "819d53ad-e32a-41b3-94ae-7ccd3f1cc7d5", "content": "### Everything else

- **Measurements take digits, always.** Anything with a unit: 220 nodes, 11 minutes, 7.4 hours, 90 days, 38 seconds, 1,900 nodes.
- **Counts of ordinary things** spell out one to nine and use digits from 10: "three clusters", "12 namespaces". Mixed in one sentence, go with digits.
- **Commas from 1,000 up.** No "1.9k nodes", not even on social.
- **Keep the decimal the source gave you.** 7.4 hours stays 7.4 hours. Don't round to "about seven hours", and don't add precision the source lacks.
- **Approved sentences stay as approved.** The report line says "more than six hours", spelled out, and that's how it runs in every piece. The same goes for "more than 140 customers", which never becomes "140+". Legal approved the sentence, and this guide doesn't get to tidy it.
- **Don't do arithmetic on claims.** Lowmoor went from 4 hours to 11 minutes. Do not convert that into a percentage or an "x times faster". The figures we can stand behind are the two figures we were given. Same for adding results from different customers together.
- **No "up to".** "Up to" numbers are a best case wearing a fact's clothes. Give the median, or say which run you mean.
- **No tildes or "approx."** in published copy. If a figure is an estimate, say "about".

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "4. Numbers", "Everything else"], "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "a1cb5f0e-a0a0-4e46-9bcf-3ae99202023b", "content": "## Hero copy

The hero says what the product does and who it's for, in that order. Lead with what happens to the reader's workload. Our tagline can sit in the hero of the brand page, but it doesn't describe a product, so product pages shouldn't rely on it.

Good, product page:

> **Contain runtime failures before they spread**
> Wickhold Quenchline detects bad behavior in Kubernetes and isolates a pod, freezes a process or drains a node, under the policy you set.
> [Book a demo]

Good, posture page:

> **Know which misconfiguration to fix first**
> Wickhold Evenburn tracks drift across cloud and cluster, finds each exposure path and gives your team a fix order.
> [See a sample report]

Good, early access page:

> **Set policy for what AI agents can call**
> Wickhold Leashgate, in early access, applies tool-call policy at runtime and limits what a compromised agent can do.
> [Request early access]

Good, report page:

> **The Wickhold Containment Report 2026**
> A survey of 412 platform and security leaders on how long containment takes, and where the hours go.
> [Read the report]

Good, brand page:

> **Small fires stay small.**
> Wickhold is the runtime security company for teams that run Kubernetes.
> [See how it works]

Bad, from a 2025 agency concept:

> **Next-level cloud security for the modern enterprise**
> One powerful platform. Total confidence. Peace of mind at every layer of your stack.

Nothing in that hero says what the software does. It would fit a mattress company if you swapped "stack" for "bed".

", "heading_path": ["Landing pages", "Hero copy"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/landing-page-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "c1079d42-ff19-496b-9bbf-e72c382dc03d", "content": "## Page skeleton and word budget

| Section | Budget (words) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Hero: headline, one sentence, CTA | 40 | Must make sense with no scrolling |
| Proof strip: customer logos or one number | 25 | One row, no carousel |
| What it does: three blocks at most | 150 | Concrete actions, not themes |
| How it works or how you roll it out | 100 | Steps. Commands if the audience is technical |
| Customer proof: one result, one quote | 70 | A full sentence with the number and the source |
| FAQ: three questions at most | 80 | Real questions from sales calls |
| Closing CTA | 15 | Same action as the hero |
| **Total** | **480** | Leaves 20 words of slack |

CTAs follow the shared CTA format in the email templates. Use one primary CTA per page, repeated at the top and bottom with the same wording. A secondary link is allowed for a technical reader who is not ready for a form, like the docs or the rollout guide.

", "heading_path": ["Landing pages", "Page skeleton and word budget"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/landing-page-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "c1483026-3308-4a52-8cf9-e6314d11b35f", "content": "## 6. Grammar and punctuation

- **American spelling** in all copy, including copy going to UK and EU readers. Containerize, not containerise.
- **Oxford comma**, always. It has settled more than one argument in Kubernetes prose, where lists of nouns can double as lists of objects.
- **Active voice** with a named actor, wherever the actor is known. "Wickhold Quenchline drained the node." If the passive is hiding who did it and that person is us, it goes.
- **Tense.** Past for what happened, present for what the product does, and nothing in the future except where a date is public.
- **Contractions** are fine in the blog, on social and in email. Skip them on legal pages and in anything aimed at a board.
- **Colons** are our favorite punctuation mark and they're doing fine. Use them to introduce the fact.
- **Semicolons** at most once a page. If there are two, one wants to be a full stop.
- **Em dashes** rarely in body copy. Most are a full stop that lost its nerve. Spaced en dashes are not a substitute.
- **Parentheses** for the short aside only. If the aside matters, promote it to a sentence.
- **Quotation marks:** double, with commas and full stops inside, American style, except for literal strings in technical writing where the punctuation would change the meaning. Single quotes only inside double.
- **Italics:** titles of reports and the occasional stress only. They disappear on Soot grounds and in email.
- **Bold:** for scanning in long documents, once or twice per section. Bold on a landing page means the design isn't working.
- **Ampersands:** only in proper names. Plain "and" in headlines too.
- **"And/or"** is a legal term. Pick one.
- **Slashes** as a shortcut ("platform/security teams") get rewritten: "platform and security teams".

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "6. Grammar and punctuation"], "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "ca65b949-2e3b-43fc-b1a9-0f6770fb82d8", "content": "## CTA format for all channels

This lives here because the email team wrote it down first, and it now applies to every channel: email, landing pages, paid, social, the blog, event pages.

A CTA, the call to action on a button or a link, is at most four words, and it starts with a verb. The same CTA wording rules apply wherever the button sits. "Learn more" and "Click here" are banned everywhere, including as link text inside a sentence.

| Fine | Not fine |
|---|---|
| Read the report | Learn more |
| Book a demo | Click here |
| See the rollout guide | Click here to see the rollout guide |
| Request early access | Early access request |
| Save your seat | Your seat is waiting for you |

Say what happens on the other side of the click. "Get started" is allowed but weak, so use something more specific if you can.

", "heading_path": ["Email templates", "CTA format for all channels"], "relative_path": "brand/templates/email-templates.md"}, {"chunk_id": "ee7ebdc2-770e-478f-b74d-48f65cec36ad", "content": "## Review

Every landing page hero is a first use for that page and goes through Brand. Paid landing pages also go to Legal for the claims on the page, and the image goes along with them, because a screenshot can make a claim too.

Allow two working days for Brand. Campaign deadlines are not exempt, so book it when the page is scoped.
", "heading_path": ["Landing page imagery", "Review"], "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/landing-page-imagery.md"}, {"chunk_id": "f85915ac-8ed5-47a1-b0b7-df460f5be9ef", "content": "## 3. Banned claims

| Do not say | Say instead, or do this | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| "prevents prompt injection" | "limits what a compromised agent can do" | Leashgate acts on tool calls. It does not read intent and it cannot promise that an agent will not be manipulated. The claim is false as a matter of product design |
| "FedRAMP Authorized", "FedRAMP certified" | See section 4 | Neither is true |
| "GDPR compliant" | Use the regional rules | Regional wording sits there, and the ban is not limited to that region |
| "breach-proof", "unhackable", "impossible to escape" | Describe the containment action | No security product can support an absolute |
| "zero false positives", "100% detection", "catches everything" | Give a sourced figure or say nothing | We hold no such evidence |
| "guarantee", "guaranteed", "warranty" outside a contract | Remove | These words have legal effect. Service credits live in the order form |
| "the leading", "the fastest", "No. 1", "the only" | Remove, or bring me the comparison data | Superlatives need current comparative substantiation, and we do not hold any |
| "certified by", "endorsed by", "partner of" for any standards body or open-source project | Remove | Using eBPF or Helm is not an endorsement from anyone |
| "saves $X", any return-on-investment figure | Remove | We have no approved financial outcome for any customer |

Two refinements, because they keep coming back:

"Helps prevent" is a banned claim dressed up. A qualifier in front of a promise does not make it a limited promise.

"Compliance-ready" and "audit-ready" were requested in June for a trust page and refused. Wickhold can describe what the product records. Whether a customer passes an audit depends on the customer and the auditor.

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "1. Length"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "2ed35bac-e511-4a05-b03f-f56a94ab438a", "content": "## 3. Citations

**Short first.** Most sentences run under twenty words. The long ones earn it by carrying a real sequence of events.

Humor depends on the audience, see each persona.

A blog intro must cite a market statistic. Put it in the first two sentences, in the citation format from the style guide, and follow it with one sentence that says why this post exists. ", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "2. The intro"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "c1483026-3308-4a52-8cf9-e6314d11b35f", "content": "## 6. Grammar and punctuation

- **American spelling** in all copy, including copy going to UK and EU readers. Containerize, not containerise.
- **Oxford comma**, always. It has settled more than one argument in Kubernetes prose, where lists of nouns can double as lists of objects.
- **Active voice** with a named actor, wherever the actor is known. "Wickhold Quenchline drained the node." If the passive is hiding who did it and that person is us, it goes.
- **Tense.** Past for what happened, present for what the product does, and nothing in the future except where a date is public.
- **Contractions** are fine in the blog, on social and in email. Skip them on legal pages and in anything aimed at a board.
- **Colons** are our favorite punctuation mark and they're doing fine. Use them to introduce the fact.
- **Semicolons** at most once a page. If there are two, one wants to be a full stop.
- **Em dashes** rarely in body copy. Most are a full stop that lost its nerve. Spaced en dashes are not a substitute.
- **Parentheses** for the short aside only. If the aside matters, promote it to a sentence.
- **Quotation marks:** double, with commas and full stops inside, American style, except for literal strings in technical writing where the punctuation would change the meaning. Single quotes only inside double.
- **Italics:** titles of reports and the occasional stress only. They disappear on Soot grounds and in email.
- **Bold:** for scanning in long documents, once or twice per section. Bold on a landing page means the design isn't working.
- **Ampersands:** only in proper names. Plain "and" in headlines too.
- **"And/or"** is a legal term. Pick one.
- **Slashes** as a shortcut ("platform/security teams") get rewritten: "platform and security teams".

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "6. Grammar and punctuation"], "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "ca3468d9-9da9-4734-a3d6-9c0497716473", "content": "## 5. Statistics: 12-month age limit

A market statistic may not be older than 12 months at publication. This is the limit on how old a statistic can be, and it is measured on the day the piece goes out, not the day it was drafted. A post queued in March for release in May is checked against May.

The limit applies to market and survey statistics only. It covers any figure that describes the industry, the market, or a population of teams. It does not apply to customer results such as the Lowmoor and Ostler outcomes, or to product metrics such as the lab figures, which have their own qualifier.

The age of a statistic runs from the publication date of its source. Fieldwork dates do not matter. A report re-quoted in a newer article keeps its original date, so a 2026 article quoting a 2024 survey is a 2024 statistic.

Applied to our own reports:

| Source | Published | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Wickhold Containment Report 2026 | April 14, 2026 | Usable for publication through April 14, 2027 |
| Wickhold Field Report 2024 | 2024 | Past the 12 months limit |
| Wickhold Field Report 2023 | 2023 | Past the 12 months limit |

The two Containment Report statistics in section 1 are the only market statistics of ours inside the limit today. The Field Report figures still appear in old decks and old posts. That is an archive problem and not a permission. Do not reuse them. Do not reword them to make them feel new, and do not refer to them as "historically" true.

Fresh third-party statistics are allowed without coming to me first, with the source link and the date of the source in the copy. The source must be a named publisher and the figure must appear on the page you link to. A figure found in a vendor's blog, quoting another vendor's blog, gets traced to the original or is dropped. The third party's name still has to clear the competitor rules.

When the 2027 Containment Report is published, section 1 will be updated and the 2026 figures remain usable until they reach the limit. Old assets stay in the archive as they are. They are not re-promoted once a market statistic in them has expired. Paid and email reuse counts as publication.

This lives here because the email team wrote it down first, and it now applies to every channel: email, landing pages, paid, social, the blog, event pages.

The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. This post explains how regulated security teams can assess vendor status and organize posture work. The report surveyed 412 platform and security leaders.

## Separate a vendor’s status from your own readiness

A vendor’s documented status and your organization’s audit preparation answer different questions. Start by asking what the vendor holds or is pursuing, which service or product the statement covers, and what documentation the vendor can provide. Record the answer in the vendor review rather than translating it into a broader conclusion.

Wickhold holds SOC 2 Type II, renewed January 2026. Wickhold is pursuing FedRAMP Moderate authorization. These are two distinct statements. Neither, on its own, establishes that a customer’s environment meets an audit requirement or that a particular deployment fits a customer’s needs.

For a review, keep the wording and evidence together. Note the date you checked the status, who confirmed it, and which service or scope the evidence describes. If a status is still in process, record that accurately. Don’t turn a plan, conversation, or pending step into a completed authorization. If the vendor provides a report under agreed access terms, note where your team stores it and who can review it.

Then make the internal decision explicit: what evidence does your organization need before it approves the vendor, and who owns that decision? Security, procurement, legal, and the service owner may need different details. A short record of the question, evidence, owner, and next step gives the review a clear path without implying that the vendor’s status completes your work.

## Keep audit preparation in your own workflow

Your team controls its own preparation. Begin with the systems, owners, and evidence your review actually covers. A useful working record can include the system or service, the relevant control or requirement, the evidence location, its owner, and the next review date. Keep gaps visible rather than smoothing them into a general status like “ready.”

For each finding, assign a person to assess it and a next action. Some findings need investigation. Others need a change, a documented exception, or a decision from the control owner. Record what the team chose and why. A report can help people see what to examine, but your team still decides how to address a finding and what evidence supports that decision.

This distinction matters when several teams share responsibility. A security leader may own the review process; a platform engineer may understand the affected workload; and an application owner may know the operational impact of a change. Give each person a defined part of the work. Agree on how the team will track decisions and when it will revisit open items.

Treat the record as a working tool, not a promise about an audit outcome. The usefulness of the process depends on your organization’s scope, evidence, and decisions. A clear list of owners and next actions can make posture work easier to coordinate without claiming that a vendor or a product makes the organization audit-ready.

## Use posture reporting to decide what to investigate

Wickhold Evenburn reports drift, exposure paths, and a fix order. That gives a team information to review and prioritize. It does not change a customer’s environment by itself. Engineers and security owners still need to assess the reported issue, decide what action fits their environment, and make or approve that change.

A practical review starts with the report, not an assumption about what the product has done. Confirm what the finding describes and which workload or configuration it concerns. Check the path and the surrounding context. Then decide whether the suggested order fits your team’s risk, ownership, and current work. If it does not, record the reason and the decision-maker rather than treating the order as an automatic instruction.

That process can connect posture work to an existing review queue. Assign an owner, note what evidence the owner needs, and track the decision and follow-up. If the team accepts a fix, it can manage that change through its normal workflow. If it defers the work, record who accepted the risk and when the team will review it again. The report helps inform the decision; it does not make the decision for you.

## Keep containment separate from posture work

Wickhold Quenchline provides supporting context for runtime containment, which is different from Evenburn’s reporting role. Quenchline takes a containment action only in contain mode. In observe mode, it records what it would have done. Its actions are isolating a pod’s network, freezing a process, and draining a node.

That distinction helps teams assess what they are evaluating. Evenburn reports drift and exposure paths; it does not contain anything. Quenchline can take the listed containment actions in contain mode; it does not patch the image an application came from. Keep those functions separate in a review, and ask which workflow, operating mode, and team decision apply to the task in front of you.

## Set the next step before the review ends

On Monday, choose one vendor review or posture queue to examine. Write down the question the team needs to answer, the evidence it will check, and the person responsible for the next action. Keep the vendor’s documented status separate from your organization’s audit preparation, and use posture reports as input to your team’s decisions.

{"brand_rules": {"evidence": [{"chunk_id": "383000ed-25fc-4fa8-8a32-0a9cb7da5f80", "content": "## How the sentences go

**Short first.** Most sentences run under twenty words. The long ones earn it by carrying a real sequence of events.

**Verbs do the work.** Name who did what. "Quenchline froze the process" over "the process was frozen". Past tense for incidents, present tense for what the product does.

**End early.** Our most common edit is deleting the last line of a paragraph. Writers tend to add one that restates the point in a nicer rhythm. Readers don't need it. This goes double for the final line of a piece.

**Ration the fire.** The tagline is "Small fires stay small." It carries the metaphor so the copy doesn't have to. A piece gets at most one fire image, and many pieces should have none. Nothing ignites, sparks, blazes or fans the flames. Slow Burn Summit gets to keep its name.

**Plain words for plain things.** "Use", "start", "stop", "run". Reach for the fancier word and the reader assumes something is being hidden.

**Don't argue with the reader's experience.** Telling a platform engineer that alerts are overwhelming is telling them what they had for breakfast. Start from what they know and add something.

2. **The context.** Two or three sentences on why it matters to someone running clusters or answering for them.

- A LinkedIn post is 180 words at most. Count everything, including the link line.
- About the first 200 characters show before the "see more" cut on most phones. The news has to fit in that space.
- Short paragraphs, one to three lines each, with a blank line between them.

- Image guidance sits with the visual rules. Every company page post gets one image, except short hiring notes.

The voice stays the same. How much of it you get changes with the room.

**Landing pages.** The flattest we get. Mechanical, confident, short. The reader is deciding whether to spend ten more minutes, so tell them what the thing does on a cluster and let them go. "Wickhold Quenchline isolates the pod, freezes the process or drains the node, then writes down what it did."

**Blog.** The most room to think. Brand-voice posts walk through how something fails. Dov's posts can argue, and they should. A good post leaves the reader able to do one thing they could not do before, even if they never buy. Avoid the summary paragraph at the end. If the post worked, the reader was there.

**LinkedIn.** The company page is brand voice. Founder posts are where the personality lives. A post runs about 200 words, which suits one story and one point. Write as a person with a job, not a thought leader: no line breaks after every sentence, no "here's what I learned", no lists of lessons from an outage.

**X.** One fact, or one observation, in a dry tone. The account does not chase the news and does not reply to arguments about vendors. It's fine for a post to be plain. "The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. That is most of a night shift."

**Email.** One person writing to one person who is busy. Say why you are writing in the first sentence. Assume it is being read on a phone in a hallway. No "I hope this finds you well", and since these are brand emails, no "I" at all unless Maren signed it. Customer notices are the exception to everything else in this list and sound like the incident channel at the top of this document.

**Product UI and error text.** The closest thing we have to pure voice. What happened, what state things are in, what to do. "Containment action failed on node `ip-10-2-14-7`: agent unreachable. **Case studies.** Third person, numbers up front, the customer's team as the subject of most sentences. Enough detail about their environment that a peer recognizes it. A case study that could describe any customer describes none of them.

There are two voices at Wickhold, and they have one hard line between them.

**Founder voice is first person singular, and it is signed.** Maren writes as "I". Her posts carry her name. She gets to have feelings and doubts, tell a story from a bad night in 2017, and be wrong in public. Dov's technical posts work the same way and are signed "Dov".

**Brand voice never says "I" or "we think".** Website, product pages, company LinkedIn, the company X account, email, decks, reports: no first person singular, ever. "We believe", "we feel" and "in our view" are "we think" in different shoes, and they go too.

**Brand voice uses "Wickhold" or "we" for facts only.** Things that happened, things that are true of the company, things a lawyer could check.

| Fine in brand voice | Not in brand voice |
|---|---|
| We renewed SOC 2 Type II in January 2026. | We think SOC 2 matters. |
| Wickhold serves more than 140 customers. | I've talked to a lot of platform teams. |
| Containment is where incidents are won or lost. | We believe containment is where incidents are won or lost. |

The third row is the useful one. Brand voice still holds opinions. It states them as flat sentences, the way the on-call lead does, and lets the reader disagree. "We think" adds nothing except a hedge.

Practicalities. Nobody else writes as "I" in Wickhold content. Kofi's developer posts and anything from the wider team run in brand voice under a byline, because a byline is credit and a founder post is a person speaking for themselves. Customer quotes are quotes and say whatever was approved. If the content team drafts for Maren, she reads it and changes it before her name goes on, and a post that she has not read does not go out. In the spring a joint Maren-and-Dov byline was tried on one post; "I" became unreadable after two paragraphs, so that was dropped. One author per post.

Grammar and punctuation

- **American spelling** in all copy, including copy going to UK and EU readers. Containerize, not containerise.
- **Oxford comma**, always. It has settled more than one argument in Kubernetes prose, where lists of nouns can double as lists of objects.
- **Active voice** with a named actor, wherever the actor is known. "Wickhold Quenchline drained the node." If the passive is hiding who did it and that person is us, it goes.
- **Tense.** Past for what happened, present for what the product does, and nothing in the future except where a date is public.
- **Contractions** are fine in the blog, on social and in email. Skip them on legal pages and in anything aimed at a board.
- **Colons** are our favorite punctuation mark and they're doing fine. Use them to introduce the fact.
- **Semicolons** at most once a page. If there are two, one wants to be a full stop.
- **Em dashes** rarely in body copy. Most are a full stop that lost its nerve. Spaced en dashes are not a substitute.
- **Parentheses** for the short aside only. If the aside matters, promote it to a sentence.
- **Quotation marks:** double, with commas and full stops inside, American style, except for literal strings in technical writing where the punctuation would change the meaning. Single quotes only inside double.
- **Italics:** titles of reports and the occasional stress only. They disappear on Soot grounds and in email.
- **Bold:** for scanning in long documents, once or twice per section. Bold on a landing page means the design isn't working.
- **Ampersands:** only in proper names. Plain "and" in headlines too.
- **"And/or"** is a legal term. Pick one.
- **Slashes** as a shortcut ("platform/security teams") get rewritten: "platform and security teams".
