Noor Eskelund. Last edit 12 August 2026, after the Leashgate early access posts. Ask in the brand channel before you ask me by email.

LinkedIn is the one channel where CISOs, platform leads and our own hiring pipeline all look at the same feed. Most of what we post there is read on a phone, between meetings, by someone who has never heard of us. Write for that person.

", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "1b2ec0a3-937b-43d7-a777-88143fa3b565", "content": "## Tone by channel

The voice stays the same. How much of it you get changes with the room.

**Landing pages.** The flattest we get. Mechanical, confident, short. The reader is deciding whether to spend ten more minutes, so tell them what the thing does on a cluster and let them go. "Wickhold Quenchline isolates the pod, freezes the process or drains the node, then writes down what it did."

**Blog.** The most room to think. Brand-voice posts walk through how something fails. Dov's posts can argue, and they should. A good post leaves the reader able to do one thing they could not do before, even if they never buy. Avoid the summary paragraph at the end. If the post worked, the reader was there.

**LinkedIn.** The company page is brand voice. Founder posts are where the personality lives. A post runs about 200 words, which suits one story and one point. Write as a person with a job, not a thought leader: no line breaks after every sentence, no "here's what I learned", no lists of lessons from an outage.

**X.** One fact, or one observation, in a dry tone. The account does not chase the news and does not reply to arguments about vendors. It's fine for a post to be plain. "The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. That is most of a night shift."

**Email.** One person writing to one person who is busy. Say why you are writing in the first sentence. Assume it is being read on a phone in a hallway. No "I hope this finds you well", and since these are brand emails, no "I" at all unless Maren signed it. Customer notices are the exception to everything else in this list and sound like the incident channel at the top of this document.

**Product UI and error text.** The closest thing we have to pure voice. What happened, what state things are in, what to do. "Containment action failed on node `ip-10-2-14-7`: agent unreachable. The pod is still running. Retry or drain the node." Chirpy empty states were tried in 2025 and came out after a customer saw one during a real incident.

**Case studies.** Third person, numbers up front, the customer's team as the subject of most sentences. Enough detail about their environment that a peer recognizes it. A case study that could describe any customer describes none of them.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "Tone by channel"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "33d10c5d-c881-4d79-95fa-1edc60d3c984", "content": "## 1. Claims approved as written

| Topic | Approved wording | Evidence held by |
|---|---|---|
| Customer count | "more than 140 customers" | Finance, reconciled quarterly |
| Market, time to contain | "41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident" | Wickhold Containment Report 2026 |
| Market, median | "the median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours" | Wickhold Containment Report 2026 |
| Lowmoor Credit Union | Time to contain fell from 4 hours to 11 minutes, 220 nodes | Signed customer approval |
| Ostler Grocers | 63% fewer open critical misconfigurations in 90 days, 1,900 nodes | Signed customer approval |
| SOC 2 | Wickhold holds SOC 2 Type II, renewed January 2026 | Legal |
| Agent policy | "limits what a compromised agent can do" | Legal and product |
| Company | Founded in March 2019 in Denver, Colorado | Legal |
| Funding | Series B of $46M in June 2024, led by Marlbank Partners | Legal |

The Containment Report was published on April 14, 2026, and surveyed 412 platform and security leaders. Give the survey size when the copy has room for it. The legal entity is Wickhold, Inc. Contracts, order forms, privacy notices and page footers use that form. Marketing copy uses Wickhold.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "1. Claims approved as written"], "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "383000ed-25fc-4fa8-8a32-0a9cb7da5f80", "content": "## How the sentences go

**Short first.** Most sentences run under twenty words. The long ones earn it by carrying a real sequence of events.

**Verbs do the work.** Name who did what. "Quenchline froze the process" over "the process was frozen". Past tense for incidents, present tense for what the product does.

**End early.** Our most common edit is deleting the last line of a paragraph. Writers tend to add one that restates the point in a nicer rhythm. Readers don't need it. This goes double for the final line of a piece.

**Ration the fire.** The tagline is "Small fires stay small." It carries the metaphor so the copy doesn't have to. A piece gets at most one fire image, and many pieces should have none. Nothing ignites, sparks, blazes or fans the flames. Slow Burn Summit gets to keep its name.

**Plain words for plain things.** "Use", "start", "stop", "run". Reach for the fancier word and the reader assumes something is being hidden.

**Don't argue with the reader's experience.** Telling a platform engineer that alerts are overwhelming is telling them what they had for breakfast. Start from what they know and add something.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "How the sentences go"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "412b98db-a59b-4fa4-afb4-aada12ba8243", "content": "Certification status: sheet kept by Priit Salonen. Last checked 2 October 2026.

Sales, this is the sheet to use before you answer a security questionnaire. If a deck or an old email says something different, the deck or the email is out of date.

| Program | Status | What you may say |
|---|---|---|
| SOC 2 Type II | Held. Renewed January 2026 | "Wickhold holds SOC 2 Type II." |
| FedRAMP Moderate | In process. Not held | "Wickhold is pursuing FedRAMP Moderate authorization." |

**FedRAMP.** Never claim FedRAMP authorization or certification. The approved wording above is the only wording. It goes in copy exactly as written, including the word "pursuing".

These are banned in every channel, spoken or written: "FedRAMP Authorized", "FedRAMP certified", "FedRAMP Ready", "FedRAMP compliant", "FedRAMP equivalent", "built to FedRAMP standards". Agency buyers read those words literally, and a false statement to a federal buyer is a contract and legal problem, whatever the deal size.

The status changes when authorization is complete and published, and this sheet says so. An assessor's visit, a sponsor conversation, or a positive meeting does not change it. Do not give prospects a target date. We do not publish one. If a federal prospect presses, the answer is the sentence above and an offer to connect them with me.

Good, in an answer to a questionnaire:

> Wickhold holds SOC 2 Type II, renewed January 2026. Wickhold is pursuing FedRAMP Moderate authorization. We can share the SOC 2 report under NDA.

Bad:

> We're basically FedRAMP Authorized, the paperwork is just finishing up.

**SOC 2.** The report goes out under NDA through the account team, never by public link. Say "Type II" every time. Say "held" or "renewed", and do not say "SOC 2 certified", because SOC 2 ends in an attestation report and not a certificate.

**Questionnaires and RFPs.** Security questionnaires go through the account team, and any answer about certifications is copied from this sheet. If a form offers only "Yes" or "No" for FedRAMP, answer "No", and use the comments box for the approved sentence. Do not tick a box in the hope of explaining later.

", "heading_path": [], "relative_path": "brand/legal/certifications-status.md"}, {"chunk_id": "41f8d6b1-1744-475c-b7dd-9cafc7d5a3e6", "content": "## Structure

Most company posts follow the same order.

1. **The fact.** What shipped, what was measured, what happened. Put the number here if there is one.
2. **The context.** Two or three sentences on why it matters to someone running clusters or answering for them.
3. **The way out.** One link, with a short instruction in front of it.

Then stop. If you have a second point, it is a second post next week.

", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Structure"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "4efa700b-1645-41eb-89bc-1d8aeb1b7fb2", "content": "### Review before publishing

Most work needs one reviewer. Riskier work needs more.

| Type of work | Review |
|---|---|
| Routine social post or email from an approved template | A peer in marketing |
| New blog post or landing page | Peer, plus Noor's team for brand |
| Any technical how-to or product detail | Developer relations |
| Anything with a new claim, statistic, customer name or certification mention | Legal, before design starts, except third-party statistics under section 5 of the approved claims |
| Anything signed by a founder | The founder personally, with no exceptions |
| Press releases | Ilse and Legal |

Legal's turnaround is set in the approved claims. Brand review takes two working days. If a deadline can't take that, say so at the start of the work and not the night before. Anything already on the approved claims list needs no further sign-off for the claim itself, which is the reason to use it word for word.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "11. Governance", "Review before publishing"], "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "668f858f-133e-4581-b3b0-c0ca0a2f6f13", "content": "## Founder voice and brand voice

There are two voices at Wickhold, and they have one hard line between them.

**Founder voice is first person singular, and it is signed.** Maren writes as "I". Her posts carry her name. She gets to have feelings and doubts, tell a story from a bad night in 2017, and be wrong in public. Dov's technical posts work the same way and are signed "Dov".

**Brand voice never says "I" or "we think".** Website, product pages, company LinkedIn, the company X account, email, decks, reports: no first person singular, ever. "We believe", "we feel" and "in our view" are "we think" in different shoes, and they go too.

**Brand voice uses "Wickhold" or "we" for facts only.** Things that happened, things that are true of the company, things a lawyer could check.

| Fine in brand voice | Not in brand voice |
|---|---|
| We renewed SOC 2 Type II in January 2026. | We think SOC 2 matters. |
| Wickhold serves more than 140 customers. | I've talked to a lot of platform teams. |
| Containment is where incidents are won or lost. | We believe containment is where incidents are won or lost. |

The third row is the useful one. Brand voice still holds opinions. It states them as flat sentences, the way the on-call lead does, and lets the reader disagree. "We think" adds nothing except a hedge.

Practicalities. Nobody else writes as "I" in Wickhold content. Kofi's developer posts and anything from the wider team run in brand voice under a byline, because a byline is credit and a founder post is a person speaking for themselves. Customer quotes are quotes and say whatever was approved. If the content team drafts for Maren, she reads it and changes it before her name goes on, and a post that she has not read does not go out. In the spring a joint Maren-and-Dov byline was tried on one post; "I" became unreadable after two paragraphs, so that was dropped. One author per post.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "Founder voice and brand voice"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "bd7ba1fe-13b7-4692-afd2-ef01d0dc122b", "content": "## Review

| Post contains | Who approves | Turnaround |
|---|---|---|
| No claims, no customers (hiring, event logistics) | Anyone on the brand team | Two business days |
| Product claim from the approved list | Noor | Two business days |
| Customer name or result | Noor and Priit Salonen, plus the customer's contact if we tag them | Five business days |
| Any number we haven't published before, except third-party statistics under section 5 of the approved claims | Priit Salonen | Two business days |

", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Review"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "c1483026-3308-4a52-8cf9-e6314d11b35f", "content": "## 6. Grammar and punctuation

- **American spelling** in all copy, including copy going to UK and EU readers. Containerize, not containerise.
- **Oxford comma**, always. It has settled more than one argument in Kubernetes prose, where lists of nouns can double as lists of objects.
- **Active voice** with a named actor, wherever the actor is known. "Wickhold Quenchline drained the node." If the passive is hiding who did it and that person is us, it goes.
- **Tense.** Past for what happened, present for what the product does, and nothing in the future except where a date is public.
- **Contractions** are fine in the blog, on social and in email. Skip them on legal pages and in anything aimed at a board.
- **Colons** are our favorite punctuation mark and they're doing fine. Use them to introduce the fact.
- **Semicolons** at most once a page. If there are two, one wants to be a full stop.
- **Em dashes** rarely in body copy. Most are a full stop that lost its nerve. Spaced en dashes are not a substitute.
- **Parentheses** for the short aside only. If the aside matters, promote it to a sentence.
- **Quotation marks:** double, with commas and full stops inside, American style, except for literal strings in technical writing where the punctuation would change the meaning. Single quotes only inside double.
- **Italics:** titles of reports and the occasional stress only. They disappear on Soot grounds and in email.
- **Bold:** for scanning in long documents, once or twice per section. Bold on a landing page means the design isn't working.
- **Ampersands:** only in proper names. Plain "and" in headlines too.
- **"And/or"** is a legal term. Pick one.
- **Slashes** as a shortcut ("platform/security teams") get rewritten: "platform and security teams".

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "6. Grammar and punctuation"], "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "ca65b949-2e3b-43fc-b1a9-0f6770fb82d8", "content": "## CTA format for all channels

This lives here because the email team wrote it down first, and it now applies to every channel: email, landing pages, paid, social, the blog, event pages.

A CTA, the call to action on a button or a link, is at most four words, and it starts with a verb. The same CTA wording rules apply wherever the button sits. "Learn more" and "Click here" are banned everywhere, including as link text inside a sentence.

| Fine | Not fine |
|---|---|
| Read the report | Learn more |
| Book a demo | Click here |
| See the rollout guide | Click here to see the rollout guide |
| Request early access | Early access request |
| Save your seat | Your seat is waiting for you |

Say what happens on the other side of the click. "Get started" is allowed but weak, so use something more specific if you can.

", "heading_path": ["Email templates", "CTA format for all channels"], "relative_path": "brand/templates/email-templates.md"}, {"chunk_id": "e4d55076-3313-4cf2-a4af-45a0ab945f2f", "content": "## Format

- A LinkedIn post is 180 words at most. Count everything, including the link line.
- About the first 200 characters show before the "see more" cut on most phones. The news has to fit in that space.
- Short paragraphs, one to three lines each, with a blank line between them.
- One link per post, at the end, on its own line. We tested putting links in the first comment for six weeks in 2025 and could not see a difference, and it annoyed people, so links stay in the post.
- Tag a customer only after their marketing contact has seen the post. Tag people, not company pages, when a named person spoke or wrote the thing.
- Use bullets only for real lists: three containment actions, the tiers, the steps of a rollout. A post that is all bullets reads as a slide.
- Image guidance sits with the visual rules. Every company page post gets one image, except short hiring notes.

{"brand_rules": {"evidence": [{"chunk_id": "383000ed-25fc-4fa8-8a32-0a9cb7da5f80", "content": "## How the sentences go

**Short first.** Most sentences run under twenty words. The long ones earn it by carrying a real sequence of events.

**Verbs do the work.** Name who did what. "Quenchline froze the process" over "the process was frozen". Past tense for incidents, present tense for what the product does.

**End early.** Our most common edit is deleting the last line of a paragraph. Writers tend to add one that restates the point in a nicer rhythm. Readers don't need it. This goes double for the final line of a piece.

**Ration the fire.** The tagline is "Small fires stay small." It carries the metaphor so the copy doesn't have to. A piece gets at most one fire image, and many pieces should have none. Nothing ignites, sparks, blazes or fans the flames. Slow Burn Summit gets to keep its name.

**Plain words for plain things.** "Use", "start", "stop", "run". Reach for the fancier word and the reader assumes something is being hidden.

**Don't argue with the reader's experience.** Telling a platform engineer that alerts are overwhelming is telling them what they had for breakfast. Start from what they know and add something.

", "end_line": 222, "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "How the sentences go"], "ref": "383000ed-25fc-4fa8-8a32-0a9cb7da5f80", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "start_line": 209}]}}

{"channel_rules": {"evidence": [{"chunk_id": "08ed6196-965b-4faa-9751-01ebf0e4f4a2", "content": "# LinkedIn playbook

Noor Eskelund. Last edit 12 August 2026, after the Leashgate early access posts. Ask in the brand channel before you ask me by email.

LinkedIn is the one channel where CISOs, platform leads and our own hiring pipeline all look at the same feed. Most of what we post there is read on a phone, between meetings, by someone who has never heard of us. Write for that person.

", "end_line": 6, "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook"], "ref": "08ed6196-965b-4faa-9751-01ebf0e4f4a2", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md", "start_line": 1}, {"chunk_id": "41f8d6b1-1744-475c-b7dd-9cafc7d5a3e6", "content": "## Structure

Most company posts follow the same order.

1. **The fact.** What shipped, what was measured, what happened. Put the number here if there is one.
2. **The context.** Two or three sentences on why it matters to someone running clusters or answering for them.
3. **The way out.** One link, with a short instruction in front of it.

Then stop. If you have a second point, it is a second post next week.

", "end_line": 36, "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Structure"], "ref": "41f8d6b1-1744-475c-b7dd-9cafc7d5a3e6", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md", "start_line": 27}, {"chunk_id": "e4d55076-3313-4cf2-a4af-45a0ab945f2f", "content": "## Format

- A LinkedIn post is 180 words at most. Count everything, including the link line.
- About the first 200 characters show before the "see more" cut on most phones. The news has to fit in that space.
- Short paragraphs, one to three lines each, with a blank line between them.
- One link per post, at the end, on its own line. We tested putting links in the first comment for six weeks in 2025 and could not see a difference, and it annoyed people, so links stay in the post.
- Tag a customer only after their marketing contact has seen the post. Tag people, not company pages, when a named person spoke or wrote the thing.
- Use bullets only for real lists: three containment actions, the tiers, the steps of a rollout. A post that is all bullets reads as a slide.
- Image guidance sits with the visual rules. Every company page post gets one image, except short hiring notes.

", "end_line": 26, "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Format"], "ref": "e4d55076-3313-4cf2-a4af-45a0ab945f2f", "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md", "start_line": 17}]}}

{"asset_sources": {"evidence": [{"chunk_id": "06ede73b-42e2-4a1d-8774-10eb6d36ca3a", "content": "### Product behavior

Wickhold Quenchline takes a containment action only in contain mode. In observe mode it records what it would have done. Copy describing automatic containment must therefore be true of contain mode and should say so where a reader could assume otherwise. Containment actions are isolating a pod's network, freezing a process and draining a node. Do not add to the list without product confirmation.

Wickhold Evenburn reports drift, exposure paths and a fix order. It does not change a customer's environment by itself, and copy should not imply that it does.

", "end_line": 72, "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "2. Claims that need a qualifier", "Product behavior"], "ref": "06ede73b-42e2-4a1d-8774-10eb6d36ca3a", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md", "start_line": 67}, {"chunk_id": "1b2ec0a3-937b-43d7-a777-88143fa3b565", "content": "## Tone by channel

The voice stays the same. How much of it you get changes with the room.

**Landing pages.** The flattest we get. Mechanical, confident, short. The reader is deciding whether to spend ten more minutes, so tell them what the thing does on a cluster and let them go. "Wickhold Quenchline isolates the pod, freezes the process or drains the node, then writes down what it did."

**Blog.** The most room to think. Brand-voice posts walk through how something fails. Dov's posts can argue, and they should. A good post leaves the reader able to do one thing they could not do before, even if they never buy. Avoid the summary paragraph at the end. If the post worked, the reader was there.

**LinkedIn.** The company page is brand voice. Founder posts are where the personality lives. A post runs about 200 words, which suits one story and one point. Write as a person with a job, not a thought leader: no line breaks after every sentence, no "here's what I learned", no lists of lessons from an outage.

**X.** One fact, or one observation, in a dry tone. The account does not chase the news and does not reply to arguments about vendors. It's fine for a post to be plain. "The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. That is most of a night shift."

**Email.** One person writing to one person who is busy. Say why you are writing in the first sentence. Assume it is being read on a phone in a hallway. No "I hope this finds you well", and since these are brand emails, no "I" at all unless Maren signed it. Customer notices are the exception to everything else in this list and sound like the incident channel at the top of this document.

**Product UI and error text.** The closest thing we have to pure voice. What happened, what state things are in, what to do. "Containment action failed on node `ip-10-2-14-7`: agent unreachable. The pod is still running. Retry or drain the node." Chirpy empty states were tried in 2025 and came out after a customer saw one during a real incident.

**Case studies.** Third person, numbers up front, the customer's team as the subject of most sentences. Enough detail about their environment that a peer recognizes it. A case study that could describe any customer describes none of them.

", "end_line": 122, "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "Tone by channel"], "ref": "1b2ec0a3-937b-43d7-a777-88143fa3b565", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "start_line": 105}, {"chunk_id": "3410ca50-9f2f-46c3-90e9-d1ff5cff3651", "content": "### Vocabulary that belongs to the products

Each product has a small set of terms. Use them exactly, because customers see the same words in the console.

- **Quenchline:** containment action (isolate a pod's network, freeze a process, drain a node), default containment policy, contain mode, observe mode.
- **Evenburn:** drift, exposure path, fix order.
- **Leashgate:** tool-call policy, agent identity, blast radius of an agent.

", "end_line": 250, "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "5. Brand architecture", "Vocabulary that belongs to the products"], "ref": "3410ca50-9f2f-46c3-90e9-d1ff5cff3651", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md", "start_line": 243}, {"chunk_id": "5b924c2e-d5ac-458e-9271-f95a845d565a", "content": "### Admit limits

One of the company values, and the one marketing finds hardest. Every product we sell has an edge. Wickhold Evenburn finds drift and exposure paths; it does not contain anything. Quenchline contains what is running; it does not patch the image it came from. Saying so costs a little in the moment and buys a lot of belief for the next claim on the page. Engineers look for the catch. When they find we already named it, they keep reading.

", "end_line": 80, "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "What Wickhold believes", "Admit limits"], "ref": "5b924c2e-d5ac-458e-9271-f95a845d565a", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "start_line": 77}, {"chunk_id": "668f858f-133e-4581-b3b0-c0ca0a2f6f13", "content": "## Founder voice and brand voice

There are two voices at Wickhold, and they have one hard line between them.

**Founder voice is first person singular, and it is signed.** Maren writes as "I". Her posts carry her name. She gets to have feelings and doubts, tell a story from a bad night in 2017, and be wrong in public. Dov's technical posts work the same way and are signed "Dov".

**Brand voice never says "I" or "we think".** Website, product pages, company LinkedIn, the company X account, email, decks, reports: no first person singular, ever. "We believe", "we feel" and "in our view" are "we think" in different shoes, and they go too.

**Brand voice uses "Wickhold" or "we" for facts only.** Things that happened, things that are true of the company, things a lawyer could check.

| Fine in brand voice | Not in brand voice |
|---|---|
| We renewed SOC 2 Type II in January 2026. | We think SOC 2 matters. |
| Wickhold serves more than 140 customers. | I've talked to a lot of platform teams. |
| Containment is where incidents are won or lost. | We believe containment is where incidents are won or lost. |

The third row is the useful one. Brand voice still holds opinions. It states them as flat sentences, the way the on-call lead does, and lets the reader disagree. "We think" adds nothing except a hedge.

Practicalities. Nobody else writes as "I" in Wickhold content. Kofi's developer posts and anything from the wider team run in brand voice under a byline, because a byline is credit and a founder post is a person speaking for themselves. Customer quotes are quotes and say whatever was approved. If the content team drafts for Maren, she reads it and changes it before her name goes on, and a post that she has not read does not go out. In the spring a joint Maren-and-Dov byline was tried on one post; "I" became unreadable after two paragraphs, so that was dropped. One author per post.

", "end_line": 104, "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "Founder voice and brand voice"], "ref": "668f858f-133e-4581-b3b0-c0ca0a2f6f13", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md", "start_line": 85}, {"chunk_id": "c1483026-3308-4a52-8cf9-e6314d11b35f", "content": "## 6. Grammar and punctuation

- **American spelling** in all copy, including copy going to UK and EU readers. Containerize, not containerise.
- **Oxford comma**, always. It has settled more than one argument in Kubernetes prose, where lists of nouns can double as lists of objects.
- **Active voice** with a named actor, wherever the actor is known. "Wickhold Quenchline drained the node." If the passive is hiding who did it and that person is us, it goes.
- **Tense.** Past for what happened, present for what the product does, and nothing in the future except where a date is public.
- **Contractions** are fine in the blog, on social and in email. Skip them on legal pages and in anything aimed at a board.
- **Colons** are our favorite punctuation mark and they're doing fine. Use them to introduce the fact.
- **Semicolons** at most once a page. If there are two, one wants to be a full stop.

- **Parentheses** for the short aside only. If the aside matters, promote it to a sentence.
- **Quotation marks:** double, with commas and full stops inside, American style, except for literal strings in technical writing where the punctuation would change the meaning. Single quotes only inside double.
- **Italics:** titles of reports and the occasional stress only. They disappear on Soot grounds and in email.
- **Bold:** for scanning in long documents, once or twice per section. Bold on a landing page means the design isn't working.
- **Ampersands:** only in proper names. Plain "and" in headlines too.
- **"And/or"** is a legal term. Pick one.
- **Slashes** as a shortcut ("platform/security teams") get rewritten: "platform and security teams".

", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "1475f7bc-8d87-4eb3-9fc9-4dece12a6a55", "content": "## Approved

", "heading_path": ["Customer logo and quote policy", "Approved"], "relative_path": "brand/legal/customer-logo-and-quote-policy.md"}, {"chunk_id": "1b2ec0a3-937b-43d7-a777-88143fa3b565", "content": "## Tone by channel

The voice stays the same. How much of it you get changes with the room.

**Landing pages.** The flattest we get. Mechanical, confident, short. The reader is deciding whether to spend ten more minutes, so tell them what the thing does on a cluster and let them go. "Wickhold Quenchline isolates the pod, freezes the process or drains the node, then writes down what it did."

**Blog.** The most room to think. Brand-voice posts walk through how something fails. Dov's posts can argue, and they should. A good post leaves the reader able to do one thing they could not do before, even if they never buy. Avoid the summary paragraph at the end. If the post worked, the reader was there.

**LinkedIn.** The company page is brand voice. Founder posts are where the personality lives. A post runs about 200 words, which suits one story and one point. Write as a person with a job, not a thought leader: no line breaks after every sentence, no "here's what I learned", no lists of lessons from an outage.

**X.** One fact, or one observation, in a dry tone. The account does not chase the news and does not reply to arguments about vendors. It's fine for a post to be plain. "The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. That is most of a night shift."

**Email.** One person writing to one person who is busy. Say why you are writing in the first sentence. Assume it is being read on a phone in a hallway. No "I hope this finds you well", and since these are brand emails, no "I" at all unless Maren signed it. Customer notices are the exception to everything else in this list and sound like the incident channel at the top of this document.

**Product UI and error text.** The closest thing we have to pure voice. What happened, what state things are in, what to do. "Containment action failed on node `ip-10-2-14-7`: agent unreachable. The pod is still running. Retry or drain the node." Chirpy empty states were tried in 2025 and came out after a customer saw one during a real incident.

**Case studies.** Third person, numbers up front, the customer's team as the subject of most sentences. Enough detail about their environment that a peer recognizes it. A case study that could describe any customer describes none of them.

Keep the node count with the result. The Lowmoor outcome belongs to a 220-node estate and the Ostler outcome to a 1,900-node estate, and neither may be stated as what a new customer should expect. Do not convert the Lowmoor result into a percentage or a multiple. Nobody approved that arithmetic. ", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "2. Claims that need a qualifier", "Customer results"], "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "2ed35bac-e511-4a05-b03f-f56a94ab438a", "content": "## 3. Citations

**Citations give the source name, the year and the link, in brackets, right after the claim.**

The shape, exactly:

```text
41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].
```

- Source name in full, as the source spells it.
- Comma, year. Comma, link. The full stop for the sentence goes outside the bracket.
- Link goes to the report or page itself, not a press release about it and not a search result. In a PDF or on a slide print the link out, because hyperlinks do not survive a screenshot.
- Use the same form everywhere, including LinkedIn and X. Yes, it's long on X. Plan the post around it.
- Two sources for one claim: two brackets. Do not merge them.
- A source we did not produce gets its own name in the bracket, even when a Wickhold page quotes it. Cite the original.
- In long pieces (report summaries, the blog), mention the survey base once near the first figure: "a survey of 412 platform and security leaders".

We tried numbered footnotes on the blog through most of 2025 and dropped them. The claim got quoted on LinkedIn, the footnote stayed behind, and the number went around with no source. A bracket travels with the sentence.

Customer results don't take a bracket when the customer is named in the sentence and the case study is linked from the page. Naming them is the source.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "3. Citations"], "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "383000ed-25fc-4fa8-8a32-0a9cb7da5f80", "content": "## How the sentences go

**Short first.** Most sentences run under twenty words. The long ones earn it by carrying a real sequence of events.

**Verbs do the work.** Name who did what. "Quenchline froze the process" over "the process was frozen". Past tense for incidents, present tense for what the product does.

**End early.** Our most common edit is deleting the last line of a paragraph. Writers tend to add one that restates the point in a nicer rhythm. Readers don't need it. This goes double for the final line of a piece.

**Ration the fire.** The tagline is "Small fires stay small." It carries the metaphor so the copy doesn't have to. A piece gets at most one fire image, and many pieces should have none. Nothing ignites, sparks, blazes or fans the flames. Slow Burn Summit gets to keep its name.

**Plain words for plain things.** "Use", "start", "stop", "run". Reach for the fancier word and the reader assumes something is being hidden.

**Don't argue with the reader's experience.** Telling a platform engineer that alerts are overwhelming is telling them what they had for breakfast. Start from what they know and add something.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "How the sentences go"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "41f8d6b1-1744-475c-b7dd-9cafc7d5a3e6", "content": "## Structure

Most company posts follow the same order.

1. **The fact.** What shipped, what was measured, what happened. Put the number here if there is one.
2. **The context.** Two or three sentences on why it matters to someone running clusters or answering for them.
3. **The way out.** One link, with a short instruction in front of it.

Then stop. If you have a second point, it is a second post next week.

", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Structure"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "4efa700b-1645-41eb-89bc-1d8aeb1b7fb2", "content": "### Review before publishing

Most work needs one reviewer. Riskier work needs more.

| Type of work | Review |
|---|---|
| Routine social post or email from an approved template | A peer in marketing |
| New blog post or landing page | Peer, plus Noor's team for brand |
| Any technical how-to or product detail | Developer relations |

Cite only customers listed as approved below. That covers names, logos, quotes, results, case studies and any description that would let a reader work out who the customer is. A customer who likes us on a call has not approved anything.

", "heading_path": ["Customer logo and quote policy"], "relative_path": "brand/legal/customer-logo-and-quote-policy.md"}, {"chunk_id": "668f858f-133e-4581-b3b0-c0ca0a2f6f13", "content": "## Founder voice and brand voice

There are two voices at Wickhold, and they have one hard line between them.

**Founder voice is first person singular, and it is signed.** Maren writes as "I". Her posts carry her name. She gets to have feelings and doubts, tell a story from a bad night in 2017, and be wrong in public. Dov's technical posts work the same way and are signed "Dov".

**Brand voice never says "I" or "we think".** Website, product pages, company LinkedIn, the company X account, email, decks, reports: no first person singular, ever. "We believe", "we feel" and "in our view" are "we think" in different shoes, and they go too.

**Brand voice uses "Wickhold" or "we" for facts only.** Things that happened, things that are true of the company, things a lawyer could check.

| Fine in brand voice | Not in brand voice |
|---|---|
| We renewed SOC 2 Type II in January 2026. | We think SOC 2 matters. |
| Wickhold serves more than 140 customers. | I've talked to a lot of platform teams. |
| Containment is where incidents are won or lost. | We believe containment is where incidents are won or lost. |

The third row is the useful one. Brand voice still holds opinions. It states them as flat sentences, the way the on-call lead does, and lets the reader disagree. "We think" adds nothing except a hedge.

Practicalities. Nobody else writes as "I" in Wickhold content. Kofi's developer posts and anything from the wider team run in brand voice under a byline, because a byline is credit and a founder post is a person speaking for themselves. Customer quotes are quotes and say whatever was approved. If the content team drafts for Maren, she reads it and changes it before her name goes on, and a post that she has not read does not go out. In the spring a joint Maren-and-Dov byline was tried on one post; "I" became unreadable after two paragraphs, so that was dropped. One author per post.

", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Review"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "c1483026-3308-4a52-8cf9-e6314d11b35f", "content": "## 6. Grammar and punctuation

- **American spelling** in all copy, including copy going to UK and EU readers. Containerize, not containerise.
- **Oxford comma**, always. It has settled more than one argument in Kubernetes prose, where lists of nouns can double as lists of objects.
- **Active voice** with a named actor, wherever the actor is known. "Wickhold Quenchline drained the node." If the passive is hiding who did it and that person is us, it goes.
- **Tense.** Past for what happened, present for what the product does, and nothing in the future except where a date is public.
- **Contractions** are fine in the blog, on social and in email. Skip them on legal pages and in anything aimed at a board.
- **Colons** are our favorite punctuation mark and they're doing fine. Use them to introduce the fact.
- **Semicolons** at most once a page. If there are two, one wants to be a full stop.
- **Em dashes** rarely in body copy. Most are a full stop that lost its nerve. Spaced en dashes are not a substitute.
- **Parentheses** for the short aside only. If the aside matters, promote it to a sentence.
- **Quotation marks:** double, with commas and full stops inside, American style, except for literal strings in technical writing where the punctuation would change the meaning. Single quotes only inside double.
- **Italics:** titles of reports and the occasional stress only. They disappear on Soot grounds and in email.
- **Bold:** for scanning in long documents, once or twice per section. Bold on a landing page means the design isn't working.
- **Ampersands:** only in proper names. Plain "and" in headlines too.
- **"And/or"** is a legal term. Pick one.
- **Slashes** as a shortcut ("platform/security teams") get rewritten: "platform and security teams".

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "6. Grammar and punctuation"], "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "ca65b949-2e3b-43fc-b1a9-0f6770fb82d8", "content": "## CTA format for all channels

This lives here because the email team wrote it down first, and it now applies to every channel: email, landing pages, paid, social, the blog, event pages.

A CTA, the call to action on a button or a link, is at most four words, and it starts with a verb. The same CTA wording rules apply wherever the button sits. "Learn more" and "Click here" are banned everywhere, including as link text inside a sentence.

| Fine | Not fine |
|---|---|
| Read the report | Learn more |
| Book a demo | Click here |
| See the rollout guide | Click here to see the rollout guide |
| Request early access | Early access request |
| Save your seat | Your seat is waiting for you |

Say what happens on the other side of the click. "Get started" is allowed but weak, so use something more specific if you can.

", "heading_path": ["Email templates", "CTA format for all channels"], "relative_path": "brand/templates/email-templates.md"}, {"chunk_id": "e4d55076-3313-4cf2-a4af-45a0ab945f2f", "content": "## Format

- A LinkedIn post is 180 words at most. Count everything, including the link line.
- About the first 200 characters show before the "see more" cut on most phones. The news has to fit in that space.
- Short paragraphs, one to three lines each, with a blank line between them.
- One link per post, at the end, on its own line. We tested putting links in the first comment for six weeks in 2025 and could not see a difference, and it annoyed people, so links stay in the post.
- Tag a customer only after their marketing contact has seen the post. Tag people, not company pages, when a named person spoke or wrote the thing.
- Use bullets only for real lists: three containment actions, the tiers, the steps of a rollout. A post that is all bullets reads as a slide.
- Image guidance sits with the visual rules. Every company page post gets one image, except short hiring notes.

{"brand_preferences": [], "rule_pack": {"evidence": [{"chunk_id": "06ede73b-42e2-4a1d-8774-10eb6d36ca3a", "content": "### Product behavior

Wickhold Quenchline takes a containment action only in contain mode. In observe mode it records what it would have done. Copy describing automatic containment must therefore be true of contain mode and should say so where a reader could assume otherwise. Containment actions are isolating a pod's network, freezing a process and draining a node. Do not add to the list without product confirmation.

Wickhold Evenburn reports drift, exposure paths and a fix order. It does not change a customer's environment by itself, and copy should not imply that it does.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "2. Claims that need a qualifier", "Product behavior"], "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "08ed6196-965b-4faa-9751-01ebf0e4f4a2", "content": "# LinkedIn playbook

Noor Eskelund. Last edit 12 August 2026, after the Leashgate early access posts. Ask in the brand channel before you ask me by email.

LinkedIn is the one channel where CISOs, platform leads and our own hiring pipeline all look at the same feed. Most of what we post there is read on a phone, between meetings, by someone who has never heard of us. Write for that person.

", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "1b2ec0a3-937b-43d7-a777-88143fa3b565", "content": "## Tone by channel

The voice stays the same. How much of it you get changes with the room.

**Landing pages.** The flattest we get. Mechanical, confident, short. The reader is deciding whether to spend ten more minutes, so tell them what the thing does on a cluster and let them go. "Wickhold Quenchline isolates the pod, freezes the process or drains the node, then writes down what it did."

**Blog.** The most room to think. Brand-voice posts walk through how something fails. Dov's posts can argue, and they should. A good post leaves the reader able to do one thing they could not do before, even if they never buy. Avoid the summary paragraph at the end. If the post worked, the reader was there.

**LinkedIn.** The company page is brand voice. Founder posts are where the personality lives. A post runs about 200 words, which suits one story and one point. Write as a person with a job, not a thought leader: no line breaks after every sentence, no "here's what I learned", no lists of lessons from an outage.

**X.** One fact, or one observation, in a dry tone. The account does not chase the news and does not reply to arguments about vendors. It's fine for a post to be plain. "The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. That is most of a night shift."

**Email.** One person writing to one person who is busy. Say why you are writing in the first sentence. Assume it is being read on a phone in a hallway. No "I hope this finds you well", and since these are brand emails, no "I" at all unless Maren signed it. Customer notices are the exception to everything else in this list and sound like the incident channel at the top of this document.

**Product UI and error text.** The closest thing we have to pure voice. What happened, what state things are in, what to do. "Containment action failed on node `ip-10-2-14-7`: agent unreachable. The pod is still running. Retry or drain the node." Chirpy empty states were tried in 2025 and came out after a customer saw one during a real incident.

**Case studies.** Third person, numbers up front, the customer's team as the subject of most sentences. Enough detail about their environment that a peer recognizes it. A case study that could describe any customer describes none of them.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "Tone by channel"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "3410ca50-9f2f-46c3-90e9-d1ff5cff3651", "content": "### Vocabulary that belongs to the products

Each product has a small set of terms. Use them exactly, because customers see the same words in the console.

- **Quenchline:** containment action (isolate a pod's network, freeze a process, drain a node), default containment policy, contain mode, observe mode.
- **Evenburn:** drift, exposure path, fix order.
- **Leashgate:** tool-call policy, agent identity, blast radius of an agent.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "5. Brand architecture", "Vocabulary that belongs to the products"], "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "383000ed-25fc-4fa8-8a32-0a9cb7da5f80", "content": "## How the sentences go

**Short first.** Most sentences run under twenty words. The long ones earn it by carrying a real sequence of events.

**Verbs do the work.** Name who did what. "Quenchline froze the process" over "the process was frozen". Past tense for incidents, present tense for what the product does.

**End early.** Our most common edit is deleting the last line of a paragraph. Writers tend to add one that restates the point in a nicer rhythm. Readers don't need it. This goes double for the final line of a piece.

**Ration the fire.** The tagline is "Small fires stay small." It carries the metaphor so the copy doesn't have to. A piece gets at most one fire image, and many pieces should have none. Nothing ignites, sparks, blazes or fans the flames. Slow Burn Summit gets to keep its name.

**Plain words for plain things.** "Use", "start", "stop", "run". Reach for the fancier word and the reader assumes something is being hidden.

**Don't argue with the reader's experience.** Telling a platform engineer that alerts are overwhelming is telling them what they had for breakfast. Start from what they know and add something.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "How the sentences go"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "41f8d6b1-1744-475c-b7dd-9cafc7d5a3e6", "content": "## Structure

Most company posts follow the same order.

1. **The fact.** What shipped, what was measured, what happened. Put the number here if there is one.
2. **The context.** Two or three sentences on why it matters to someone running clusters or answering for them.
3. **The way out.** One link, with a short instruction in front of it.

Then stop. If you have a second point, it is a second post next week.

", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Structure"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "4efa700b-1645-41eb-89bc-1d8aeb1b7fb2", "content": "### Review before publishing

Most work needs one reviewer. Riskier work needs more.

| Type of work | Review |
|---|---|
| Routine social post or email from an approved template | A peer in marketing |
| New blog post or landing page | Peer, plus Noor's team for brand |
| Any technical how-to or product detail | Developer relations |
| Anything with a new claim, statistic, customer name or certification mention | Legal, before design starts, except third-party statistics under section 5 of the approved claims |
| Anything signed by a founder | The founder personally, with no exceptions |
| Press releases | Ilse and Legal |

Legal's turnaround is set in the approved claims. Brand review takes two working days. If a deadline can't take that, say so at the start of the work and not the night before. Anything already on the approved claims list needs no further sign-off for the claim itself, which is the reason to use it word for word.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "11. Governance", "Review before publishing"], "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "5b924c2e-d5ac-458e-9271-f95a845d565a", "content": "### Admit limits

One of the company values, and the one marketing finds hardest. Every product we sell has an edge. Wickhold Evenburn finds drift and exposure paths; it does not contain anything. Quenchline contains what is running; it does not patch the image it came from. Saying so costs a little in the moment and buys a lot of belief for the next claim on the page. Engineers look for the catch. When they find we already named it, they keep reading.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "What Wickhold believes", "Admit limits"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "668f858f-133e-4581-b3b0-c0ca0a2f6f13", "content": "## Founder voice and brand voice

There are two voices at Wickhold, and they have one hard line between them.

**Founder voice is first person singular, and it is signed.** Maren writes as "I". Her posts carry her name. She gets to have feelings and doubts, tell a story from a bad night in 2017, and be wrong in public. Dov's technical posts work the same way and are signed "Dov".

**Brand voice never says "I" or "we think".** Website, product pages, company LinkedIn, the company X account, email, decks, reports: no first person singular, ever. "We believe", "we feel" and "in our view" are "we think" in different shoes, and they go too.

**Brand voice uses "Wickhold" or "we" for facts only.** Things that happened, things that are true of the company, things a lawyer could check.

| Fine in brand voice | Not in brand voice |
|---|---|
| We renewed SOC 2 Type II in January 2026. | We think SOC 2 matters. |
| Wickhold serves more than 140 customers. | I've talked to a lot of platform teams. |
| Containment is where incidents are won or lost. | We believe containment is where incidents are won or lost. |

The third row is the useful one. Brand voice still holds opinions. It states them as flat sentences, the way the on-call lead does, and lets the reader disagree. "We think" adds nothing except a hedge.

Practicalities. Nobody else writes as "I" in Wickhold content. Kofi's developer posts and anything from the wider team run in brand voice under a byline, because a byline is credit and a founder post is a person speaking for themselves. Customer quotes are quotes and say whatever was approved. If the content team drafts for Maren, she reads it and changes it before her name goes on, and a post that she has not read does not go out. In the spring a joint Maren-and-Dov byline was tried on one post; "I" became unreadable after two paragraphs, so that was dropped. One author per post.

", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Review"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "c1483026-3308-4a52-8cf9-e6314d11b35f", "content": "## 6. Grammar and punctuation

- **American spelling** in all copy, including copy going to UK and EU readers. Containerize, not containerise.
- **Oxford comma**, always. It has settled more than one argument in Kubernetes prose, where lists of nouns can double as lists of objects.
- **Active voice** with a named actor, wherever the actor is known. "Wickhold Quenchline drained the node." If the passive is hiding who did it and that person is us, it goes.
- **Tense.** Past for what happened, present for what the product does, and nothing in the future except where a date is public.
- **Contractions** are fine in the blog, on social and in email. Skip them on legal pages and in anything aimed at a board.
- **Colons** are our favorite punctuation mark and they're doing fine. Use them to introduce the fact.
- **Semicolons** at most once a page. If there are two, one wants to be a full stop.
- **Em dashes** rarely in body copy. Most are a full stop that lost its nerve. Spaced en dashes are not a substitute.
- **Parentheses** for the short aside only. If the aside matters, promote it to a sentence.
- **Quotation marks:** double, with commas and full stops inside, American style, except for literal strings in technical writing where the punctuation would change the meaning. Single quotes only inside double.
- **Italics:** titles of reports and the occasional stress only. They disappear on Soot grounds and in email.
- **Bold:** for scanning in long documents, once or twice per section. Bold on a landing page means the design isn't working.
- **Ampersands:** only in proper names. Plain "and" in headlines too.
- **"And/or"** is a legal term. Pick one.
- **Slashes** as a shortcut ("platform/security teams") get rewritten: "platform and security teams".

This lives here because the email team wrote it down first, and it now applies to every channel: email, landing pages, paid, social, the blog, event pages.

A CTA, the call to action on a button or a link, is at most four words, and it starts with a verb. The same CTA wording rules apply wherever the button sits. "Learn more" and "Click here" are banned everywhere, including as link text inside a sentence.

| Fine | Not fine |
|---|---|
| Read the report | Learn more |
| Book a demo | Click here |
| See the rollout guide | Click here to see the rollout guide |
| Request early access | Early access request |
| Save your seat | Your seat is waiting for you |

Say what happens on the other side of the click. "Get started" is allowed but weak, so use something more specific if you can.

- A LinkedIn post is 180 words at most. Count everything, including the link line.
- About the first 200 characters show before the "see more" cut on most phones. The news has to fit in that space.
- Short paragraphs, one to three lines each, with a blank line between them.
- One link per post, at the end, on its own line. We tested putting links in the first comment for six weeks in 2025 and could not see a difference, and it annoyed people, so links stay in the post.
- Tag a customer only after their marketing contact has seen the post. Tag people, not company pages, when a named person spoke or wrote the thing.
- Use bullets only for real lists: three containment actions, the tiers, the steps of a rollout. A post that is all bullets reads as a slide.
- Image guidance sits with the visual rules. Every company page post gets one image, except short hiring notes.

| Step | Who | When |
|---|---|---|
| Outline | Editor (Kofi for engineering posts, Noor for the rest) | Before anyone writes 1,000 words |
| Technical read | An engineer who did not write it | Draft complete |
| Copy edit | Brand team | After the technical read |
| Claims check | Priit, for any customer, certification or number, except third-party statistics under section 5 of the approved claims | As the approved claims set out |
| Paste test | Second engineer, code posts only | Day before publish |

Allow two weeks from outline to publish. Report posts in April move faster because Legal has already checked the numbers.

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "6. Review"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "2dfe4ee1-b5b7-475f-aa8a-47e4ee921cb3", "content": "## 1. Length

Blog posts run 900 to 1,400 words. That range counts the body, including captions and code comments you wrote yourself, but not the code output you pasted.

Under 900 words, it's probably a release note or a LinkedIn post. Over 1,400 words, split it in two or cut the history section. We all write the history section first because it's easy, and nobody needs it. The report, the docs and the rollout guide are the place for anything longer.

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "1. Length"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "43519095-47d5-42a8-b0b4-9efdf2334158", "content": "# Writing for the Wickhold blog

*Kofi Anselm wrote the first version in May 2026 for the two contractors we brought in after the Containment Report. Noor edited it in July. Send fixes to either of us.*

The blog has one job: get a platform engineer or a security lead to trust that the people here have held the pager. Traffic is a side effect. A post that gets a staff engineer to forward it to their team beats a post that ranks for a keyword and gets skimmed.

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "6fabfd1d-c817-4def-a0d5-bc9821112094", "content": "## 4. Shape of a post

A title that says what the reader will get. Then the intro. Then three to five sections with descriptive headings. Then an ending that tells the reader what to do on Monday.

Titles we liked:

- Contain mode, one namespace at a time
- What drift looks like after a Helm upgrade
- The six hours after detection
- Writing your first tool-call policy for Wickhold Leashgate, in early access

Titles we rewrote:

- "5 Kubernetes Security Mistakes You're Making Right Now" became "Five findings we see in most new clusters"
- "Everything You Need To Know About eBPF" became "What our eBPF agent can and can't see"

Section headings should still make sense if they're all someone reads. "Background" and "The solution" tell the reader nothing.

End on the practical next step, then one call to action to the most relevant page. Don't summarize what you just said. If the post was good, they remember. Don't add a paragraph about Wickhold at the bottom either, as the footer handles that.

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "4. Shape of a post"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "9792dec6-922e-42ef-aded-9a7b0bc70f03", "content": "## 2. The intro

A blog intro must cite a market statistic. Put it in the first two sentences, in the citation format from the style guide, and follow it with one sentence that says why this post exists. The rule is there because engineers are more willing to keep reading once they know the problem is measured and someone has measured it honestly.

Statistics are subject to the age limit in the approved claims, so check the date before you reuse an intro from an older post.

Market statistics are figures about the market or a surveyed population. Our own customer results and benchmark numbers belong further down the post, and they don't satisfy this requirement.

Good:

> The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. Most of the teams we talk to can tell you how long detection took. Far fewer can tell you what happened in the hours after. This post is about those hours.

Good:

> 41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. A lot of that time goes to one question: who is allowed to touch the workload? Here is how to settle that question before the page goes off.

Bad, because it has no statistic and no reason to read on:

> Kubernetes has changed how modern teams ship software, and with that change come new security challenges.

Bad, because a customer result is doing the job of a market statistic:

> Lowmoor Credit Union cut time to contain from 4 hours to 11 minutes. Here's how your team can get the same results.

A vendor’s documented status and your organization’s audit preparation answer different questions. For a review, keep the wording and evidence together. Note the date you checked the status, who confirmed it, and which service or scope the evidence describes. ## Keep audit preparation in your own workflow

Your team controls its own preparation. Begin with the systems, owners, and evidence your review actually covers. A useful working record can include the system or service, the relevant control or requirement, the evidence location, its owner, and the next review date. Keep gaps visible rather than smoothing them into a general status like “ready.”

For each finding, assign a person to assess it and a next action. Some findings need investigation. Others need a change, a documented exception, or a decision from the control owner. Record what the team chose and why. A report can help people see what to examine, but your team still decides how to address a finding and what evidence supports that decision.

This distinction matters when several teams share responsibility. Wickhold Quenchline takes a containment action only in contain mode. In observe mode it records what it would have done. Copy describing automatic containment must therefore be true of contain mode and should say so where a reader could assume otherwise. Containment actions are isolating a pod's network, freezing a process and draining a node. Do not add to the list without product confirmation.

Wickhold Evenburn reports drift, exposure paths and a fix order. It does not change a customer's environment by itself, and copy should not imply that it does.

Use the quote as it stands in the signed approval, with the person's name, title and company. Do not trim it so that the meaning shifts, stitch two quotes together, or update a title without asking. The written approval sits with Legal. If someone on the list changes jobs, stop using the quote until Legal has confirmed it.

Approvals cover website, email, social, sales decks, reports and event slides. They do not cover paid advertising or press releases. Each of those goes back to the customer through the account owner, one asset at a time.

Logos come from the brand library, in the supplied one-color versions. Don't recolor one, crop it, or take it from the customer's website. On a logo wall, keep the customers in alphabetical order so that nobody reads an endorsement ranking into it. Don't tag either company, or its people, on social unless the account owner has checked first. Blog posts run 900 to 1,400 words. That range counts the body, including captions and code comments you wrote yourself, but not the code output you pasted.

Under 900 words, it's probably a release note or a LinkedIn post. Over 1,400 words, split it in two or cut the history section. We all write the history section first because it's easy, and nobody needs it. The report, the docs and the rollout guide are the place for anything longer.

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "1. Length"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "2ed35bac-e511-4a05-b03f-f56a94ab438a", "content": "## 3. Citations

**Citations give the source name, the year and the link, in brackets, right after the claim.**

The shape, exactly:

```text
41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].
```

- Source name in full, as the source spells it.
- Comma, year. Comma, link. The full stop for the sentence goes outside the bracket.
- Link goes to the report or page itself, not a press release about it and not a search result. In a PDF or on a slide print the link out, because hyperlinks do not survive a screenshot.
- Use the same form everywhere, including LinkedIn and X. Yes, it's long on X. Plan the post around it.
- Two sources for one claim: two brackets. Do not merge them.
- A source we did not produce gets its own name in the bracket, even when a Wickhold page quotes it. Cite the original.
- In long pieces (report summaries, the blog), mention the survey base once near the first figure: "a survey of 412 platform and security leaders".

We tried numbered footnotes on the blog through most of 2025 and dropped them. The claim got quoted on LinkedIn, the footnote stayed behind, and the number went around with no source. A bracket travels with the sentence.

Customer results don't take a bracket when the customer is named in the sentence and the case study is linked from the page. Naming them is the source.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "3. Citations"], "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "33d10c5d-c881-4d79-95fa-1edc60d3c984", "content": "## 1. Claims approved as written

The Containment Report was published on April 14, 2026, and surveyed 412 platform and security leaders. Give the survey size when the copy has room for it. The legal entity is Wickhold, Inc. Contracts, order forms, privacy notices and page footers use that form. Marketing copy uses Wickhold.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "1. Claims approved as written"], "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "383000ed-25fc-4fa8-8a32-0a9cb7da5f80", "content": "## How the sentences go

**Short first.** Most sentences run under twenty words. The long ones earn it by carrying a real sequence of events.

**Verbs do the work.** Name who did what. "Quenchline froze the process" over "the process was frozen". Past tense for incidents, present tense for what the product does.

**End early.** Our most common edit is deleting the last line of a paragraph. Writers tend to add one that restates the point in a nicer rhythm. Readers don't need it. This goes double for the final line of a piece.

**Ration the fire.** The tagline is "Small fires stay small." It carries the metaphor so the copy doesn't have to. A piece gets at most one fire image, and many pieces should have none. Nothing ignites, sparks, blazes or fans the flames. Slow Burn Summit gets to keep its name.

**Plain words for plain things.** "Use", "start", "stop", "run". Reach for the fancier word and the reader assumes something is being hidden.

**Don't argue with the reader's experience.** Telling a platform engineer that alerts are overwhelming is telling them what they had for breakfast. Start from what they know and add something.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "How the sentences go"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "3b54ef64-c087-4b32-a84a-a649f3d76cd6", "content": "## Tone by audience

Humor depends on the audience, see each persona.

The personas hold the working rules for each reader, including what goes first. What follows is only the register, meaning how the voice sounds once you have chosen your content.

**CISOs.** Level and measured. Assume the reader will forward your paragraph to an audit committee without editing it, and write something they can forward. Risk, time and board language are their native terms: exposure, time to contain, residual risk, ownership. Short sentences, complete ones, no shorthand. Every sentence should survive being read aloud in a room that includes a lawyer.

**Platform engineers.** A good pull-request comment from a colleague you respect. Exact, brief, assumes competence, and shows its working. If there is a YAML snippet that makes the point, the prose can get out of its way. Marketing English reads as noise here and the page will be closed.

**DevSecOps.** These readers sit between the review queue and the pipeline, and they spend their days being the person who says no. Write to someone who is outnumbered: practical, on their side, and specific about what lands in their queue and what stays out of it.

**Compliance leads.** Careful nouns. This reader will notice the difference between "supports" and "meets", and will quote you. Their persona is still being written, so if the piece is aimed mainly at them, ask Noor before guessing.

**Customers mid-incident.** Pure 3am voice. Nothing about the product, nothing about the relationship, no reassurance that isn't backed by a fact. What we see, what we've done, when the next update comes.

**Finance and procurement.** They read a small part of what we write and they read it closely. Plain sentences, the price in the standard form, the terms where they expect them. Anything that sounds like enthusiasm reads to them as a negotiating position.

**Journalists.** Assume no interest in the product and real interest in what is happening to teams. Offer the finding, the method and a person to talk to. Don't send them a story with a hook in it; they have their own.

**Candidates and the community.** Warmer, plainer, and allowed to mention that the work is interesting. The same no-drama rules hold. Nobody here is a rockstar.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "Tone by audience"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "412b98db-a59b-4fa4-afb4-aada12ba8243", "content": "Certification status: sheet kept by Priit Salonen. Last checked 2 October 2026.

Sales, this is the sheet to use before you answer a security questionnaire. If a deck or an old email says something different, the deck or the email is out of date.

| Program | Status | What you may say |
|---|---|---|
| SOC 2 Type II | Held. Renewed January 2026 | "Wickhold holds SOC 2 Type II." |
| FedRAMP Moderate | In process. Not held | "Wickhold is pursuing FedRAMP Moderate authorization." |

**FedRAMP.** Never claim FedRAMP authorization or certification. The approved wording above is the only wording. It goes in copy exactly as written, including the word "pursuing".

These are banned in every channel, spoken or written: "FedRAMP Authorized", "FedRAMP certified", "FedRAMP Ready", "FedRAMP compliant", "FedRAMP equivalent", "built to FedRAMP standards". Agency buyers read those words literally, and a false statement to a federal buyer is a contract and legal problem, whatever the deal size.

The status changes when authorization is complete and published, and this sheet says so. An assessor's visit, a sponsor conversation, or a positive meeting does not change it. Do not give prospects a target date. We do not publish one. If a federal prospect presses, the answer is the sentence above and an offer to connect them with me.

Good, in an answer to a questionnaire:

> Wickhold holds SOC 2 Type II, renewed January 2026. Wickhold is pursuing FedRAMP Moderate authorization. We can share the SOC 2 report under NDA.

Bad:

> We're basically FedRAMP Authorized, the paperwork is just finishing up.

**SOC 2.** The report goes out under NDA through the account team, never by public link. Say "Type II" every time. Say "held" or "renewed", and do not say "SOC 2 certified", because SOC 2 ends in an attestation report and not a certificate.

**Questionnaires and RFPs.** Security questionnaires go through the account team, and any answer about certifications is copied from this sheet. If a form offers only "Yes" or "No" for FedRAMP, answer "No", and use the comments box for the approved sentence. Do not tick a box in the hope of explaining later.
